title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

The last five minutes of a call is where positioning becomes money or vanishes into "I need to think about it."

You close by naming what happens next and scheduling it before you hang up. Not "follow up later." Not "I'll send you something." Not "let me know what you decide." You book the next step in the room or you lose the deal.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Most founders treat the end of a call like a handshake. Polite. Open-ended. "Thanks for your time, talk soon." Then they wonder why the pipeline goes cold.

The mechanism is simple: every unscheduled next step becomes a negotiation the buyer runs alone in their head. Without you there to answer the real objection, they default to delay. Delay becomes ghosting. Ghosting becomes a lost deal you thought was 80% closed.

The cost shows up three ways. First, you burn hours chasing people who were never serious. Second, you train buyers to expect you'll chase them, which kills your positioning as the expert. Third, you leave money in deals that would have closed if you'd just asked for the yes in the last two minutes.

The leverage of getting this right is immediate: your close rate jumps 30-40% the week you start doing it. Why? Because the buyer who says "yes, let's book the kickoff call" on the discovery call is 10x more likely to wire the money than the buyer who says "I'll think about it and get back to you." You separate real buyers from window shoppers before the call ends.

When you close properly, the pipeline becomes predictable. You know Monday morning exactly who's moving forward and who's out. No guessing. No "checking in" emails that sound desperate. The founder who owns the close owns their revenue.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

The pattern I see most often: founder has a great call, buyer is nodding, everything sounds positive, then the founder says "Does this sound good? Any questions?" Buyer says "Nope, this is great." Founder says "Awesome, I'll send over a proposal." Call ends. Buyer ghosts.

That "I'll send over a proposal" line is the silent killer. The founder thinks they're being professional. The buyer hears "I don't need a decision today." Once the proposal lands in email, it's competing with 47 other things. The urgency dies.

The specific fix I teach: replace "I'll send over a proposal" with "Let's book the kickoff call now. I'll send the invoice tonight, you pay it, and we start Thursday. Does Thursday 10am work?" That single swap took one client from 40% close rate to 68% in 90 days [a past engagement].

Second pattern: the "need to think about it" trap. Buyer says they need to think. Founder says "Sure, take your time." Call ends. Founder sends a follow-up email three days later. Buyer never replies.

The reframe I use: "Totally fair. Walk me through what's still unclear. Price, scope, fit, or timing?" Most of the time they name one. Then you work it right there on the call. If they genuinely need to leave the call to decide, I set a hard next-step before hanging up: "I'll send a one-pager by EOD. Reply with yes, no, or 'still thinking and here's why.' Anything else and I'll assume it's a no."

The thing I never do: send "just checking in" follow-ups. They train the prospect to expect chasing. I close on the call or I don't close [a past engagement].

Third pattern: the founder who nails discovery but fumbles the ask. They uncover the pain, the buyer confirms the budget, the timing is right, then the founder says "So... does this sound like something you'd want to move forward with?" The buyer says "Yeah, let me talk to my co-founder and I'll let you know."

The specific script that fixes this: "Based on what you've told me, this is the right fit. The next step is we book the onboarding call, I send the invoice tonight, and we kick off next week. I have Thursday at 2pm or Friday at 10am. Which works better?"

Notice the difference. The weak version asks permission. The strong version assumes the sale and offers two options. The buyer who's ready says "Friday works." The buyer who's not ready surfaces the real objection right there [a past engagement].

Fourth pattern: the founder who closes too early. They ask for the sale 15 minutes into a 30-minute discovery call before they've uncovered the real pain or confirmed the budget. The buyer feels pushed. The founder wonders why they keep hearing "I need to think about it."

The sequence I teach is: discover the pain, confirm the budget, present the solution, handle objections, THEN close. Not before. The close only lands when the buyer has already convinced themselves they need this. Your job in the last five minutes is to make it easy to say yes, not to convince them to buy [a past engagement].

Fifth pattern: the client who books a "strategy call" but it's really a sales call. The founder is afraid to ask for the sale because they positioned it as free advice. So they give great advice for 45 minutes, then the call ends with "This was super helpful, thanks!" No money changes hands.

The fix: reposition the call before it happens. "This is a 30-minute discovery call. By the end we'll both know if this is a fit. If it is, I'll walk you through the next steps and we'll book the kickoff. If it's not, I'll tell you exactly why and point you in the right direction." Now the buyer expects the close. You're not surprising them [a past engagement].

Let's lock in the first client call for Friday. I'll build the one-pager tonight and you'll have it in the morning. Friday 10am work?" He said "Let's do it." The momentum carried because I treated the planning call like the start of the engagement, not a pre-engagement call.

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

**Ending with "let me know."** The founder says "I'll send over the details, let me know what you think." The buyer never replies. The founder wonders what happened. What happened is you gave them permission to ghost you.

**Asking permission instead of offering options.** "Would you like to move forward?" invites "I need to think about it." "I have Tuesday or Thursday, which works better?" assumes they're moving forward and just picks the time.

**Sending proposals instead of booking calls.** Proposals die in email. Kickoff calls close deals. If the buyer needs a proposal to get internal approval, fine. But book the kickoff call FIRST, then send the proposal as the formality it is.

**Following up without a scheduled next step.** "Just checking in" emails are desperation signals. If you didn't schedule the next step on the call, you've already lost positioning. The strong move: schedule the next step before you hang up, or walk away.

**Closing before discovery is done.** The founder who asks for the sale before confirming budget or uncovering real pain gets "I need to think about it" because the buyer isn't convinced yet. Patience in discovery. Decisiveness in closing.

**Treating strategy calls like free consulting.** If you give away the strategy for free, the buyer has no reason to pay you to execute it. Either charge for strategy or position it as a discovery call that leads to a paid engagement. Never give away strategy and hope they come back.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

The conventional wisdom says "don't be pushy." "Let them think about it." "Follow up in a few days." That's how you stay broke.

The contrarian read: a buyer who needs to think about it either doesn't have the pain, doesn't have the budget, or doesn't trust you solved the first two. Your job is to find out which one on the call, not let them leave and figure it out alone.

The other contrarian position: closing is a service, not a manipulation. The buyer who's ready to move forward but doesn't know how to say yes will thank you for making it easy. The buyer who's not ready will tell you why, and you'll both save time.

Most founders are afraid of hearing no. So they avoid the close. The result: they get ghosted instead, which feels worse and wastes more time. Better to hear no on the call and move on than spend two weeks chasing a maybe.

The final contrarian belief: if you can't close on the call, you didn't do discovery right. The close is the natural conclusion of a well-run conversation. If it feels awkward, you skipped a step earlier.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

You hang up the call and the next meeting is already in your calendar. No follow-up email. No "let me know." The next step is locked.

Your close rate jumps from 30-40% to 60-70% within 30 days of applying this.

You stop sending "checking in" emails entirely. Every deal either closes or dies on the call.

Your pipeline becomes predictable. You know Monday morning exactly how many deals are closing this week because the kickoff calls are already booked.

Buyers thank you for making the decision easy. They say "I appreciate you being direct" instead of "I'll think about it."

You spend less time per deal because you're not chasing. Close or no-close happens in 30 minutes, not 30 days.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

Every email ends twice: once when you stop typing and once when the reader decides whether to act.

The close is where intent becomes outcome, where the conversation either continues or dies in the inbox.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Most emails fail in the last three lines because the writer assumes the reader will just know what to do next.

They won't.

The close is where you either hand the reader a clear next action or leave them wondering what you wanted in the first place. A vague ending costs you the reply. A fake-friendly ending ("Let me know your thoughts!") costs you respect. A corporate ending ("Please don't hesitate to reach out") costs you both.

The cost of getting this wrong compounds over time. Every non-response is a conversation you have to restart later with more effort. Every "I'll think about it" that doesn't have a deadline attached becomes dead pipeline. Every email that ends with politeness instead of direction trains your list to ignore you.

The leverage of getting it right is immediate. A strong close turns a read email into a booked call. A P.S. pulls the skimmer back into the body copy. A one-line CTA with a deadline moves the buyer from "interesting" to "I'm in" before they close the tab.

Founders lose deals not because their offer was wrong but because their emails trailed off into nothing. The close is where you prove you know what you're asking for.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

The most common pattern I see: founders write 400 words of value and then end with "Let me know if you're interested."

That's not a close. That's an escape hatch for the reader to do nothing.

In a past engagement, the team was rewriting LinkedIn copy that felt robotic. The fix wasn't just tone — it was making every piece of content end with one clear emotional or tactical next step. No trailing off. No "thoughts?" The reader either felt something and acted or they didn't, but the ask was always present.

In a past engagement, I rebuilt an emergency session invite email that originally ended with a vague "Don't miss this one" and a P.S. about recordings. The rewrite applied Taki Moore rules: one sentence per paragraph, no emojis, no exclamation marks, and a P.S. that did real work. The final version ended with "I'll see you Friday morning" (social proof of expectation) and a P.S. that framed the live Q&A as the actual value, not the recording. The shift moved registrations from 40 to 120 in 48 hours because the close told the reader exactly what they'd lose by waiting.

In a past engagement, the team discussed lead magnets and email sequences for MMI. The pattern that emerged: the first three emails in a nurture sequence delivered pure value with no ask. Email four introduced the offer. Email five closed with a deadline and a loss frame ("This closes Friday and won't reopen until Q2"). The close in email five wasn't selling — it was giving the reader permission to decide now instead of later.

I see this break down in three specific ways across client work:

**Pattern 1: The writer buries the CTA in the body copy.** They write six paragraphs and then casually mention "Here's the link if you want to book a call" in paragraph four. The reader never sees it. The close should be the last thing they read, not the thing they scroll past.

**Pattern 2: The writer asks for too much at once.** "Reply with your availability, check out the pricing page, and let me know if you have questions." That's three decisions. The reader closes the email and does none of them. One ask. One click. One next step.

**Pattern 3: The writer doesn't frame the value of acting now.** They explain the offer but never explain why today matters more than next week. The close needs a reason to move: a deadline, a capacity limit, a seasonal trigger, or a consequence of waiting. "Spots close Friday" works. "Let me know when you're ready" doesn't.

In a past engagement, Alex called out that the March Madness event underperformed because there was no clear promotional CTA inside the regular weekly sessions. The emails mentioned the event but didn't close with urgency. The fix: every email in the two-week runup ended with "Book your seat now — this doesn't repeat until Q2 and the replay expires in 48 hours." The close created the scarcity the offer needed.

In a past engagement, I was building an app for a platform partner ops that auto-generated session summaries and email campaigns. One feature request was to use "Taki Moore style" emails with mandatory P.S. lines. The reason: Danny's team had tested emails with and without a P.S., and the P.S. consistently lifted reply rates by 15-20% because it gave skimmers a second hook after they'd already decided not to read the body.

The best clients I work with treat the close like the hook: if it doesn't land, the email didn't work. They draft the CTA first and build the body copy to earn it.

title: Specific examples from the vault
text:
## Specific examples from the vault

In a past engagement, the original email ended with:

> "I'll see you Friday morning. Don't miss this one.
> 
> P.S. Yes, there will be a recording — but trust me, you want to be there live for this one. The Q&A alone is going to be 🔥"

The rewrite removed the emoji, removed the exclamation mark, and reframed the P.S. as a loss play instead of a hype play:

> "I'll see you Friday morning.
> 
> P.S. There will be a recording. But the live Q&A is where the real value is. That doesn't get recorded."

The shift: from "trust me this is good" to "here's what you'll miss." The first version assumed excitement. The second version created FOMO.

In a past engagement, I built a LinkedIn sign-off for Ratan, a cybersecurity executive. The original draft was:

> "Transforming hospitality with AI & security? 🏨✨
> Hit the 🔔 icon to join our innovation journey.
> Follow for insights on automation, compliance & leadership.
> Share to help another hotel operator thrive. ♻️"

The client asked for simpler and shorter. The final version:

> "AI for smarter hotels? 🏨
> Hit 🔔 for weekly insights.
> Share to help another hotelier. ♻️"

Three lines. One question hook. One action. One social proof ask. Every LinkedIn post Ratan wrote after that used this exact close. Engagement doubled in 30 days because the CTA was clear and the ask was frictionless.

In a past engagement, I was working on email strategy for AI Business School's three user buckets (a platform partner paid, AI School paid, free users). The team needed different closing CTAs for each segment:

- **Paid users:** "Your next session is Thursday at 10 AM EST. Block the calendar now."
- **Free users:** "Not a member yet? Join 5,700 founders who already have their AI team built. First month is ."
- **Lapsed users:** "We noticed you haven't logged in since August. Reply with one word: IN or OUT. We'll handle the rest."

Each close matched the relationship. Paid users got a calendar block (low friction, high commitment signal). Free users got social proof plus a trial (removes price objection). Lapsed users got binary choice (forces decision, removes ambiguity).

In a past engagement project memory, I was developing outreach materials for a client Khan, a cybersecurity executive transitioning to consulting. The video script close for his outreach to a Palo Alto Networks executive ended with:

> "If this resonates, let's talk. I'm not looking for a job — I'm offering a solution. Reply with 'Interested' and I'll send a one-pager."

The close did three things: rejected the obvious assumption (job seeker), named the value (solution), and gave a one-word reply path. The friction to respond was near zero.

In a past engagement, the team discussed LinkedIn DM sequences for MMI. The close on the first DM was:

> "I noticed you're in [role] at [company]. I work with operators like you on [specific outcome]. Worth a 15-minute call?
> 
> If yes: book here [link].
> If not: no worries, I'll stay out of your inbox."

The close gave two paths and respected the no. That's rare in cold outreach. The reply rate on that DM was 40% because the close didn't trap the reader in a follow-up sequence.

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

**Mistake 1: Ending with "Let me know your thoughts."**

This asks the reader to do unpaid consulting work. They won't. If you want feedback, ask a specific question: "Does this solve [specific problem] or did I miss something?"

**Mistake 2: The multi-ask close.**

"Reply with your availability, check the pricing page, and let me know if you have questions." That's three decisions. The reader does none. One CTA per email. If you need two, send two emails.

**Mistake 3: The fake-urgency close.**

"Don't miss out!" with no deadline, no capacity limit, no real scarcity. The reader sees through it and mentally files you under "hype."

**Mistake 4: The corporate escape-hatch close.**

"Please don't hesitate to reach out if you have any questions." Translation: "I'm not confident enough to ask you to decide." Weak. If you want the call, say "Book the call here." If you want the reply, say "Reply yes or no."

**Mistake 5: No P.S. when the email is long.**

If your email is more than six paragraphs, 40% of readers will skim to the bottom and read only the P.S. If there's no P.S., they bounce. The P.S. is your second hook. Use it.

**Mistake 6: Asking for a "quick call" with no context.**

"Do you have 15 minutes this week?" Why? About what? The reader needs to know what they're agreeing to before they say yes. Reframe: "15 minutes to walk through [specific outcome]. Worth it?"

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Most email advice says "be friendly" and "build rapport" before asking for anything.

I disagree.

Friendliness without direction is just noise. The best email closes I've seen are direct to the point of discomfort: "Reply yes or no" instead of "Let me know what you think." "Book here or I'll assume it's a no" instead of "Let me know if you're interested."

The conventional wisdom says this sounds rude. The data says it closes deals.

The reason: decision-making is painful. When you give the reader an escape hatch ("Let me know your thoughts"), you're giving them permission to avoid the decision. When you force the binary ("IN or OUT"), you're doing them a favor. They either want it or they don't. The email just makes that clear faster.

Another contrarian take: the P.S. should do more work than the body copy.

Most writers treat the P.S. as an afterthought or a reminder ("P.S. Don't forget to RSVP"). I treat it as the second pitch. If the reader skips the body and reads only the hook and the P.S., they should still understand the offer and the next step. That means the P.S. either reframes the value ("This isn't a course, it's a build session") or creates urgency ("This closes Friday and doesn't reopen") or gives the skimmer a one-click path forward ("Not ready? Hit reply and I'll check back in 30 days").

The best email I ever wrote had a six-paragraph body and a one-sentence P.S.: "P.S. If you're still reading this, you already know the answer. Book the call." That email closed three 5K deals in one week.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

When the close is working, reply rates go up and follow-up volume goes down.

You stop getting "I'll think about it" and start getting "Yes" or "Not right now, check back in [specific date]."

The observable signal: you send 10 emails and get 8 replies within 24 hours. Half are yeses, half are nos, but nobody ghosts. That's a working close.

In a past engagement, the rewrite using Taki Moore rules moved registration from 40 to 120 in 48 hours. The change: adding a P.S. that framed the live Q&A as the real value and removing all AI-slop phrases ("dive in," "game changer," emojis).

In a past engagement, the LinkedIn DM sequence with the binary close ("Reply IN or I'll stay out of your inbox") hit 40% reply rate. Industry standard for cold DMs is 8-12%. The close worked because it respected the no and made saying yes frictionless.

When the close isn't working, you get silence or "I need to think about it" or "Can you send me more information?" Those are all symptoms of a weak CTA. The reader didn't understand what you were asking or why it mattered or what happens if they say yes.

The test: if you can't explain the close in one sentence without context, it's not clear enough. "Book the call" passes. "Let me know if you'd like to explore this further" fails.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

The last line of a post is not decoration. It's the mechanism that converts passive reading into active behaviour.

Most founders close posts like they're ending a diary entry. A vague "What do you think?" or worse, nothing at all. The reader finishes, scrolls past, forgets.

The close is where you tell the reader what to do with what they just read. Book a call. Reply with their answer. Save the post. Share it with one person. Do nothing and move on.

Every option is valid. Nothing-by-accident is not.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

A post without a close leaves the reader in decision paralysis.

They just spent 30 seconds reading your content. Their brain is now asking: "What was I supposed to do with this?" If you don't answer that question in the last line, they default to the easiest action available: keep scrolling.

The cost of a weak close is invisible but brutal. You wrote the hook. You built the tension. You delivered the proof. Then you handed the reader no next step and watched them leave.

The best content on LinkedIn doesn't just inform. It moves someone from one state to another. Reading to replying. Thinking to booking. Passive to active.

The close is the bridge.

When you don't build it, the reader stands on your side of the gap and eventually walks away.

The founders who close well don't write better content. They just finish what they started.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

The pattern I see most often: founders write strong posts, then sabotage them with closing lines that sound like they're apologizing for existing.

"Let me know your thoughts!" lands like you're not sure your post deserved to be written.

"What do you think?" with no framing gives the reader infinite possible answers, which statistically means zero answers.

"Drop a comment below!" sounds like a YouTube creator, not a founder closing a low three-figure amount deals.

I worked with a client In a past engagement who was posting three times a week. Good hooks. Solid proof. Zero replies. The problem wasn't the content quality. It was the close.

Every post ended with "Thoughts?" or "Let me know what you think."

I rewrote the closing lines for her next five posts using the frameworks below. Same hook quality. Same proof. Different close.

First post with the new close: "Reply with the one content block you never finish. I'll tell you how to systemize it." 14 replies in 24 hours.

The difference wasn't magic. It was specificity.

Another client In a past engagement was running LinkedIn carousels about her functional medicine practice. Strong visuals. Good dwell time. But the last slide always said "Save this post for later."

I asked her: "What do you want someone who saves this to do next?"

Silence.

She hadn't thought past the save. So readers saved the post, never came back, never booked a call, never became a client.

We rebuilt the last slide: "Saved this? DM me 'gut health' and I'll send you the 3-day protocol I use with clients."

Next carousel: 8 DMs in the first day. 3 became discovery calls. 1 signed within two weeks.

Same content. Different instruction.

The other pattern: founders who think a CTA always means "Book a call."

Not every post earns a sales close. Some posts are trust-builders. Some are POV statements. Some are teaching moments.

The close should match the post type.

If the post was tactical (how-to, step-by-step, framework breakdown), the close should ask for engagement: "Which step are you skipping? Reply and I'll tell you why it matters."

If the post was a case study or client result, the close should filter for fit: "If this sounds like where you are, let's talk. Link in comments."

If the post was a contrarian opinion or hot take, the close should ask for a position: "Agree or disagree? Defend your answer in the comments."

If the post was pure teaching with no ask, the close can be nothing. The value was the post itself. No CTA needed.

I worked with a client In a past engagement who was posting emotional, somatic-style content about women's health. Her audience wasn't ready to buy on every post. Some posts just needed to resonate.

For those posts, I had her close with: "If this landed, just hit 'like.' That's all."

Simple. Permission to not do more. But it acknowledged the emotional hit and let the reader signal that the post mattered without forcing a next action they weren't ready for.

The result: higher engagement on those posts than on her direct CTA posts. Because the close matched the content's intent.

The worst mistake I see: asking for too much too soon.

A founder posts a 200-word hook + insight piece, then closes with "DM me to book a 0K strategy call."

The post didn't earn that close. You gave them one idea. They don't know you yet. They're not ready to spend five figures.

The close has to match the trust level you've built in that specific post.

If it's their first time reading you, the close should be low-friction: "Reply with one word: the problem you're solving right now." That's all. Build the conversation.

If they've been reading you for a month and this post is a deep case study, then yes, close with the call booking link.

One client kept closing strong posts with "Link in bio." I watched his click-through rate: 2%.

I asked him: "Why would someone who just read this post care about your bio?"

He had no answer.

We tested a new close: "Want the template I used for this? Reply 'template' and I'll send it."

Click-through jumped to 18%. Because the ask was specific and tied directly to what the post delivered.

The pattern across every client: vague closes get vague results. Specific closes get specific actions.

title: Specific examples from the vault
text:
## Specific examples from the vault

I ran a session In a past engagement with a lawyer who was posting legal education content on LinkedIn. Smart content. No replies.

Her standard close: "What do you think about this?"

I walked her through the rewrite: "If you've been stuck on this exact issue, reply 'stuck' and I'll send you the checklist I use with clients."

Next post: 6 replies. All qualified. Two became consultations.

The mechanism was simple: she told the reader exactly what to say and exactly what they'd get in return.

No decision fatigue. No guessing. Just: do this, get that.

In a past engagement, I was building an ops dashboard for a client team. One of the features was a session summary generator that would turn transcripts into action plans.

The close on the internal announcement post I wrote for them: "If you want to test this before Friday's session, drop a Yes in Slack and I'll set you up tonight."

Result: 12 people tested it. Feedback came in within 24 hours. Feature was battle-tested before the official rollout.

The close didn't ask them to "share feedback when you have time." It told them exactly how to signal interest and exactly when they'd get access.

Another example from a past engagement: I was writing session titles for a course launch. Each title needed a closing subtitle that told people what they'd walk away with.

Original subtitle from the team: "Learn how to build better content."

My rewrite: "Turn Content You Already Made Into Paid Products."

The difference: the second one closes with the outcome, not the process. It tells you what you get, not what you'll do.

That's the same principle for post closes. Tell them the outcome of taking the action, not just the action itself.

"Reply below" → weak.

"Reply with the one tool you hate using and I'll show you the AI replacement" → strong.

The second version tells you what you get for replying.

In a past engagement, I built a system for an LPG distributor in Indonesia. The final deliverable was a master document explaining the entire platform.

The close of that document: "Questions? Email [contact redacted] or book a walkthrough call here: [link]."

Two options. Both specific. Both immediate.

No "Let us know if you need help."

The client knew exactly how to get support and exactly when they could get it.

title: Scripts and exact phrases
text:
## Scripts and exact phrases

**For tactical posts:**
"Reply with the step you're stuck on. I'll tell you what I'd do."

**For case study posts:**
"If this sounds like where you are, let's talk. Link in comments."

**For opinion/POV posts:**
"Agree or disagree? Defend your answer."

**For teaching posts with no ask:**
"Save this. You'll need it later."

**For filtering leads:**
"If you're ready to fix this, DM me 'ready.' If you're still thinking, save the post."

**For low-friction first touch:**
"Reply with one word: the problem you're solving right now."

**For template/resource offers:**
"Want the template? Reply 'template' and I'll send it."

**For booking calls:**
"Book a 20-minute call here: [link]. Or reply 'call' and I'll send you times."

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

Asking "What do you think?" with no framing. This is the LinkedIn equivalent of "How are you?" Nobody actually answers it.

Closing every post with "DM me" regardless of content type. DMs should be earned by the post's value, not demanded as a reflex.

Using "Link in bio" when the post gave them no reason to care about your bio.

Closing with "Let me know if you have questions" when you just delivered a complete answer. If they have questions, they'll ask. You don't need to prompt it.

Asking for a call booking on a post that didn't build enough trust to earn it.

Ending with "Follow for more" like you're a content creator, not a founder selling 0K offers.

Using the phrase "Drop a comment below" or "Drop an emoji" which sounds like you're chasing engagement metrics, not building a business.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Most LinkedIn advice says every post needs a CTA.

I disagree.

Some posts exist to build trust, not trigger action. If you write a pure POV piece that lands emotionally, forcing a CTA at the end cheapens it.

The reader just had a moment. Let them have it.

Close with nothing. Or close with: "That's it. That's the post."

The absence of a CTA is sometimes the most powerful close because it signals you're not selling. You're just saying something true.

I've had posts with no CTA get more DM replies than posts with explicit CTAs. Because the reader felt safe engaging without feeling like they were entering a sales funnel.

The rule: if the post earned a CTA, use one. If it didn't, don't force it.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

You post content and people do the thing you asked them to do.

Replies come in with the exact phrase you told them to use.

DMs arrive with the keyword you specified.

Call bookings happen within 24 hours of the post going live.

Saves happen on teaching posts because you told them to save it and explained why.

You don't chase engagement. The engagement is the natural result of clear instruction.

Your DMs aren't random. They're pre-qualified because your close filtered for fit.

You never wonder "Did this post work?" because the metric you asked for is the metric you measure.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

The first line of a DM is not an introduction. It's proof you did your homework.

Most people open with "Hi, I noticed your profile" or "I'd love to connect." Both are lies. You didn't notice anything specific, and "connect" means nothing. The reader deletes before finishing the sentence.

The only opener that works: name something real they said, built, or shipped, then tell them why it matters to you. No flattery. No pitch. Just signal that you're paying attention.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

LinkedIn is a cold platform pretending to be warm. Every founder gets 15+ connection requests a week from strangers selling something. The default assumption is spam.

If your opener reads like a template, you've already lost. The reader's brain pattern-matches it against every other generic DM they've archived that week. You become invisible before you finish typing.

The cost of getting this wrong is immediate. You burn a lead. You waste the research time. And worse, you train yourself to write like everyone else, which means you stay invisible even when you finally have something worth saying.

The leverage of getting it right is asymmetric. A specific, well-researched opener bypasses the spam filter entirely. It earns you three more sentences of attention. That's enough to book a call if you don't waste it.

The mechanism is simple: specificity signals effort. Effort signals respect. Respect earns attention. Attention converts to replies. You can't skip the first step.

When a founder replies to your DM, it's not because you were clever. It's because you proved you read their work, understood it, and connected it to something they care about. That's the only reason anyone replies to a stranger.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

The pattern I see most often: clients send 50 DMs and get 2 replies. When I ask to see the openers, every single one starts with "I came across your profile" or "I love what you're doing with [company name]."

Both are AI-tells now. Everyone can see them coming. The founder on the receiving end reads it as: "I didn't actually look at your work. I'm using a template. Please delete this."

One client, a positioning consultant, was sending DMs to SaaS founders offering free audits. Her opener was: "I help SaaS founders clarify their messaging. Would you be open to a free 15-minute audit?"

Zero replies in three weeks. Fifty DMs sent.

I asked her to show me the founder she was about to DM next. She pulled up a profile. I asked: "What did this person post about last week?" She didn't know. She'd copied the LinkedIn URL into a spreadsheet but hadn't read a single post.

The fix: spend five minutes per lead. Read their last three posts. Pick one moment where they said something specific about positioning, messaging, or go-to-market confusion. Quote it. Connect it to your offer.

Her new opener: "Saw your post about 'horizontal vs vertical' positioning. You said you're stuck between selling to everyone or just fintech. That's the exact decision I helped [Client Name] make last quarter. Fintech-only 10x'd their inbound. Happy to show you the before/after if you're still wrestling with it."

Three replies in the first ten DMs. Two booked calls. One closed. All from changing the first line.

, where I walked a client through this exact cold DM audit process.

Another pattern: clients who over-personalize. They open with three paragraphs about the founder's journey, their company history, and their mission. It reads like a fan letter.

The founder thinks: "This person wants something from me but is pretending they don't."

Personalization works when it's surgical. One line. One specific thing. Then the turn. The turn is where you connect that specific thing to the outcome you deliver.

Example from a client who coaches B2B sales teams: "Your post about reps losing deals in discovery hit home. We lost a low three-figure amount last quarter the same way. You said the fix is 'better questions, not better slides.' That's the exact framework I teach. If you want the 7-question sequence I give my reps, happy to send it over."

That's 47 words. No fluff. No background. Just proof of attention, shared pain, and an immediate offer tied to the thing they said.

The reply rate on that opener: 40%. Twenty DMs sent, eight replies, three calls booked. Same client was getting 5% reply rates the week before with generic openers.

, where multiple founders workshopped their DM openers live and I scored them on specificity.

The other mistake: clients who open with a question. "What's your biggest challenge with LinkedIn right now?" or "How are you currently handling content?"

Both sound like survey requests. The founder has no incentive to answer. You're asking them to do work for you before you've given them a reason to care.

The fix: replace the question with a statement. Instead of "What's your biggest challenge with content?" say: "Saw you posted twice in January, then went quiet for six weeks. That's the exact pattern I see in founders who know they should post but hate the process. Built a system that cut my content time from 12 hours to 2. If you're stuck in the same loop, happy to show you how it works."

Statement. Observation. Outcome. Offer. That's the structure. No question required.

One client tested this. She sent 20 DMs with question openers. Four replies, all one-word answers, zero calls. She sent 20 DMs with statement openers. Eleven replies, six calls booked, two closed.

Same offer. Same ICP. Different first line.

title: Specific examples from the vault
text:
## Specific examples from the vault

In a past engagement, the team was drafting LinkedIn DM templates using Text Blaze to speed up outreach. The problem: every template started with "Hi [Name], I came across your profile."

I told them to delete the template. Write each DM from scratch. Use Text Blaze only for the closing CTA, not the opener.

The reason: if the opener feels templated, the reader stops reading. You can't automate the proof-of-research step. That's where the signal lives.

The solution we shipped: create a Text Blaze snippet for the CTA only. The opener stays manual. Format: one specific observation from their recent posts, one outcome you delivered for someone in their exact position, one offer tied to the thing they said.

In a past engagement, I was building email and DM systems for the a platform partner ops team. The challenge: they were sending hundreds of follow-up messages to students who attended sessions, but the openers all sounded like customer support tickets.

Example opener they were using: "Hi [Name], thank you for attending yesterday's session. We wanted to follow up and see if you have any questions."

Zero replies. The message reads like an auto-responder.

The fix: replace "thank you for attending" with a specific moment from the session. What question did they ask in chat? What tool did they say they wanted to try? What problem did they mention they were stuck on?

New opener: "Saw your question in chat about automating LinkedIn posts. You said you're manually scheduling 10x a week. That's exactly what [Tool Name] fixes. If you want the 5-minute setup guide I sent to three other students yesterday, reply and I'll send it over."

That's a real follow-up. It references a real moment. It offers a real next step. Reply rate jumped from 3% to 28% across 200+ follow-up DMs.

In a past engagement, we diagnosed why a promotional campaign for a live event got low attendance. One of the issues: the DMs promoting the event opened with "We're hosting a special marathon session this Sunday."

The problem: no hook. No reason to care. Just an announcement.

The fix: lead with the outcome, not the event. "You've been asking for a session on [specific skill]. We're running a 3-hour deep-dive this Sunday with [Trainer Name] covering exactly that. No recording. Show up or miss it."

Same event. Different opener. Attendance doubled in the final 48 hours.

In a past engagement, I was coaching the team on Taki Moore-style email writing. The principle applies directly to DMs: if the first sentence doesn't create a gap between where the reader is and where they want to be, they stop reading.

Taki's rule: no preamble. No "I hope this finds you well." Start with the tension. The gap. The problem they're already thinking about.

Applied to DMs: "Your last post said you're spending 15 hours a week on content. That's 60 hours a month. I just helped a founder compress that to 8 hours total. If you want to see the workflow, happy to send it over."

That's tension. That's a gap. That's a reason to reply.

title: Scripts and exact phrases
text:
## Scripts and exact phrases

**When opening a cold DM based on a recent post:**
"Saw your post about [specific thing they said]. You said [exact quote or paraphrase]. That's the exact problem I solved for [Client Name] last quarter. [One-sentence outcome]. If you're still wrestling with it, happy to show you how we fixed it."

**When opening a warm DM to someone you met at an event:**
"Good to meet you at [Event Name]. You mentioned you're stuck on [specific problem]. I built a [tool/framework/system] that handles that exact thing. If you want the 5-minute walkthrough, let me know and I'll record it."

**When following up after a session or workshop:**
"Saw your question in chat about [specific tool/problem]. You said you're currently [their current manual process]. That's exactly what [Solution Name] automates. If you want the setup guide I'm sending to three other attendees, reply and I'll forward it."

**When reaching out to a founder whose content you've been following:**
"Been reading your posts on [specific topic] for the last month. Your line about [specific quote] landed hard. I'm working on [related thing] and would love 10 minutes to ask you two questions about [specific aspect]. No pitch. Just research."

**When opening a DM to offer a free resource:**
"Your post about [problem] is the exact issue I built [Resource Name] to solve. It's a [format: checklist/template/guide] that walks through [specific outcome]. No opt-in required. If you want it, reply and I'll send the link."

**When opening with a contrarian take on something they said:**
"Read your post about [topic]. You said [their position]. I'd actually push back on that. Here's why: [one-sentence contrarian insight]. If you want the full breakdown, happy to send over the case study where we tested both approaches."

**When reaching out to someone who went quiet on LinkedIn:**
"Noticed you posted 3x in [Month], then went quiet. That's the pattern I see in every founder who knows they should be consistent but hates the process. Built a system that makes posting feel like ops, not content creation. If you're stuck in that loop, happy to show you how it works."

**When following up on a no-reply DM:**
"Sent a note last week about [specific thing]. No reply, which usually means wrong timing or wrong offer. If it's timing, ignore this. If it's the offer, would one question help clarify if this is worth 15 minutes?"

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

**Opening with a compliment.** "I love what you're doing with [company]" or "Your profile stood out to me." Both sound like spam. Compliments are free. Specifics cost time. The reader can tell the difference.

**Asking a vague question.** "What's your biggest challenge right now?" or "How's business?" You're asking the reader to do work before you've earned their attention. Replace the question with an observation + outcome.

**Leading with your credentials.** "I'm a [title] who helps [ICP] do [thing]." Nobody cares who you are until they know why they should. Lead with their problem, not your resume.

**Writing three paragraphs before the offer.** The first line should create tension. The second line should show you've solved it before. The third line should offer the next step. Anything longer than that is wasting attention.

**Using "I noticed" or "I came across."** Both are filler. Cut them. Start with the specific thing. "Saw your post about X" is stronger than "I noticed you posted about X."

**Asking for a call before you've delivered value.** "Would you be open to a quick call?" is the fastest way to get ignored. Replace it with: "If you want [specific thing], reply and I'll send it over." Value first, call second.

**Personalizing the wrong things.** Mentioning their company name, their location, or their job title is not personalization. That's mail-merge. Personalization is quoting something they said and connecting it to an outcome you delivered.

**Hedging the offer.** "If you're interested" or "Let me know if this resonates" or "No pressure." All of it sounds weak. Make the offer direct. "Reply and I'll send it" is stronger than "Let me know if you'd like me to send it."

One client opened every DM with "Hope you're having a great week!" It's filler. It trains the reader that your message is low-priority. Cut it. Start with the thing that matters.

Another client ended every DM with "Looking forward to hearing from you!" It sounds like a form letter. Replace it with a clear next step. "Reply with yes and I'll send the guide by end of day."

, where I audited a client's DM templates and flagged every phrase that made them sound like a bot.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Most LinkedIn advice says "personalize your outreach." That's not wrong. It's just incomplete.

Personalization without a clear outcome is wasted effort. You can spend 10 minutes researching someone, write a beautiful opener that references their work, and still get ignored if you don't tell them what happens next.

The contrarian position: specificity is not the goal. The goal is earned attention. Specificity is just the tool.

That means you can write a less-personalized DM and still win if the outcome you're offering is clear, immediate, and tied to something they said publicly.

Example: "Saw your post about losing deals in discovery. I built a 7-question framework that closes 40% more deals in the same pipeline. If you want it, reply and I'll send the doc."

Is that deeply personalized? No. It doesn't mention their company, their team size, or their specific challenges. But it's specific enough to prove you read their post, and the outcome is clear enough to justify a reply.

The over-personalization trap is real. Clients spend 20 minutes researching someone, write a 200-word DM that sounds like a biography, and wonder why they didn't reply. The answer: too much input, not enough output. You gave them information, not a reason to act.

The better move: spend 5 minutes. Find one thing. Connect it to one outcome. Make one offer. Send it. Move on.

Another contrarian take: cold DMs work better than warm intros for testing messaging. With a warm intro, the reader is doing you a favor. They're more likely to reply even if your message is weak. That gives you false validation.

With a cold DM, the reader has no obligation. If they reply, it's because your message earned it. That's the real test.

I tell clients: write 10 cold DMs before you ask for a single warm intro. If your cold DMs don't get replies, your warm intros won't convert either. Fix the message first.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

You send 20 DMs. You get 8 replies within 48 hours. Four of them book calls. Two close.

The replies don't say "Thanks for reaching out." They say "This is exactly what I needed. When can we talk?"

The founders you DM start checking your profile before they reply. You see profile views from every person you messaged. That's the signal your opener worked.

You stop needing to send follow-ups. The first DM earns a reply or it doesn't. When it does, the conversation moves immediately to scheduling.

Your clients start asking you to teach them how you write DMs. That's the real proof. When operators who close deals for a living want to learn your method, you've built something repeatable.

You can open a cold DM thread, read the first message you sent, and feel zero embarrassment. It's specific. It's clear. It's useful. That's the bar.

Before: 50 DMs sent, 3 replies, 0 calls booked, weeks of follow-up.

After: 20 DMs sent, 8 replies, 4 calls booked, 2 closed, no follow-up required.

The difference is the first line.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

The first five words of your email are the only ones that matter.

Everything else is negotiable.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Most founders write emails backwards.

They spend 30 minutes on the body, five seconds on the subject line, and zero time on the opening sentence.

Then they wonder why nobody reads past line two.

The cost of getting this wrong compounds silently.

Your best offer gets ignored because the subject line sounds like spam. Your strongest insight dies in paragraph three because the hook didn't land. Your follow-up gets deleted unread because the opening sentence promised nothing worth trading time for.

The mechanism is simple: your reader makes three binary decisions in three seconds.

Decision one: do I open this? (Subject line)

Decision two: do I keep reading? (First sentence)

Decision three: do I care enough to act? (Everything else)

If you lose at decision one or two, nothing else you wrote matters. The body could be perfect. The offer could be irresistible. The CTA could be clear. But if the reader never got there, you built a house with no door.

The leverage of getting this right is asymmetric. A subject line that earns the open means every word after that costs you nothing extra. An opening sentence that lands means the reader is now bought in, now looking for reasons to stay instead of reasons to leave.

That shift — from looking for an exit to looking for value — is the only thing email marketing actually sells.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

Most of the founders I work with think their email problem is a writing problem.

It's not. It's a framing problem.

They open with context the reader doesn't need yet. "Hi [Name], hope you're doing well. I wanted to reach out because..." By the time they get to the actual point, the reader is already gone.

The pattern I see most often: the founder buries the value proposition in paragraph two or three, after spending paragraph one explaining who they are or why they're writing.

Here's what that looks like in real campaigns I've reviewed.

A client running AI training workshops for solopreneurs was sending follow-up emails that opened with: "Thanks for attending last week's session on Claude Skills. I hope you found it valuable." Dead on arrival. The reader already knows they attended. They don't need a recap. They need a reason to read the next sentence.

We rewrote it to: "The skill you built last Tuesday is sitting in your Claude account doing nothing." Immediate tension. The reader now has a problem they didn't know they had 10 seconds ago, and they keep reading to find out how to fix it.

Another client — consultant selling 5K engagements — was opening cold outreach with: "I noticed your company recently raised a Series B and I'd love to discuss how we might work together." Generic. Forgettable. No specificity. No hook.

We rewrote to: "Your last three LinkedIn posts all mention the same problem: you're closing deals but losing them in onboarding." That line pulled from a past engagement where we diagnosed exactly this pattern. The specificity signaled research. The problem signaled relevance. The open rate jumped from 18% to 41%.

The common thread across every workshop, every coaching session, every content review: the founder knows what they want to say, but they open with setup instead of impact.

They write "I wanted to share some thoughts on..." when they should write "You're doing five jobs that one Claude Skill could handle for you."

They write "Following up on our conversation..." when they should write "Here's the exact script we talked about, ready to use today."

The shift I make in every session: cut the first two sentences. Start where the value starts.

In a past engagement, we worked through exactly this. The original draft opened with "It's Danny. I don't do emergency sessions lightly." Weak. Self-referential. No cost to the reader if they stop reading.

Final version opened with: "You can now text Claude a task from your phone, walk away, and come back to the work done on your computer." Immediate specificity. Immediate outcome. The reader now knows exactly what's in it for them in the first 12 words.

That's the pattern that repeats across every vertical, every offer type, every audience: value first, context second, credentials never.

title: Specific examples from the vault
text:
## Specific examples from the vault

In a past engagement, we built an email for a March Madness Marathon event. The original subject line was: "🚨 I had to call an emergency session. This just dropped and it changes everything."

Emoji. Vague urgency. No specificity. The reader has no idea what "this" is or why they should care.

We tested three alternatives. The one that landed: "I texted Claude from the airport." Seven words. No emoji. Pure specificity. The reader immediately knows this is about Claude, about mobile-first workflows, and about something the sender actually did (not just hyped). Open rate doubled.

The opening sentence in that email originally read: "I just spent the last 48 hours playing with something Anthropic quietly dropped last week and I genuinely couldn't wait until next month's curriculum to show you this."

Too long. Too many qualifiers ("just," "genuinely," "quietly"). Too much setup before the payoff.

Final version: "You can now text Claude a task from your phone, walk away, and come back to the work done on your computer." The value is in the first sentence. The reader knows immediately if this applies to them.

In a past engagement, we debriefed why an event underperformed. One of the diagnoses: the promotional emails started with "The goal of March Madness was to have a much higher attendance..." Context nobody asked for. The reader doesn't care about your internal goals. They care about their outcome.

The corrected approach for future events: "Three hours. Multiple trainers. Everything that's changed in AI and LinkedIn in the last few months, covered in one session built specifically for you." Outcome-first. Specificity-first. The reader knows in 20 words if this is worth their time.

In a past engagement, we rebuilt trainer documentation for AI Business School. The email delivering that doc originally opened with: "Here's the updated session guide for March 2026." Functional. Forgettable. No hook.

Revised to: "The March curriculum is live. Open the doc and you'll see every session title, every tool, every deliverable, color-coded by week." The specificity makes the action clear. The reader knows what to expect before they click.

Every example follows the same structure: cut the preamble, start with the specific outcome or specific tension, give the reader a reason to stay in the first 10 words.

title: Scripts and exact phrases
text:
## Scripts and exact phrases

Here are the opening lines that reliably perform across client emails, workshop invites, and cold outreach:

"You're doing five jobs manually that one Claude Skill could handle for you."

"The skill you built last Tuesday is sitting in your Claude account doing nothing."

"Your last three LinkedIn posts all mention the same problem: you're closing deals but losing them in onboarding."

"You can now text Claude a task from your phone, walk away, and come back to the work done on your computer."

"I texted Claude from the airport and landed to a full week's work done."

"Three hours. Multiple trainers. Everything that's changed in AI and LinkedIn in the last few months, covered in one session built specifically for you."

"Here's the exact script we talked about, ready to use today."

"The March curriculum is live. Open the doc and you'll see every session title, every tool, every deliverable, color-coded by week."

Every line starts with outcome, tension, or specificity. Never context. Never credentials. Never "hope this finds you well."

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

Opening with "I wanted to reach out because..." Dead. The reader doesn't care why you wanted to reach out. They care what's in it for them.

Opening with "Hope you're doing well." Generic filler that signals you have nothing urgent to say.

Opening with "Following up on our conversation..." Weak unless you immediately name the specific thing you're following up on. "Following up" by itself is vague. "Here's the pricing breakdown we talked about Friday" is specific.

Burying the value proposition in paragraph two or three. If the reader has to scroll to find out why they should care, they won't scroll.

Using emojis in professional emails. In a past engagement, we explicitly removed the 🚨 emoji from the subject line because it cheapened the message. Emojis signal hype. Plain text signals substance.

Opening with "I'm excited to share..." or "I'd love to discuss..." Self-referential. The reader doesn't care about your excitement. They care about their outcome.

Starting with credentials before value. "As the founder of Purely Personal..." tells the reader nothing about what they get. "You're spending 12 hours a week on content that Claude could compress to 2" tells them everything.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Conventional wisdom says emails should "build rapport" before asking for anything.

Wrong.

Rapport is a luxury you earn after you've already proven relevance.

If your opening sentence doesn't immediately signal "this applies to you," the reader deletes the email before rapport has a chance to matter.

The other bad advice: "personalize every email."

Personalization is only valuable if it proves you did research that changes the offer. "I saw you recently posted about X" is generic unless it leads to a specific insight the reader didn't have before.

"Your last three posts mention the same problem" is personalization that works because it names a pattern the reader may not have noticed themselves.

"I noticed your company raised a Series B" is personalization that doesn't work because it's public information that adds no insight.

The third myth: subject lines should create curiosity.

Curiosity without context is just confusion. "You won't believe what happened next" might work for clickbait. It doesn't work when you're asking someone to spend 10 minutes reading your email or 60 minutes on your call.

Better: specificity that makes the reader instantly know if this is relevant. "I texted Claude from the airport" creates curiosity anchored in a concrete outcome. The reader knows this is about mobile AI workflows before they open the email.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

Open rates above 40% on cold outreach. Above 60% on warm follow-ups. Above 80% on workshop invites to existing clients.

Reply rates above 10% on cold emails (not autoresponders — real replies that move the conversation forward).

The reader responds within 24 hours instead of a week, because the opening line landed hard enough that they couldn't ignore it.

Clients forward your emails to their teams without being asked, because the value was immediately clear and the format was clean enough to share.

You stop hearing "I didn't have time to read the whole thing" because the first sentence made the whole thing worth reading.

Before: emails that sit in the inbox for days, then get archived unread.

After: emails that get opened within an hour, read to the end, and acted on the same day.

The observable signal: you're booking more calls from fewer emails, because every email you send now earns the read instead of hoping for it.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

Your first line is the only line that matters.

Everything else — the body, the proof, the CTA — dies if the hook doesn't land. The reader sees your name, your face, and one sentence. That's the decision window. Scroll or stop. There is no third option.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Most founders write hooks that sound like they're reading from a script at a corporate town hall.

"In today's fast-paced world…" "Imagine if…" "Here's a hot take…"

These are AI tells. They signal "skip this" before the second line even loads.

The cost is invisible but catastrophic. A founder spends 90 minutes writing a post. The body is sharp. The proof is real. The CTA converts. But the hook is generic, so 95% of their audience scrolls past in 0.8 seconds. The post gets 14 likes from the founder's inner circle and zero pipeline movement.

LinkedIn's algorithm amplifies engagement in the first 60 minutes. If the hook doesn't stop the scroll in that window, the post is dead. It doesn't matter how good the rest of it is. The platform buries it. The founder posts again next week with the same result. Six months later they're burned out, blaming "the algorithm" or "content saturation," when the real problem was line one.

The leverage of getting this right is asymmetric. A founder who masters hooks can write mediocre bodies and still book calls. A founder with weak hooks and brilliant bodies gets ignored. The first line is the entire game.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

The pattern I see most often: founders open with a question or an "imagine if" construction because that's what they've been taught.

"What if I told you there's a better way to [do the thing]?"

"Have you ever wondered why [obvious problem]?"

These hooks test well in copywriting courses. They fail on LinkedIn because everyone is using them. The reader's brain has learned to filter them as noise.

I had a client — SaaS founder, strong offer, smart positioning — who was posting 3x a week and getting 8–12 likes per post. I pulled up his last 10 posts. Every single hook opened with a question. [a past engagement] documents the session where we diagnosed this. His body content was solid. His proof was specific. But every hook sounded like a landing page above the fold.

The reframe I gave him: "Stop asking permission to make a point. Just make the point."

We rewrote his next hook from "What if your sales team could close 30% more deals with one simple change?" to "Your sales team is leaving 30% of revenue on the table because they're asking the wrong question in discovery."

Same promise. Different entry. The post went from 11 likes to 140 and booked two calls.

Another pattern: founders who've worked with ghostwriters or agencies inherit hooks that sound like ad copy.

"Buckle up." "Let's dive in." "This changed everything."

These are instant credibility killers. They position the founder as someone who outsourced their voice to a junior copywriter who learned to write from Gary Vee circa 2019. [a past engagement] shows the audit I ran on a client's profile after they came off a six-month ghostwriting engagement. 14 of 16 posts opened with phrases from the AI-slop list. The comments were full of "great post!" reactions from other people using the same ghostwriter. Zero clients.

I also see founders who open with qualifiers because they're trying to avoid sounding arrogant.

"I'm not an expert, but…" "This might be controversial, but…" "Just my two cents…"

These hedges sound humble. They read as insecure. The reader's brain interprets them as "this person doesn't believe what they're about to say." [a past engagement] includes a breakthrough moment with a client who opened every post with a disclaimer. I asked her: "If you walked into a sales call and opened with 'I'm not sure if this will work for you,' what would happen?" She laughed and said the prospect would leave. Same dynamic on LinkedIn. The hook either earns the reader's attention or it doesn't. Hedging forfeits the round.

The flip side: founders who overcorrect and open with fake controversy.

"Hot take: [thing everyone already agrees with]."

"Unpopular opinion: you should focus on results."

These hooks promise tension and deliver platitudes. The reader feels baited. They don't engage. They scroll faster next time. [a past engagement] shows a carousel hook that fell into this trap: "Your 10,000 followers mean nothing if your bank account shows zero." The line itself is fine. But calling it a "hot take" or "unpopular opinion" would've killed it. The hook works because it states a specific tension without announcing that it's supposed to be provocative.

The strongest hook pattern I've seen across clients: open with a specific claim or a specific moment, not a setup for a claim.

One client — personal branding coach for executives — was opening posts with "Let me tell you about the time I…" I told him to cut "let me tell you" and just start with the moment. His next post opened: "I spent a low three-figure amount on a rebrand that tanked my pipeline in three weeks." That post booked four discovery calls. The body was identical to posts he'd written before. The only change was the hook.

title: Specific examples from the vault
text:
## Specific examples from the vault

The best hook I've seen from a client came from a past engagement: "I got 1,558 likes on a LinkedIn post and booked zero calls."

The post was about vanity metrics versus pipeline. But the hook worked because it named a real number, implied a problem, and made the reader ask "how is that possible?" No setup. No "imagine if." Just the tension, stated plainly.

Another example from the same client: "Most founders post content. Almost none of them ship a system."

That hook worked because it rejected the obvious assumption (posting is the goal) and named a specific alternative (shipping a system). The reader either agrees and keeps reading, or disagrees and comments. Both outcomes are wins. The line earns engagement because it has a position.

[a past engagement] documents a session title workshop where we applied the same principle to event promotion. The original title was "March Madness Marathon: Learn AI Skills." Generic. No tension. We rewrote it to "Create 5 Lead-Generating Posts From Any Content in 30 Minutes." The new title wasn't a hook for a post, but it followed hook logic: specific action, specific deliverable, specific timeframe. Attendance doubled.

I had a founder who sold consulting services to mid-market SaaS companies. His posts were getting 20–30 likes but no inbound. I pulled his last 15 hooks. 12 of them opened with "Here's how to [do the thing]." The pattern was invisible to him because he'd written those hooks over six months. To a reader seeing them in a feed, they all looked identical.

We tested a new pattern: open with the outcome of NOT doing the thing, then pivot to the solution in line two.

Old hook: "Here's how to run a discovery call that converts."

New hook: "Your discovery calls are converting at 22% because you're asking 'what's your budget' in the first five minutes."

The new hook worked because it diagnosed a specific mistake before offering a fix. The reader who makes that mistake stops scrolling. The reader who doesn't make that mistake keeps scrolling, which is fine — they weren't the ICP anyway.

[a past engagement] shows a workshop brief where we applied hook logic to session titles. The original session title was "AI for Marketing." Too broad. No tension. We rewrote it to "Turn Content You Already Made Into Paid Products." The new title worked as a hook because it named a specific transformation the reader could visualize. Same content. Different entry point. Signups increased 40%.

One pattern that consistently underperforms: opening with a personal story setup.

"Three years ago, I was broke and desperate. Today, I run a seven-figure agency. Here's what changed."

The line-by-line narrative works in long-form content or YouTube videos where the reader has already committed to watching. On LinkedIn, the reader hasn't committed to anything yet. The hook has to earn the next sentence. "Three years ago" doesn't do that. It asks the reader to trust that the story will be worth their time before they've seen any proof.

The reframe: open with the insight or the result, THEN flashback to the story in the body if it adds value.

Better hook: "I doubled my agency revenue by firing 60% of my clients." Now the reader wants to know how. The story can show up in paragraph three as proof.

title: Scripts and exact phrases
text:
## Scripts and exact phrases

**Contrarian + specific format:**

"Most [people in your niche] do [common behavior]. Almost none of them [the thing that actually works]."

Example: "Most founders post content. Almost none of them ship a system."

**Outcome-of-inaction format:**

"Your [thing] is [underperforming metric] because you're [specific mistake]."

Example: "Your LinkedIn DMs are converting at 11% because you're pitching in message two."

**The specific moment format:**

"[Concrete event with a number]."

Example: "I spent a low three-figure amount on a rebrand that tanked my pipeline in three weeks."

**The rejected assumption format:**

"[Thing people believe] isn't the problem. [Actual thing] is."

Example: "Your LinkedIn isn't a brand problem. It's a workflow problem."

**The tension-without-resolution format:**

"[Specific outcome that shouldn't be possible, stated plainly]."

Example: "I got 1,558 likes on a LinkedIn post and booked zero calls."

**The specific number + timeframe format:**

"[Action verb] [specific deliverable] in [specific time]."

Example: "Create 5 lead-generating posts from any content in 30 minutes."

**The diagnostic format:**

"If [observable behavior], then [underlying problem you diagnose]."

Example: "If you're explaining your offer in three sentences, you don't have an offer yet."

**The reversal format:**

"Everyone says [conventional wisdom]. The opposite is true: [your position]."

Example: "Everyone says 'post daily.' The opposite is true: post when you have something worth saying."

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

**Opening with a question instead of a claim.**

The reader's brain treats questions as a request for permission. "Should you care about this?" The answer is "probably not" and they scroll. A claim forces engagement: "Here's what's true. Agree or disagree." Questions are lazy hooks that signal the founder doesn't trust their point.

**Using "imagine if" or "what if" constructions.**

These are 2019 Facebook ad hooks that have been beaten to death. The reader's pattern-matching system flags them as generic copy and scrolls before processing the rest of the sentence. They also delay the actual point by an entire line, which is fatal when you have 0.8 seconds to capture attention.

**Opening with a qualifier or a hedge.**

"I'm not an expert, but…" "This might be controversial, but…" "Just my opinion, but…" These phrases undermine the hook before it's even delivered. They position the founder as unsure. If you're unsure, don't post it. If you're sure, don't apologize for being sure.

**Announcing that you're about to say something interesting.**

"Here's a hot take…" "Buckle up…" "Let's dive in…" These are meta-hooks. They narrate the post instead of starting the post. The reader doesn't care that you think your take is hot. They care whether the take is actually useful. Lead with the take, not the announcement.

**Opening with a setup sentence that goes nowhere.**

"In today's fast-paced world, businesses need to adapt." This is corporate jargon posing as a hook. It says nothing specific. It could apply to any business in any industry in any decade. The reader's brain discards it as filler and moves on.

**Starting with a story without establishing why the reader should care.**

"Three years ago I was sitting in a coffee shop…" The reader doesn't know you yet. They don't know if your story is worth their time. You have to earn the right to tell the story by opening with the insight or the outcome first. Story-first hooks work in long-form where the reader has already committed. They fail on LinkedIn where commitment costs attention.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Most people think hooks need to be clever or creative or "thumb-stopping."

That's backwards.

The best hooks are the most boring ones — if you define boring as "direct and specific." A hook that says "Your LinkedIn isn't a brand problem, it's a workflow problem" isn't clever. It's a diagnosis. But it works because it rejects an assumption the reader holds and names a specific alternative.

The founder who chases "creative" hooks ends up writing lines that sound impressive but say nothing. "Unlock your potential." "The future of work is here." "Are you ready to transform your business?" These hooks perform in creative director portfolios. They die on LinkedIn because they don't give the reader a reason to stop.

Another contrarian take: weak hooks are better than no hooks.

I've seen founders spend 30 minutes trying to craft the perfect opening line and end up not posting at all. That's worse than posting with a mediocre hook. A mediocre hook teaches you what doesn't work. No post teaches you nothing. The goal isn't perfection. The goal is iteration speed. Post, measure, adjust.

I also push back on the idea that hooks need to be "scroll-stoppers." That phrase comes from paid ads where you're interrupting someone who wasn't looking for you. On LinkedIn, your audience opted in by connecting with you or following you. The hook's job isn't to interrupt. It's to reward the reader for stopping. Big difference.

The other thing nobody says: hooks work best when they're written last, not first.

Most founders write the hook, then build the body around it. That's why their posts feel forced. The body is trying to justify a hook that was written in a vacuum. I teach clients to write the body first, extract the core insight, then write the hook as a distilled version of that insight. The hook becomes a promise the body keeps, not a thesis the body tries to prove.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

You know the hook is working when the comments section fills up with two types of responses: "This is exactly what I needed to hear" and "I completely disagree, here's why."

Both are wins. Agreement means you articulated something the reader felt but couldn't name. Disagreement means you stated a position clearly enough to provoke a reaction. What you don't want is silence, or worse — "great post!" comments from people who didn't read past the hook.

Observable signal: profile views spike within 24 hours of posting. The reader saw the hook, clicked through to see who you are, and is now evaluating whether to connect or follow. That's the hook doing its job.

Another signal: you start getting DMs that quote your hook back to you. "I saw your post about LinkedIn being a workflow problem, not a brand problem — can we talk?" That's pipeline movement. The hook moved someone from passive consumer to active buyer.

The before-and-after I see most often: founder goes from 15 likes and zero comments to 80 likes and 12 comments, with 3 of those comments coming from people outside their immediate network. The absolute numbers don't matter. What matters is the ratio shift. More engagement from strangers means the hook is pulling people in who weren't already fans.

Also: you stop needing to write explanatory second sentences. Weak hooks require a second sentence to clarify what the first sentence meant. Strong hooks stand alone. If you can delete line two and the hook still makes sense, you wrote a good hook.

Revenue signal: your sales calls start with "I read your post about [specific hook], and I think we need that." The prospect is pre-sold because the hook diagnosed a problem they have. You're not selling anymore. You're prescribing. That's what a working hook does — it shifts the sales dynamic from "convince me" to "help me."
