title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

LinkedIn is a text channel that sounds like speech, not publication.

The platform rewards posts that read like a smart operator leaning over coffee and saying something real, not an editor polishing a magazine byline. If you sound like you're performing for applause instead of talking to one person who needs to hear this exact thing today, you've already lost.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

LinkedIn is the only social platform where the feed algorithm still rewards substance over dopamine hits.

That means founders who can write in their actual voice, with their actual beliefs, naming actual numbers and clients, will consistently outperform polished ghostwriters and content agencies. The cost of generic LinkedIn voice is invisibility. Your post gets 14 likes from your colleagues, zero comments from strangers, and nobody books a call.

The leverage of getting this right is that one post written in real voice can book three calls in 48 hours. Not because it went viral. Because three of the right people read it, recognized themselves in the problem, and sent a DM.

Most founders think they need better hooks or more posting frequency. What they actually need is to stop sounding like a LinkedIn influencer and start sounding like themselves on a real sales call. The platform is not Twitter. It's not Instagram. It's a room full of operators reading on their commute, during a coffee break, or while pretending to listen to a meeting. They scroll past anything that sounds like content theatre.

When a founder writes in authentic voice, two things happen. First, they attract the exact clients who need their specific POV and experience. Second, they repel everyone else, which is the whole point. A thousand generic followers who like your posts but never buy is worse than fifty specific followers who recognize you as the exact person they need to hire.

The mechanism is simple: real voice costs the writer something to publish. Generic voice costs nothing, which is why it earns nothing back.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

The single most common LinkedIn problem I see across clients is that they write like they're trying to impress a room of strangers instead of help one specific person solve one specific problem.

A founder will draft a post about "the future of AI in marketing" with zero specifics, no named examples, no numbers, no real POV. They post it. It gets 22 likes from their network. Nobody comments. Nobody books. They conclude LinkedIn doesn't work for them. What actually doesn't work is writing like a thought leader instead of an operator.

I worked with a B2B SaaS founder who had 8,000 followers and couldn't book a single inbound call from LinkedIn a past engagement. His posts were perfectly written, grammatically correct, well-formatted with bullet points and line breaks. They were also completely invisible. The Invisibility Diagnostic scored them 1 out of 4. No voice. No POV. No specificity. No ask.

We rebuilt one post together using the exact language he used on a sales call the week before. Same story. Same client example. Same numbers. But written in his actual speaking rhythm: short sentences, plain English, one concrete thing per paragraph. He published it on a Tuesday morning. By Thursday he had twelve DMs and three booked calls. The difference wasn't the story. The difference was that version two sounded like a real human saying something they actually believe.

Another client came to me drowning in content advice from a marketing agency [a past engagement]. They had her using hooks like "Here's a hot take" and "Let me dive into this." Every post opened with a question or an "imagine if" framing. Her engagement was fine by vanity metrics but she wasn't booking work. We killed every AI-slop phrase, rewrote her last five posts to open with a specific claim instead of a question, and added one named client example to each. Within three weeks she booked two 5K engagements directly from LinkedIn DMs. Both clients told her they'd been following her for months but the recent posts finally made them think "this person has actually done this work."

The pattern I see over and over: founders writing to sound smart instead of writing to move someone closer to a buying decision [a past engagement]. They use words like "leverage" and "synergy" and "empower" because those words feel professional. What they actually do is signal that you're parroting LinkedIn instead of speaking from experience.

I had a client who ran a content agency [a past engagement]. Her posts were full of corporate jargon and vague promises. "We help brands unlock their full potential." Nobody knows what that means. We rewrote her positioning around one specific thing she'd done for one specific client: "Took a SaaS founder from 200 monthly visitors to 2,000 in 90 days using a content system they could run in 3 hours a week." That version books calls. The generic version gets ignored.

The other major pattern is founders who think LinkedIn requires a different voice than the one they use in real client conversations [a past engagement]. They talk to me on a call with clarity, directness, specificity. Then they sit down to write a LinkedIn post and suddenly they're using em dashes, starting sentences with "I believe," writing three-paragraph setups before they get to the point. I tell them to record a 60-second voice note explaining the exact thing they want to post about, then transcribe it and publish 80% of that with light editing. That's their LinkedIn voice. Not what they think LinkedIn voice should sound like.

One founder I worked with had a fantastic business teaching small business owners how to hire their first employee [a past engagement]. Her LinkedIn was completely disconnected from that work. She posted generic leadership advice and got zero traction. We rebuilt her content strategy around one question: "What would you say to a client on a sales call if they asked you this exact question?" That became the filter for every post. Within 60 days she was booking five calls a week from LinkedIn, up from zero.

The hardest part for most founders is accepting that LinkedIn rewards specificity over polish. They want to sound impressive. The platform wants you to sound useful. A post that says "I helped a client increase revenue" is meaningless. A post that says "I helped a SaaS founder increase MRR from a low three-figure amount to mid five figures in four months by rebuilding their onboarding sequence and killing their free tier" is a sales pitch disguised as a case study.

I also see founders who've hired ghostwriters or agencies to run their LinkedIn a past engagement. The content is consistent. The formatting is clean. The hooks are strong. But it doesn't sound like the founder. Clients book a call expecting one person and meet someone else. That's not a brand problem. That's a trust problem. Your LinkedIn voice should be the exact same voice someone hears when they get on a call with you. If those don't match, you're burning trust before the sale even starts.

The most successful LinkedIn voices I've seen share three traits: they sound like spoken English, they cite specific examples with numbers, and they don't hedge [a past engagement]. No "in my experience" or "I believe" or "it depends." Just the claim, then the proof, then the ask. That's the structure. Everything else is decoration.

title: Specific examples from the vault
text:
## Specific examples from the vault

A coaching client came to me with classic LinkedIn paralysis [a past engagement]. She'd been posting inconsistently for six months. Some posts got traction. Most died. She couldn't figure out the pattern. We pulled her last 20 posts and ran them through the Invisibility Diagnostic. The ones that worked all had three things: they opened with a contrarian claim, they cited a specific client by vertical and outcome, and they ended with a question that cost something to answer. The ones that died opened with questions or "imagine if" framings, had no specifics, and ended with "What do you think?" That's a recipe for likes from your network and zero DMs from strangers.

I had a B2B founder who'd been told by a marketing consultant that LinkedIn posts should be "inspirational" [a past engagement]. So he posted quotes and motivational content. Got decent engagement. Booked zero calls. I asked him what he talked about on actual sales calls. He said "I walk them through the exact three mistakes I see in their sales process and show them how I'd fix it in 30 days." I told him to post that. He resisted because it felt too specific, too prescriptive, too salesy. He posted it anyway. Booked four calls in 72 hours. Closed two. That's a low three-figure amount in revenue from one post that "felt too salesy."

Another example: a founder running a productized service [a past engagement]. Her LinkedIn was full of educational content about best practices in her industry. Well-researched. Well-written. Zero client acquisition. We rebuilt her content around case studies structured as before/after transformations. "Client came to me with X problem. Here's what we changed. Here's the result in 60 days." Every post cited a real client, real numbers, real timeline. Her inbound rate tripled in 30 days. She told me later that prospects were coming to sales calls pre-sold because they'd read three of those posts and already knew she could deliver the result.

I worked with a founder who thought his LinkedIn voice should be "professional and polished" [a past engagement]. Every post was grammatically perfect, formatted with clean line breaks, opened with a strong hook. It also sounded like it was written by a committee. I had him record a voice note answering "Why did you start your business?" and transcribed it. The difference was night and day. The voice note had personality, specificity, real emotion. We used that as the template for his next five posts. Engagement doubled. More importantly, the people engaging were qualified buyers, not random LinkedIn lurkers.

One client had the opposite problem [a past engagement]. Her posts were too casual. She wrote exactly how she talked, which was great for authenticity but terrible for structure. No clear point. No CTA. Just rambling observations. We kept her voice but added structure: open with one claim, support with one example, close with one question. Her engagement stayed high but now it converted. Three new clients in 60 days, all from LinkedIn DMs that started with "I've been reading your posts for weeks and I need to work with you."

A founder in the coaching space told me his LinkedIn wasn't working because "the algorithm hates me" [a past engagement]. I pulled his last ten posts. Every single one opened with a question. "Have you ever wondered why...?" "What if you could...?" "Are you struggling with...?" The algorithm doesn't hate questions. People do. A question hook asks the reader to work before you've earned it. We rewrote his last post to open with a claim instead: "Most coaches price too low because they don't understand positioning." Same underlying message. Totally different structure. The rewritten version got 4x the comments and two inbound leads. The original got 11 likes.

I've also seen the opposite failure mode: founders who think LinkedIn requires aggressive Gary Vee-style energy [a past engagement]. All caps. Exclamation points. Hype. That works for Gary because he's Gary. For a B2B consultant selling 5K engagements, it reads as desperation. I tell clients: write like you're explaining something important to a smart colleague who doesn't have time for bullshit. That's the tone. Not hype. Not monotone corporate. Confident operator.

title: Scripts and exact phrases
text:
## Scripts and exact phrases

"Write this post like you're explaining it to one specific person who needs to hear it, not a room full of strangers."

"If you wouldn't say this sentence out loud on a sales call, delete it."

"Open with a claim, not a question. Questions ask the reader to work before you've earned it."

"Name the client. Name the outcome. Name the timeline. If you can't name specifics, you don't have a story worth posting."

"Your LinkedIn voice should sound exactly like your voice on a sales call. If those don't match, you're burning trust."

"One sentence per paragraph. Period. No exceptions."

"No em dashes. Ever. Use a period or a comma."

"If you catch yourself writing 'I believe' or 'in my experience,' delete it and just state the thing."

"The test: read the post out loud. If you'd be embarrassed to say it to a paying client, rewrite it."

"Hooks should feel like spoken speech, not 'Here's a hot take' or 'Let me dive in.'"

"End with a question that costs something to answer, or an invitation to DM, or nothing. Never end with 'What do you think?'"

"If a post scores below 3 out of 4 on the Invisibility Diagnostic, don't publish it."

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

Starting sentences with "I" too often. It signals insecurity. State the claim first, then cite yourself as the source if needed.

Using em dashes to connect thoughts that should be two sentences. Em dashes are a crutch. Kill them all.

Opening with questions or "imagine if" framings. These were hooks in 2019. Now they're instant skips. Open with a specific contrarian claim instead.

Writing in paragraph blocks instead of one sentence per line. LinkedIn is read on mobile. Dense paragraphs die. One sentence. Blank line. Next sentence. That's the format.

Using AI-slop phrases like "dive in," "unlock," "game changer," "here's the reality," "let that sink in." These are instant tells that you're not writing in your own voice.

Posting educational content with no POV. "Here are 5 tips for better LinkedIn posts" teaches nothing and books zero calls. "Here's the one mistake I see in 90% of LinkedIn posts that kills engagement" is a position. Positions attract clients. Tips attract likes.

Ending posts with "What do you think?" or "Agree?" These are engagement bait tactics that work for influencers and fail for B2B founders. End with a real question, a specific invitation, or nothing.

Not citing specifics. "I helped a client grow their business" is worthless. "I helped a SaaS founder increase MRR from 2K to a low three-figure amount in 90 days" is a pitch. Always cite the vertical, the metric, and the timeframe.

Overthinking hooks. The best hooks sound like the first sentence you'd say if someone asked you about this topic over coffee. Not "Buckle up" or "This is going to blow your mind." Just the claim.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Most LinkedIn advice tells you to post daily, optimize for the algorithm, use trending formats, ride viral topics.

I think that's backwards.

Post when you have something specific to say to one specific person. The algorithm rewards consistency but it rewards voice more. A founder posting three times a week in authentic voice will outperform a founder posting daily in generic voice every single time.

The LinkedIn influencer playbook is: hook with a hot take, structure with line breaks, close with engagement bait, repeat. That works if your goal is followers. It fails if your goal is clients. Clients don't book calls because you went viral. They book calls because you demonstrated specific expertise on a specific problem they currently have.

The other contrarian belief: short posts outperform long posts for B2B founders. Everyone says "LinkedIn loves long-form content now." What LinkedIn actually loves is content that holds attention. If you can make your point in six sentences, publish six sentences. Adding three paragraphs of filler to hit some imaginary word count threshold just dilutes the message.

I also reject the idea that LinkedIn requires a "LinkedIn voice" different from your real voice. Your real voice is the only voice that converts. Everything else is costume.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

The signal is not likes. The signal is DMs.

When your LinkedIn voice is dialed in, you'll get messages from people you've never met saying "I've been reading your posts for weeks and I think you're exactly who I need to hire." Those messages come from strangers who've read three to five posts and concluded you understand their problem better than anyone else they're following.

Another signal: people quoting your posts back to you on sales calls. "I read your post about X and it described my exact situation." That means your posts are functioning as sales collateral, which is the whole point.

You'll also notice your posts start attracting comments from qualified buyers, not just LinkedIn randos. A post written in real voice with specific examples attracts people who have that specific problem. A post written in generic voice attracts people who like collecting content.

The number to watch is not followers. It's booked calls per month from LinkedIn DMs. If that number is zero, your voice isn't working. If that number is five-plus, your voice is dialed in and the only question is whether you're posting enough.

Before: posting three times a week, getting 40 likes per post, zero inbound leads. After: posting twice a week, getting 25 likes per post, booking eight calls a month. That's what success looks like. Lower vanity metrics, higher revenue.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

You talk to a client on a 1:1 call the same way you'd talk to a founder sitting across from you at coffee. Not friendlier. Not more formal. The exact same energy.

The moment you switch into "coaching voice" — softer tone, more questions, careful phrasing — you've already lost the session.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Most coaches sound like therapists. They ask permission before pushing. They validate before challenging. They hedge every sharp observation with "I could be wrong, but…"

That works if the client came to feel better. It doesn't work if they came to fix something broken in their business.

The founder sitting across from you is paying low four figures to mid four figures a month because their LinkedIn isn't working. Their offer isn't landing. Their content sounds like everyone else. Their pipeline went quiet three weeks ago and they don't know why.

They don't need a friend. They need an operator who's seen this pattern 47 times and knows exactly what breaks first.

When you sound like a coach, they treat you like a coach. They nod. They agree. They say "that's a great point" and then do nothing. When you sound like the person who already solved this for someone else last Tuesday, they write it down and ship it by Friday.

The cost of sounding too careful: the client leaves the call feeling heard but not moved. The cost of sounding too direct: nothing, if you're right. The best clients want to be told what's broken and how to fix it. The worst clients want to be told they're already doing great.

You're not optimizing for the worst clients.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

The pattern repeats in almost every first session. The founder opens with "I'm not sure what's wrong, but my LinkedIn isn't working." They've been posting for three months. Getting likes. No calls booked.

The soft-coach move is to ask "What do you think might be contributing to that?" The operator move is to open their profile and say "Your positioning line says you help founders with marketing strategy. That's 400,000 people. No one books a call with 'marketing strategy.' What's the one problem you actually solve?"

That's the fork. One path is collaborative. One path is directive. The directive path closes faster because it names the thing the founder already suspected but didn't want to say out loud.

Client example from a past engagement: Uma came in saying he wanted executive coaching, LinkedIn branding, and to make himself more visible. Three things. All vague. The call could have spent 20 minutes exploring each one.

Instead: "What's the one thing that brings you the most income?" He said "None of them." That's the real problem. Not LinkedIn. Not visibility. The fact that he's running three businesses and none of them work.

The next move wasn't to ask more questions. The next move was to cut: "Everything else has to go. You can't be niche at all. Pick one."

He picked mindset coaching. Then the next cut: "There should never be 'or' in your ICP. You said health-conscious professionals OR small business owners. Which one?"

This is how the call actually moves. Not "let's explore your options." Cut. Cut. Cut. By minute 12 the positioning is clear. By minute 25 he has homework. By minute 30 the session is over and he knows exactly what to ship by Friday.

Another pattern from a past engagement: Ilvy opened with "I'm running coaching, supplements, Smart Coffee, Myel technology, and HNS network." Five things. The soft move is "tell me more about each." The operator move is "What's the one thing that brings you the most income?"

She said "None of them." Same answer as Uma. Same root problem.

The script from that call: "That's the problem. You're doing five things and no one can remember what you do. If I'm someone who doesn't know you and you have to sell yourself with one niche, what would it be?"

She said mindset coach. The next line: "That's all you need to focus on. Everything else has to go."

This lands because it's not a suggestion. It's a diagnosis. The founder already knows it. They've known it for six months. They just needed someone to say it with enough certainty that they can finally stop hedging.

The voice that works in these moments is the voice of someone who's already run this exact playbook 30 times. Not "I think this might help." Not "Have you considered…" Just: "Here's what's broken. Here's the fix. Here's what you ship by Friday."

from a past engagement: the same principle applies when reviewing session titles for NAS AI School. The team kept submitting titles like "How to Use Claude Code Voice Mode to Code 3x Faster" or "Create AI Agents That Monitor Your Business 24/7 with Claude /loop."

The feedback loop wasn't "What do you think about this title?" It was "This fails the 12-year-old test. A founder in Malaysia wouldn't understand '/loop.' Cut it. Rewrite."

That's coaching voice. Not softer. Sharper. The client doesn't need validation. They need the thing that's wrong named quickly so they can fix it and move on.

Another client pattern from the vault: founder comes in saying "I need to post more consistently." That's not the problem. The problem is they don't know what to post because their positioning is unclear. But if you ask "What's your positioning?" they'll give you a paragraph of corporate speak.

The move that works: open their last five posts. Read one out loud. Ask "Does this sound like you talking, or does this sound like ChatGPT?" They laugh. They know. That's the problem. Not consistency. Voice.

Once the real problem is named, the fix is obvious. They don't need a content calendar. They need a Voice DNA document Claude reads before writing anything. Session outcome: we build that document in the next 20 minutes. Homework: use it to rewrite one post. Reply with the before/after by tomorrow.

The session ends with a concrete next step. Not "think about your voice." Not "explore your tone." One rewrite. By tomorrow. That's the difference between coaching that feels good and coaching that ships results.

## Specific examples from the vault

from a past engagement, the turning point with Uma came at minute 7. He said "I don't have personal connections. I'm very good technically. I do my job very well. It's just that I don't have personal brand."

The response: "This is where my expertise is. I work with the head of AI at Intel. He's about to become CMO of OpenAI. That's not public yet. He's my client. I also work with a workshop hosthatterjee, CEO of London School of Cyber Security. After I worked with her, she hired me as CMO. The advantage with personal brand is when you know how to show outside how good you are, more opportunities open."

That's not humble. It's not "I might be able to help." It's proof. The exact clients. The exact outcomes. The exact next role they landed. This establishes authority in 90 seconds.

Then the homework assignment: "I'm going to write one post for you tonight. You tell me your story. I'm going to post it. Then you're going to see what happens."

No discussion. No "would you be open to trying…" Just: here's what we're doing. The founder either trusts you or they don't. If they trust you, they ship. If they don't, no amount of careful language will fix that.

from a past engagement, minute 20: Ilvy said she's struggling to get clients. The diagnosis: "You have no one-liner. You have no clear mission. You have no clear transformation statement for your service."

The homework: "Deliver a new one-liner, mission, vision, and clear service transformation within 24 hours. I'm also assigning you a 90-day daily video challenge. One video per day. Public accountability. Post your commitment in the group right now so you can't back out."

This is sharp. It's also kind. The kindest thing you can do for a founder who's stuck is tell them exactly what to ship and exactly when it's due.

Another moment from the same call: Ilvy asked if she could use Danny's 108 prompts, ikigai coaching methods, and custom GPT as her own services. The answer: "Yes. I'm giving you permission. Use them. Build your business with them. Just don't wait. Ship something this week."

That permission is valuable. But the real value is the push. Not "take your time." Not "let me know how it goes." Ship this week.

from a past engagement, a session with Alex (COO of NAS AI School): the brief was to build an ops dashboard for session documentation. The request came in as a long paragraph describing the general need.

The response wasn't "tell me more about your workflow." It was "I need three things: your session transcripts, your attendee data, and your feedback PDFs. Send them now. I'm building the first version today."

That's operator voice. Not asking permission. Not exploring requirements for two weeks. Just: here's what I need, here's when I'm building it, send the files.

By end of session, the dashboard had three live features: PDF upload, transcript parsing, and session summary generation. Not a spec doc. Not a roadmap. A working product.

The same pattern shows up In a past engagement: Danny asked Claude to turn a curriculum document into a branded a platform partner-style guide. The instruction wasn't "see what you can do." It was "Use yellow and orange branding. Black text. Make it beautiful. Structure it for app context ingestion."

Specific. Directive. No room for interpretation. The document shipped in one iteration.

from a past engagement, a debrief with Alex after a failed event: Alex asked "Why didn't we hit attendance goals?" The soft move would be to list contributing factors and let Alex decide. The operator move: "Wrong day. Sunday is the lowest attendance day. Marketing started too late. No promotional strategy across regular sessions. Too much content, too little time."

Five problems. Named. No hedging. Then the fix: "Next event runs on a Thursday. Two-week promo runway minimum. Every trainer plugs it in their session. Dry run cut from three hours to 30 minutes."

Alex knew what to do immediately because the diagnosis was sharp and the fix was specific.

title: Scripts and exact phrases
text:
## Scripts and exact phrases

**Opening the call:**
"Walk me through what's broken. Don't sell me your vision. Just tell me what's not working."

**When the founder is vague:**
"That's three things. Pick one. What's the one problem you solve that someone would pay a low three-figure amount to fix?"

**When they hedge:**
"You just said 'I think' twice. You know the answer. What is it?"

**When their positioning is too broad:**
"Your ICP says 'entrepreneurs and small business owners.' That's 40 million people. Cut it in half. Who specifically?"

**After they describe the problem:**
"Okay. Here's what's actually broken: [name the real problem]. Here's the fix: [one action]. Ship it by Friday and reply with proof."

**When they ask for options:**
"I'm not giving you options. Options are how you stay stuck. Here's what you're doing."

**When they say 'I need to think about it':**
"You don't. You've been thinking about it for six months. That's why you're here. What's the thing you're scared to do?"

**Ending the call:**
"You have one task. [Name the task]. Deadline is [specific day]. Don't reply with an update. Reply with the finished thing."

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

**Mistake 1: Asking too many questions.**

The founder came to you because they're stuck. If you ask them "What do you think you should do?" they'll give you the same answer they've been giving themselves for three months. It didn't work then. It won't work now.

The fix: diagnose first. Ask clarifying questions only when you genuinely don't know. Once you see the pattern, name it.

**Mistake 2: Softening the diagnosis.**

"I could be wrong, but it seems like maybe your positioning might be a little unclear?"

No. The positioning is unclear. Say it. The founder needs to hear it said with certainty. If you hedge, they'll hedge. If you commit, they'll commit.

**Mistake 3: Giving multiple options.**

"You could focus on LinkedIn, or you could try YouTube, or you could build an email list."

Options sound helpful. Options are paralysis. The founder already has too many options. That's why they're stuck. Your job is to cut the options down to one and tell them which one to ship first.

**Mistake 4: Ending the call without a concrete next step.**

"Great session. Think about what we discussed and let's reconnect next week."

This guarantees nothing ships. The call ends with one task, one deadline, one format for proof. Not "think about it." Not "let me know how it goes." Ship this by Friday and reply with the screenshot.

**Mistake 5: Talking like a coach instead of an operator.**

"How does that make you feel?" "What's coming up for you?" "Let's explore that."

These are therapy questions. They work in therapy. They don't work in business coaching. The founder doesn't need to explore their feelings. They need to fix their offer and book a sales call by Tuesday.

**Mistake 6: Not calling out when the founder is stalling.**

Founder says "I'm not ready to post yet. I need to refine my message first."

The soft coach lets that sit. The operator says "You've been refining for two months. You're not refining. You're avoiding. Write one post. Today. I'll review it. Then you post it tomorrow."

Stalling is the enemy. Your job is to name it and break it.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Most coaching wisdom says "meet the client where they are." Build rapport first. Ask questions. Let them arrive at the answer themselves.

That's wrong for founders.

Founders don't need someone to meet them where they are. They're already where they are. That's the problem. They need someone to pull them to where they need to be.

The Socratic method — asking questions until the client discovers the answer — sounds elegant. It works beautifully in academic settings. It fails in business coaching because the founder already knows the answer. They've known it for weeks. They just don't trust it enough to act.

Your job isn't to help them discover the answer. Your job is to name the answer with enough certainty that they finally trust it and ship.

The other contrarian piece: the best coaching sessions are short. 30 minutes. 45 maximum. Any longer and you're either overcomplicating the problem or the founder is stalling.

Long sessions feel productive. They're not. They're a way to avoid the discomfort of having one clear task and no excuses left.

Cut the session when the homework is clear. Don't fill the remaining time with more questions just because you booked an hour.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

The founder stops saying "I think" and starts saying "I'm doing."

They reply to your message with a screenshot of the thing they shipped, not an update about progress.

The gap between sessions shrinks. They don't need a weekly call anymore because they know how to diagnose their own sticking points and move past them.

They start talking to their own clients the same way you talk to them: direct, outcome-first, no hedging.

Their LinkedIn posts stop sounding like ChatGPT and start sounding like them on a real sales call.

The pipeline refills. They go from "I'm not getting leads" to "I have three discovery calls this week and I'm not sure how to close them."

That's the signal. When the problem shifts from "nothing's happening" to "too much is happening and I need help prioritizing," you've done your job.

Another signal: they stop asking permission. They stop saying "Do you think I should…?" and start saying "I did this. Here's what happened. What's next?"

The final signal: they refer someone else to you and the referral opens with "My friend worked with you and said you don't bullshit. That's what I need."

When the reputation is "doesn't bullshit," you're coaching the right way.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

Praise is currency. Spend it like you're broke.

The second you open with "Great question!" or "I love this!" you've revealed you have nothing to say yet. Real praise names the specific thing that worked and why it mattered. Everything else is filler.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Generic praise trains people to ignore you.

When every response opens with "this is such an important topic" or "you're absolutely right," the words become wallpaper. The recipient stops reading after the first line because they've learned nothing real follows.

Specific praise does three things generic praise can't. First, it proves you actually engaged with the work. Second, it tells the person what to do more of. Third, it gives them language to describe their own strength that they didn't have before.

The cost of getting this wrong shows up in two places. In content, opening every post or comment with sycophancy makes you invisible. Every founder on LinkedIn who starts with "Love this!" sounds identical. In coaching or sales calls, leading with praise-as-filler wastes the first 30 seconds of trust the client gave you. They came for a diagnosis. You gave them a compliment they've heard before.

The leverage of getting this right is positioning. When someone reads your feedback and thinks "they saw something I didn't see in my own work," you've earned credibility they can't revoke. That's not praise. That's analysis they paid for without knowing it.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

The pattern repeats across every type of engagement. Founders send LinkedIn posts for review. Workshop participants submit homework. Sales calls open with the prospect explaining their offer. In every case, the instinct is to open with validation before critique.

The instinct is wrong.

In a past engagement, a client sent a post for review that opened with "Most people think AI will replace them. Smart people know it won't." Generic praise would have been "Great hook!" Specific praise was: "The parallel structure works because it creates an in-group the reader wants to join. The problem is the claim is vague. Replace 'Smart people know it won't' with 'The best founders are using it to replace their 12-hour content week.' Now the reader knows what the in-group actually does."

That's not praise. That's a diagnosis with one piece of working code embedded in it. The client now has language to describe what made the hook almost work, and a concrete fix.

In a past engagement, a prospect explained their offer on a discovery call. The instinct would have been to say "That sounds like a great program!" Instead: "The transformation you described in the first 30 days is the entire offer. Everything after that is proof. Lead with that and the rest writes itself."

The prospect replied: "I've been explaining this wrong for six months." That's what specific praise unlocks. It tells them what they already have that they didn't know was valuable.

The inverse also shows up. In a past engagement, a participant submitted a hook that was genuinely weak. Generic critique would have been "This needs work." Specific critique was: "This hook has no claim. You opened with a question, which means the reader has to do work before they know why they're reading. Replace 'Have you ever wondered why some founders grow faster?' with 'Most founders post daily and stay invisible. The ones who grow post differently, not more.' Now there's a claim."

The participant rewrote it in 10 minutes. Specific praise and specific critique use the same mechanism: name the exact thing that's working or broken, then show the alternative.

In a past engagement, a founder was stuck on positioning. They'd written three versions of their one-liner and couldn't pick. Generic praise would have been "All three are solid!" Specific praise was: "Version two is the only one where I know who you serve and what they get. Versions one and three describe what you do, not what they walk away with. Ship version two."

The founder shipped it that afternoon. Praise that commits to a position gives the recipient permission to move.

The pattern also shows up in comment threads on LinkedIn. Most founders reply to every comment with "Thanks for sharing!" or "Appreciate this!" Those responses are invisible. In a past engagement, the highest-performing comments were the ones that either added a new insight or asked a follow-up question that deepened the original post.

Example from a real thread: Original post was about how most founders waste time on content that doesn't book calls. Generic comment: "So true!" Specific comment: "This is why I track pipeline per post, not likes per post. Vanity metrics killed my first business." The specific comment got 14 replies. The generic one got zero.

Praise works the same way. Generic praise is "Great post!" Specific praise is "The line about tracking pipeline instead of likes is the entire framework. That's the new north star."

In a past engagement coaching sessions, the default move when a founder makes progress is to say "Amazing work!" The better move is to name the exact moment the shift happened. Example from a past engagement: "The second you said 'I help founders build systems that run their marketing' instead of 'I do content strategy,' the offer became clear. That's the line. Use it everywhere."

The founder wrote it at the top of every sales document. Specific praise tells them what to anchor to.

The other place this shows up is in objection handling on sales calls. When a prospect says "I've tried content before and it didn't work," the instinct is to validate their concern before reframing. That's the wrong sequence. In a past engagement, the move is to reframe first, then validate second.

Example from a real call: Prospect says "I'm worried this won't work for my niche." Generic validation: "I totally understand that concern." Specific reframe: "What didn't work before was probably the execution, not the niche. If your offer is strong and the ICP is narrow, content is the most reliable channel. The question is whether you're willing to do it consistently for 90 days."

That's not praise or validation. That's a diagnosis that costs the prospect something to ignore.

title: Specific examples from the vault
text:
## Specific examples from the vault

In a past engagement, the client submitted a post that scored 2/4 on the Invisibility Diagnostic. The hook had voice and specificity but no POV or ask. Generic feedback would have been "Solid start, just needs a stronger ending." Specific feedback was: "You opened with 'Most founders waste 12 hours a week on content that doesn't book calls' — that's the claim. But the post doesn't tell me what to do instead. Add a three-step framework in the body or a single CTA at the end. Right now I believe the problem but don't know the solution."

The client added: "Here's what I do instead: 1. Audit every post against pipeline, not likes. 2. Cut anything that didn't book a call. 3. Double down on what did." The rewrite booked two calls in the first 48 hours.

In a past engagement, the prospect explained a coaching offer that promised "clarity and confidence." Generic praise would have been "That's a great outcome to promise!" Specific feedback was: "Clarity and confidence are feelings, not results. A buyer can't measure them. Replace it with 'In 90 days you'll have a one-line positioning statement that books calls, or we keep working until you do.' Now the promise is falsifiable."

The prospect rewrote the offer page that night. Booked three clients in two weeks. The shift wasn't praise. It was specificity that made the promise real.

In a past engagement, a participant submitted a LinkedIn profile headline that read "Helping founders grow." Generic feedback would have been "Good start, but make it more specific." Specific feedback was: "This headline has no ICP and no mechanism. Replace it with 'I help B2B founders build LinkedIn content systems that book 5+ calls a month without hiring a team.' Now I know who you serve, what they get, and how."

The participant changed it before the workshop ended. Three inbound DMs in the next week.

In a past engagement, the founder had written three versions of their offer. Version one: "I help entrepreneurs build their brand." Version two: "I help founders turn their LinkedIn into a client channel in 90 days." Version three: "I teach founders how to create content that converts."

Generic praise: "These are all strong!" Specific praise: "Version two is the only one with a number and a timeframe. The other two describe what you do, not what I get. Ship version two today."

The founder used it in a sales call that afternoon. Closed a a low three-figure amount engagement.

In a past engagement, the analysis of 50 top-performing posts revealed a pattern: the hooks that booked calls were the ones that rejected a common assumption in the first line. Example: "Most founders post content. Almost none of them ship a system."

Generic insight: "Contrarian hooks perform well." Specific insight: "The pattern is claim + specificity in the first sentence, then proof in the body. The hooks that don't work open with questions or 'imagine if.' The ones that work open with 'Most X do Y. The best X do Z instead.' That's the template."

That template became the default hook structure for every client In a past engagement.

In a past engagement, the founder had been stuck on pricing for three weeks. They'd written five versions of their offer, all between ,500 and low four figures. Generic advice: "Pick the one that feels right." Specific advice: "The price isn't the variable. The promise is. If you promise 'better content,' a low three-figure amount is expensive. If you promise 'a content system that books 5 calls a month in 90 days or we keep working,' a low three-figure amount is cheap. Fix the promise first."

The founder repriced at low four figures with a result-tied guarantee. Closed two clients in the next 10 days.

In a past engagement, a client asked how to handle "I need to think about it" on sales calls. Generic advice: "Give them time and follow up." Specific advice: "That phrase almost never means thinking. It means a missing piece. Ask: 'Walk me through what's still unclear. Price, scope, fit, or timing?' Most of the time they name one. Then you handle it on the call."

The client used it on the next call. Closed on the spot.

title: Scripts and exact phrases
text:
## Scripts and exact phrases

"The line about [specific thing] is the entire offer. Lead with that."

"This has no claim. You opened with a question, which means the reader has to do work before they know why they're reading."

"Version [number] is the only one where I know who you serve and what they get. Ship that."

"The transformation you described in the first 30 days is the whole program. Everything after that is proof."

"That's not a result. That's a feeling. Replace [vague outcome] with [specific measurable thing]."

"The hook works because [specific mechanism]. The problem is [specific gap]. Replace [weak part] with [working alternative]."

"This post scored [number]/4 on the Invisibility Diagnostic. Here's what's missing: [specific element]. Add [concrete fix]."

"The parallel structure creates an in-group. The claim is vague. Replace [generic line] with [specific alternative that names the action]."

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

Opening with sycophancy before the real feedback. "Great question!" trains the listener to ignore the next sentence because they've learned it's filler. Lead with the position or the diagnosis.

Praising effort instead of outcome. "I can tell you worked hard on this" is meaningless. The recipient already knows they worked hard. Tell them what worked or what didn't.

Hedging specificity with softening language. "This might be just me, but I think maybe the hook could be a bit stronger" wastes 12 words to avoid committing. Say: "The hook has no claim. Add one."

Praising everything equally. If every piece of work gets "This is great!" the recipient learns nothing about what to do more of. Specificity is the mechanism that makes praise useful.

Using praise as a setup for critique. "I love the concept, but…" signals that the praise wasn't real. If the concept is strong, say so and stop. If it's not, skip the praise and name the gap.

Complimenting the person instead of the work. "You're so talented!" doesn't help them replicate the thing that worked. "The specificity in line three is what made this post book calls" does.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Most people think praise builds confidence. It doesn't. Specificity builds confidence.

The founder who hears "Great job!" walks away with nothing new. The founder who hears "The line about tracking pipeline instead of likes is the framework — that's the new positioning" walks away with an anchor.

The other contrarian position: withholding praise isn't harsh. It's efficient. If the work isn't ready, saying "This is solid!" wastes both people's time. Saying "This has no ICP — add one in the next draft" moves the work forward.

The third hot take: praise is analysis, not emotion. The goal isn't to make someone feel good. The goal is to tell them what's working so they can do it again on purpose.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

The recipient quotes your feedback back to you three weeks later as the thing that unlocked the shift.

Your comments on LinkedIn posts get replied to more than generic "Love this!" comments because you added a new angle or asked a question that deepened the original point.

Clients implement the feedback within 24 hours instead of sitting on it because the fix was concrete enough to act on immediately.

Workshop participants cite the specific line you praised as the new standard they're holding their work to.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

Disagreement is not the enemy of the relationship. Silence is.

The moment you stop pushing back on a client who's headed toward a decision that will cost them time, money, or credibility, you're no longer serving them. You're serving your own comfort.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Most consultants lose clients not because they pushed back too hard, but because they didn't push back at all.

They nod along. They take the brief. They execute what was asked for instead of what was needed. Then the client gets mediocre results, blames the execution, and moves on.

The consultant tells themselves it was the client's fault for not listening. But the truth is simpler: the consultant never spoke up.

Pushback done right doesn't damage trust. It builds it. Because the client learns you'll tell them the truth even when it's uncomfortable. That you care more about their outcome than your invoice.

The mechanism here is simple: clients hire you because they don't have the answer. If they knew what to do, they wouldn't be paying you. So when they come in with a plan that's wrong, and you execute it anyway, you've just become expensive labour instead of a strategic partner.

The cost of not pushing back shows up three ways. First, the engagement produces weak results and nobody can figure out why. Second, the client loses confidence in your judgment because you never exercised any. Third, you train yourself to be a yes-person, which makes every future engagement harder because you've lost the muscle for disagreement.

Who suffers? The client suffers because they paid for strategy and got compliance. You suffer because you delivered work you knew wouldn't land. And the next consultant suffers because the client now believes "consultants just do what you tell them."

The leverage of getting it right is massive. One well-timed pushback in week one can save six weeks of wasted work. One honest "this won't work" can redirect an entire engagement toward the thing that will actually move the needle.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

The most common place pushback shows up is in the first strategy call when the client explains what they want built.

They'll say something like "I need 30 LinkedIn posts scheduled for the next month" or "I want a new website" or "Can you ghost-write my newsletter?"

The request sounds reasonable. It's specific. It's actionable. And it's almost always wrong.

Because what they actually need is positioning clarity, or an ICP they can speak to, or a content system that runs itself. But they're asking for the surface-level thing because they don't know the deeper problem yet.

If you take the brief and start executing, you'll deliver exactly what they asked for and they'll be disappointed. Because the 30 posts won't book calls. The website won't convert traffic. The newsletter won't build authority.

So the first pattern is: **push back on the brief, not the goal.**

Example from a past engagement: A founder came in asking for a "LinkedIn content calendar with daily posts." I asked "What's the outcome you're trying to get from daily posting?" They said "I want more inbound leads." I pushed back: "Daily posting won't get you leads if your positioning is unclear and your ICP is too broad. Let's start there."

They resisted at first. They wanted the calendar. But I held the line: "I can build you a calendar right now and you'll waste a month posting content that doesn't convert. Or we can spend two weeks getting your positioning tight, then build a content system that actually books calls. Which one do you want?"

They chose positioning. Three weeks later they had their first inbound call from a post. The calendar never would have done that.

The second pattern is: **push back when the client wants to skip the foundation work.**

Example from a past engagement: A client wanted to jump straight into building Claude Skills without doing the Voice DNA document. They said "I already know my voice, let's just start building."

I pushed back: "You might know your voice when you're speaking, but Claude doesn't. And if we skip the Voice DNA doc, every output Claude gives you will sound like AI, not you. Then you'll spend three times as long editing everything, and you'll blame the system instead of the setup."

They pushed back on my pushback: "Can't we just do a quick version?"

I held: "No. Because a quick version means I'm teaching Claude a half-version of your voice, which means every piece of content we build on top of that foundation is half-quality. It's not a shortcut. It's a trap."

They agreed. We spent four hours on the Voice DNA. Every Claude output after that required minimal editing.

The third pattern is: **push back when the client is optimizing for vanity metrics instead of pipeline.**

Example from a past engagement: A client was obsessed with getting more likes and comments on their LinkedIn posts. They wanted me to teach them "engagement hacks."

I pushed back: "Likes don't pay your bills. Are you getting booked calls from your content?"

They said no.

I pushed harder: "Then optimizing for likes is optimizing for the wrong thing. We need to rewrite your CTAs, tighten your ICP, and make every post a filtering mechanism. You'll probably get fewer likes. But you'll get more calls."

They didn't like hearing it. But they trusted the pushback. We rebuilt their content strategy around pipeline instead of vanity. Six weeks later they had four inbound discovery calls. Their engagement dropped by 20%. Their revenue opportunity went up by a low three-figure amount.

The fourth pattern is: **push back when the client wants to sound like everyone else.**

Example from a past engagement: A founder kept writing hooks that sounded like every other AI founder on LinkedIn. "AI is changing everything." "The future of work is here." Generic, safe, invisible.

I pushed back: "This sounds like a bot wrote it. And I know you didn't hire me to make you sound like a bot. What's the actual opinion you have that nobody else is saying?"

They said "I don't want to be too polarizing."

I pushed back again: "You're not polarizing. You're invisible. There's a difference. Polarizing means some people hate you. Invisible means nobody notices you at all. Which one is costing you more clients?"

That landed. They rewrote the hook with a real point of view. The post got half the likes and three DMs from qualified leads.

The fifth pattern is: **push back when the client is hiding behind process instead of making a decision.**

Example from a past engagement: A client kept saying "I need to think about it" every time we got to a decision point. Pricing, positioning, ICP, offer structure. Every conversation ended with "let me sit with this."

After the third call I pushed back: "You're not thinking. You're avoiding. What are you actually afraid of?"

Long pause.

Then they said: "I'm afraid of picking the wrong thing and wasting time."

I pushed back: "You're already wasting time by not picking anything. Sitting with it for two weeks isn't thinking. It's paralysis. Here's what we're going to do: pick one thing right now. We'll test it for 30 days. If it's wrong, we'll know in 30 days and we'll change it. But if you don't pick, you'll still be sitting here in 60 days with the same question."

They picked. We moved forward. The decision wasn't perfect but it was good enough to learn from.

The sixth pattern is: **push back when the client wants you to do the work they should be doing.**

Example from a past engagement: A client wanted me to write all their LinkedIn posts for them. They said "You're better at this than me, so why don't you just handle it?"

I pushed back: "Because then it's my voice, not yours. And your audience will feel it. They're following you, not me. If I write everything, you'll sound like a ghostwriter's version of yourself."

They pushed back: "But I don't have time to write."

I held: "That's why we're building you a system. You'll spend two hours a week instead of twelve. But you need to be in the driver's seat, not the passenger seat. Otherwise this doesn't scale after I'm gone."

They agreed. We built the system together. Six months later they're running it without me.

## Specific examples from the vault

**Example 1: The "I just need posts" client**

from a past engagement: A founder came in with a Google Doc full of content ideas. They wanted me to "just turn these into posts."

I read the doc. The ideas were fine. But there was no strategy. No ICP. No positioning. Just a list of topics.

I said: "These ideas won't work."

They were surprised: "Why not? They're all relevant to my audience."

I pushed: "Who is your audience? Name one specific person."

They couldn't. They said "founders" and "business owners" and "people who want to grow."

I pushed harder: "That's not an audience. That's everyone. If you post to everyone, nobody listens. So before we turn these into posts, tell me: who is the one person you're trying to reach, and what is the one problem you're solving for them?"

They got defensive: "I don't want to narrow it down too much. I don't want to lose opportunities."

I pushed back one more time: "You're not losing opportunities by narrowing. You're creating them. Because right now you sound like everyone else. And everyone else is invisible."

They sat with that. Then they named one ICP. We rebuilt the content strategy around that one person. The engagement stayed the same but the DM quality went up 10x.

**Example 2: The "too expensive" objection**

from a past engagement: A prospect said "Your price is higher than I expected. I need to think about it."

I could have said "No problem, take your time." But that would have been a lie. Because "I need to think about it" after a price objection means "I'm not convinced this is worth the money."

So I pushed back: "Fair. Walk me through what feels expensive. The price, the scope, the fit, or the timing?"

They said: "The price. I was expecting something closer to K."

I pushed: "Got it. So if this was K instead of a low three-figure amount, you'd move forward today?"

They hesitated. "Probably."

I pushed harder: "That hesitation tells me price isn't actually the issue. What's the real concern?"

Long pause.

Then they said: "I'm worried I'll pay for this and it won't work."

Now we had the real objection. I addressed that directly: "That's fair. Here's the guarantee: we build the system together in 90 days. If by day 90 you don't have a working content engine that books at least one inbound call, we keep working until you do. No extra cost."

They moved forward that day.

**Example 3: The "skip the Voice DNA" client**

from a past engagement: A client wanted to skip the Voice DNA document and go straight to building Claude Skills.

I said no.

They pushed: "I already know my voice. I've been writing for years."

I pushed back: "You know your voice when you're writing manually. Claude doesn't. And if we skip the Voice DNA, every output Claude gives you will sound generic. You'll spend three times as long editing. And you'll blame the tool instead of the setup."

They said: "Can't we do a shorter version?"

I pushed again: "No. Because a short version means Claude only knows half your voice. Which means every output is half-quality. It's not a shortcut. It's a mistake."

They trusted the pushback. We spent four hours building the Voice DNA doc. Every Claude output after that was 90% ready to ship.

**Example 4: The "I need time to decide" loop**

from a past engagement: A client kept ending every call with "let me think about this." Three calls in a row.

On the fourth call I pushed back: "You're not thinking. You're avoiding. What are you actually afraid of?"

They said: "I'm afraid of picking the wrong positioning and having to start over."

I pushed: "You're already starting over every two weeks by not picking anything. Here's what we're doing: you're going to pick one positioning statement right now. We'll test it for 30 days. If it's wrong, we'll know fast and we'll change it. But if you don't pick, you'll still be here in 60 days with the same question."

They picked. We moved forward. The positioning wasn't perfect but it was good enough to learn from.

**Example 5: The "just write it for me" request**

from a past engagement: A client wanted me to ghostwrite all their LinkedIn posts.

I said no.

They pushed: "But you're better at this than me."

I pushed back: "Doesn't matter. Your audience is following you, not me. If I write everything, you'll sound like a ghostwriter's version of yourself. And your audience will feel it."

They said: "I don't have time to write."

I pushed again: "That's why we're building a system. You'll go from 12 hours a week to 2. But you need to stay in the driver's seat. Otherwise this doesn't scale when I'm gone."

They agreed. We built the system together. Six months later they're running it solo.

title: Scripts and exact phrases
text:
## Scripts and exact phrases

"This won't work" — said flatly, early, before they've invested time in the wrong direction.

"Walk me through what you're actually trying to achieve" — when the request doesn't match the goal.

"That's a symptom, not the problem" — when they're solving the surface issue instead of the root cause.

"You're not thinking, you're avoiding. What are you actually afraid of?" — when they keep saying "I need to think about it."

"If I do that for you, you'll sound like me, not you. And your audience will notice" — when they want you to ghostwrite everything.

"This is optimizing for the wrong metric" — when they're chasing likes instead of pipeline.

"That hesitation tells me [X] isn't actually the issue. What's the real concern?" — after any objection that includes a pause.

"I can do exactly what you're asking, and you'll be disappointed with the result. Or we can do the thing that will actually work. Which one do you want?" — when they're asking for the wrong deliverable.

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

**Mistake 1: Softening the pushback with "just my opinion" or "you might disagree but..."**

This dilutes the message. If you believe the client is wrong, say it directly. Hedging makes them think you're unsure, which makes them ignore the advice.

**Mistake 2: Pushing back without offering an alternative.**

"That won't work" by itself is just negativity. "That won't work, here's what will" is strategy.

**Mistake 3: Pushing back after they've already started executing.**

Too late. The pushback needs to happen at the decision point, not after they've invested two weeks in the wrong direction.

**Mistake 4: Pushing back on everything.**

If you disagree with every decision, you're not a strategist, you're just difficult. Pick the battles that actually matter to the outcome.

**Mistake 5: Using questions instead of statements.**

"Do you think that's the right move?" is weak. "That's the wrong move, here's why" is clear. Questions make it sound like you're unsure. Statements make it sound like you know.

**Mistake 6: Apologizing for the pushback.**

"Sorry, but I don't think that will work" signals that you think disagreeing is wrong. It's not. Drop the "sorry."

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Most people think pushback damages client relationships. The opposite is true.

Clients don't leave because you disagreed with them. They leave because you let them waste time and money on something you knew wouldn't work, then blamed them for not listening to advice you never gave.

The consultants who get fired are the ones who nod along, execute the brief, and deliver mediocre results. The consultants who get retained are the ones who push back early, redirect the strategy, and take responsibility for the outcome.

There's a belief in the consulting world that "the client is always right" and your job is to execute what they ask for. That's not consulting. That's labour. And it's why most consultants are replaceable.

The real job is to tell the client what they need to hear, not what they want to hear. And if you can't do that because you're afraid of losing the deal, you've already lost it.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

The client starts trusting your judgment over their own instincts.

They come to you with ideas and say "tell me if this is stupid" instead of "can you build this?"

They start referring to you as the person who "tells them the truth" instead of the person who "does the work."

The pushback conversations get shorter. Because they learn to expect disagreement and they come prepared to be redirected.

You close more deals. Because prospects sense that you care about the outcome more than the invoice.

The work itself gets better. Because you're solving the real problem instead of the surface symptom.

You stop getting scope creep. Because the client trusts that if something is out of scope, you'll tell them upfront instead of quietly doing it anyway.

And the biggest signal: they come back. Not because the first engagement was comfortable, but because it worked.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

If you would be embarrassed to say it on a sales call, you cannot ship it on LinkedIn.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

The read-aloud test is the kill switch that catches every piece of AI slop, every generic hook, every corporate buzzword before it leaves your hands.

Most founders type something into Claude, scan it with their eyes, think "yeah that looks fine," and hit publish. They never speak the words out loud.

That's the gap where bad content escapes.

Because written text lies to you. Your brain autocorrects. It fills in tone. It hears your voice reading the words, not a stranger's voice.

But when you force yourself to READ THE WORDS OUT LOUD, your body reacts. Your face tenses. You hear the fakeness. You catch the phrase that sounds like a LinkedIn influencer cosplaying as you.

The cost of skipping this test is compounding invisibility. Every post you ship that doesn't sound like you trains your audience to scroll past your name. Every generic hook conditions them to expect nothing interesting from you.

And the worst part: you don't see the damage immediately. You still get likes. You still get "great post!" comments from other people who are also posting AI slop.

But the qualified buyers stop reading. They pattern-match you as "another AI-generated founder account" and move on.

The read-aloud test protects your positioning. It's the last line of defense between "content that sounds like me" and "content that sounds like everyone else using the same prompt."

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

The read-aloud test shows up in three specific patterns across 1:1 coaching sessions.

**Pattern 1: The embarrassment reflex**

A founder brings me a LinkedIn post they're about to ship. I ask them to read it out loud on the Zoom call.

Within three sentences, they pause. Their face changes. They say "oh god, I would never actually say this."

The line is always something like "In today's fast-paced business landscape, leveraging AI can unlock transformative outcomes."

They typed it. Claude generated it. It looked professional on the screen. But the second they heard it in their own voice, their body rejected it.

[a past engagement] — founder brought a post with "game-changing" in the hook. I made him read it aloud. He stopped at the word, laughed, and said "I sound like a LinkedIn bot." Rewrote the hook as "Most founders are typing into Claude and getting Claude back. Here's what I do instead." Shipped that version. Booked two calls that week.

**Pattern 2: The vocal fry test**

I train clients to read their hooks out loud in a deliberately flat, bored voice. If the hook needs your enthusiasm to land, it's a weak hook.

The best hooks create tension or curiosity in the structure of the sentence itself, not in how you perform it.

[a past engagement] — one attendee read his hook with full vocal energy: "Are you ready to UNLOCK the POWER of AI in your business?" It sounded fine when he performed it.

I made him read it again in a monotone. Dead silence. The sentence had no structural interest. It was just a question that needed hype to work.

We rewrote it as: "I spent a low three-figure amount on AI tools last month. Used two of them." Same information. No performance required. The gap between a low three-figure amount and two creates the tension.

He read that version flat. Still interesting. That's the test.

**Pattern 3: The client-facing filter**

The question I ask in every content review session: "Would you send this post privately to your highest-paying client as a message?"

Not "would you post it publicly." Would you DM it to the person who just paid you 5K?

If the answer is no, the post doesn't ship.

[a past engagement] — founder wrote a post about "the five pillars of personal brand strategy." Looked polished. Hit all the formatting rules. No AI tells in the copy.

I asked the DM question. He said "No way. This sounds like a blog post. I'd never send this to a client."

We cut four of the five pillars. Kept one. Wrote 1,200 characters on that one pillar using a specific client example. The new version passed the DM test. That's the version that shipped.

title: Specific examples from the vault
text:
## Specific examples from the vault

**Example 1: The "unlock" purge**

[a past engagement] — I ran a voice audit on a founder's last 20 LinkedIn posts. Nine of them contained the word "unlock" or "unlocking."

"Unlock your potential." "Unlocking growth." "Unlock the power of AI."

I made him read all nine posts out loud in one sitting. By post four, he was laughing. By post seven, he said "I sound like a late-night infomercial."

The word "unlock" had become a crutch. He never noticed it on screen. But the second he heard himself say it nine times in ten minutes, the pattern became obvious.

We added "unlock" to his banned words list. He hasn't used it since. His engagement went up 40% the following month.

**Example 2: The sales call transcript as content test**

[a past engagement] — founder couldn't figure out why his LinkedIn posts weren't converting. He was posting three times a week. Good formatting. No obvious AI tells.

I asked him to send me his last three sales call recordings. I transcribed them. Then I printed out his last ten LinkedIn posts.

We laid them side by side.

On the sales calls: sharp, specific, opinionated. "Most agencies will tell you to post daily. I tell my clients to post twice a week and make every post count. Here's why..."

On LinkedIn: generic, hedged, vague. "Consistency is key in content marketing. Here are some tips to help you stay on track..."

Two completely different people.

I played back a 60-second clip from his best sales call — the moment where he told a prospect "if you're not tracking which posts book calls, you're just posting into the void."

Then I made him read his most recent LinkedIn post out loud.

The gap was immediate. He said "I would never say this shit on a call."

That became the new filter. Every post had to pass this test: "Is this something I would say on a sales call, word for word?"

His next post opened with "If you're not tracking which posts book calls, you're posting into the void." Direct lift from the sales call. Booked three discovery calls that week.

**Example 3: The mom test**

[a past engagement] — I teach a variation of the read-aloud test in workshops: read your post to your mom (or any non-founder family member).

If they don't understand it, your ideal client won't either.

One attendee read his hook: "Leverage AI to synergize your go-to-market motion and unlock scalable growth levers."

His mom's response: "What does that mean?"

He tried to explain. Took him four sentences to say "use AI to get more customers faster."

That became the new hook: "Use AI to get more customers faster. Here's how I did it in 90 days."

The mom test is a forcing function. It kills corporate jargon. It kills abstraction. It kills anything that requires a business degree to parse.

**Example 4: The phone voice note method**

[a past engagement] — founder was stuck writing hooks. Everything he typed felt flat.

I had him open his phone's voice recorder and record himself talking through the post idea like he was explaining it to a friend at a coffee shop.

No script. No editing. Just raw explanation.

He sent me the audio. I transcribed it. Pulled three sentences verbatim.

"Most founders think AI will replace them. I think it'll replace everyone around them. That's why I'm building an AI team, not an AI tool."

That became the post. Word for word. No polishing.

It performed 3x better than any post he'd written at his desk.

The phone voice note method is the read-aloud test in reverse. Instead of reading written text out loud to catch the fake stuff, you speak first and write second.

Your spoken voice is always closer to your real voice than your typed voice.

title: Scripts and exact phrases
text:
## Scripts and exact phrases

**"Read this like you're on a sales call."** 
The frame I use in every content review session. Not "read it out loud." Not "read it to yourself." Read it like you're on a Zoom call with a prospect who just asked you a question.

**"If you wouldn't say it to a client, don't say it to the timeline."** 
The positioning filter. Your LinkedIn feed is a sales channel. Every post is a conversation with a potential buyer. If the language wouldn't work in that conversation, it doesn't work on LinkedIn.

**"Your face just changed. What did you hear?"** 
The reaction I call out when a founder reads a line and their expression shifts. They always hear the problem before they can articulate it. Trust the face.

**"Read it flat. No enthusiasm. Does it still work?"** 
The vocal fry test. If the hook needs your energy to land, the structure is weak.

**"Would you send this as a DM to your highest-paying client?"** 
The client-facing filter. If the answer is no, the post doesn't ship.

**"That's a line you typed. Give me the line you'd say."** 
The rewrite prompt when someone reads a sentence that's clearly written-voice, not spoken-voice. I make them close the doc and just tell me what they meant.

**"You just said that in three words. Your post said it in twenty. Use the three."** 
The compression test. Spoken language is tighter. When you read a post out loud and then explain what it means, the explanation is always shorter than the original text.

**"Read the last five posts in a row. Out loud. Does it sound like the same person wrote all five?"** 
The consistency check. Most founders have three different voices across their last ten posts because they're copying different prompts, different styles, different moods. Reading them consecutively makes the inconsistency obvious.

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

**Mistake 1: Reading silently in your head and calling it done** 
Your brain autocorrects when you read silently. You hear what you meant to write, not what you actually wrote. The only way to catch AI slop is to force it through your mouth.

**Mistake 2: Reading out loud but not listening** 
Some founders perform the test mechanically — they read the words, but they're not actually listening to how it sounds. The point isn't just vocalization. It's hearing your own voice say the words and noticing when your body rejects them.

**Mistake 3: Reading only the hook** 
The hook matters, but the body copy matters more. A great hook with a generic body is still a bad post. Read the entire thing out loud, start to finish, before you ship.

**Mistake 4: Reading after you've already published** 
The read-aloud test is a pre-publish filter, not a post-mortem. By the time you realize a post sounds wrong, 5,000 people have already scrolled past it. Do the test before you hit "Post."

**Mistake 5: Outsourcing the test to someone else** 
"I had my VA read it" doesn't count. You need to hear YOUR voice say the words. Your VA's voice tolerance is different. Your ear is the only one that matters.

**Mistake 6: Skipping the test on "short" posts** 
A three-sentence post can still sound like AI. Length doesn't protect you. Read everything out loud.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Most content advice tells you to "write like you talk."

That's wrong.

You should write like you talk to a client on a good call — not like you talk to your friend at a bar.

Spoken conversation is messy. It has filler words, false starts, tangents, verbal tics. If you transcribed a casual conversation verbatim and posted it on LinkedIn, it would be unreadable.

The read-aloud test isn't about capturing raw speech. It's about capturing the TONE and CLARITY of your best professional conversation.

The version of your voice that shows up when you're explaining something important to someone who's paying attention.

That voice is tighter than casual speech but looser than formal writing. It's the sweet spot.

The other contrarian take: not every post needs to pass the read-aloud test.

Some content formats are deliberately written-voice. Long-form breakdowns. List posts. Frameworks. These aren't meant to sound like spoken conversation. They're meant to be scanned, not read aloud.

The read-aloud test applies primarily to hooks, stories, and opinion posts — the content types that depend on voice and tone to land.

If you're writing a "7 ways to improve your sales process" post, the read-aloud test is less relevant. That's a reference document. It lives or dies on structure and clarity, not voice.

But if you're writing "Here's why most founders are wrong about pricing," you need to read it out loud. Because that post is selling a point of view, and point of view lives in voice.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

When the read-aloud test becomes a habit, you start catching problems before they're problems.

You type a sentence. You hear it wrong before you even finish typing. You delete it and start over.

The filter moves upstream. You're no longer catching bad posts at the review stage. You're catching bad LINES at the drafting stage.

Your typing rhythm changes. You write shorter sentences. You cut more. You default to simpler words.

Observable signal: your editing time drops by 50%. When every sentence is written in spoken-voice from the start, you spend less time rewriting.

Another signal: your engagement starts matching your effort. Posts you spent 20 minutes on perform the same as posts you spent 90 minutes on, because the 20-minute posts sound like you and the 90-minute posts sound like a content strategist.

The ultimate signal: people start quoting you back to yourself. In discovery calls. In DMs. In replies.

When someone says "I saw your post about X, and the line you wrote about Y — that's exactly what I needed to hear," that's confirmation the voice is landing.

Before the read-aloud test becomes a habit, nobody quotes you. They say "I saw your post" but they don't remember a single line.

After the test becomes a habit, specific lines stick. Because they sound like something a real person would actually say.
