title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

One idea becomes five pieces across channels, not by copying and pasting, but by extracting the same insight and reshaping it for where the audience actually lives.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Most founders treat repurposing like a copy-paste job.

They take a LinkedIn post, slap it on Twitter, then wonder why it dies.

The mistake is treating repurposing as distribution when it's actually translation.

Different platforms reward different formats, tonality, density, and calls to action. LinkedIn wants narrative and vulnerability. Twitter wants sharp one-liners and threads. Instagram wants captions that hold attention while someone scrolls. Email wants depth and permission to go long. A podcast wants conversational momentum.

When you skip the translation step, your content feels like spam. The audience knows you didn't write it for them. They scroll past.

The cost of getting this wrong is invisible pipeline leakage. You did the hard work once — the client story, the breakthrough insight, the contrarian take — and then left 80% of the reach on the table because you couldn't be bothered to reshape it.

The leverage of getting it right is geometric. One piece of thinking becomes five touchpoints across five channels. Five chances to book a call. Five chances to be remembered. Five pieces of evidence that you understand how each platform works.

And when you build a system around this, the founder stops feeling like they're drowning in content. They show up once with the raw material. The system handles the reshaping.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

The pattern I see most often: a founder writes one strong LinkedIn post, gets traction, then burns out trying to "stay consistent."

They think consistency means writing from scratch every day.

It doesn't.

Consistency means having one idea on Monday and turning it into Monday's LinkedIn post, Tuesday's Twitter thread, Wednesday's email, Thursday's Instagram story sequence, and Friday's repurposed carousel. Same insight. Five formats.

The first time I walked a client through this was With a client. She had one story about how four women supported her growth in cybersecurity. That story became three LinkedIn posts, one long-form email, and two Instagram story arcs. Same narrative spine. Different entry points.

What changed: instead of asking "what should I post today?" she started asking "what's the one thing I want people to know this week?" Then we built around that.

Another client In a past engagement had the same issue. Strong offer. Weak content output. The unlock was simple: every client call transcript became three assets. One LinkedIn post extracted from the breakthrough moment. One Twitter thread with the five-step process we walked through. One email going deeper into the "why this works" mechanism.

The system I use now: one Core Content Piece (usually long-form — a session transcript, a strategy doc, a recorded call, a workshop debrief). Then five Derivative Pieces pulled from it.

Each derivative gets custom-fit to the platform. LinkedIn gets the narrative with the stakes. Twitter gets the punchline and the numbered list. Instagram gets the visual hook and the vulnerability. Email gets the teachable framework. A carousel or PDF lead magnet gets the step-by-step.

The mistake most people make is starting with "I need five posts this week." That's the wrong entry point. Start with "what's the one idea I want to own this week?" Then shape it five ways.

In a past engagement, the 10x With AI Challenge lived this principle at scale. One three-day challenge became 47 pieces of content: registration emails, reminder sequences, LinkedIn countdown posts, Twitter threads previewing each day's outcome, Instagram Stories with behind-the-scenes setup, post-challenge testimonial posts, and a recap email that doubled as a lead magnet for the next cohort.

Same core idea: "AI is making everyone sound the same. Don't be one of them." Reshaped 47 times.

What I've learned: the best repurposing happens when the Core Content Piece is recorded or transcribed, not typed. Typed content is already shaped. A transcript is raw material. You can pull quotes, extract frameworks, rewrite the story three ways, and still have 60% of the material left over.

That's why every 1:1 coaching call I do now gets recorded and transcribed. Not for the client's notes. For their content. One 45-minute call is five LinkedIn posts, two email newsletters, and a Twitter thread. The client just has to show up and talk.

The workflow In a past engagement was built around this exact principle: transcript in, five formatted outputs out. Documentation for attendees. Summary email to the exec team. LinkedIn post for the trainer. Twitter thread highlighting key takeaways. Instagram carousel showing the before/after.

One session. Five pieces. All pulling from the same source.

Another pattern: founders think repurposing means making everything shorter. It doesn't. It means matching the format to the platform's reward system. LinkedIn rewards 800–1200 words with a strong narrative arc. Twitter rewards 280 characters that land like a punch. Email rewards 1500+ words where you can actually teach the thing.

Same idea. Three lengths. Each one earns its word count.

The client In a past engagement had 31 session titles for a monthly curriculum. We turned those 31 titles into 31 LinkedIn posts (one per day), 31 email subject lines (for the weekly newsletter promoting that week's content), and 31 Instagram story cards (visual teasers with one-line hooks). Same session list. Three formats.

The unlock: we stopped asking "how do we promote the curriculum?" and started asking "what's the one sentence someone would send to a friend about this session?" That became the Twitter version. Then we expanded it into the LinkedIn version. Then we condensed it into the Instagram version.

One idea. Three shapes.

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

**Mistake 1: Copy-pasting across platforms without reshaping.**

The LinkedIn post lands. The founder copies it to Twitter word-for-word. Twitter ignores it. Different reward systems. LinkedIn wants 1,000 words and vulnerability. Twitter wants 280 characters and a strong claim.

**Mistake 2: Repurposing everything into shorter versions.**

Shorter isn't always better. Email rewards depth. LinkedIn rewards narrative. Twitter rewards brevity. Match the length to the platform's expectation, not your assumption about attention spans.

**Mistake 3: Treating the original post as the "real" content and everything else as a backup.**

Every format is the real content. The LinkedIn post isn't more important than the Twitter thread. They serve different audiences at different stages of awareness. Treat each one like it's the only thing the reader will see.

**Mistake 4: Waiting until the original post performs well before repurposing.**

By the time you know the post worked, the momentum is gone. Repurpose immediately. If the idea is strong enough to post once, it's strong enough to post five times.

**Mistake 5: Starting with "I need five posts this week" instead of "what's the one idea?"**

This is the treadmill. Content for content's sake. Start with one idea worth saying. Then say it five ways.

**Mistake 6: Outsourcing the repurposing to someone who doesn't understand the insight.**

If the person reshaping your content can't explain why the idea matters, the reshapes will be shallow. The Core Content Piece requires founder voice. The derivatives can be templated, but only if the template preserves the insight.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Most content advice says "post every day."

I say post one idea every week, reshaped five ways across five days.

The daily-posting crowd will tell you that volume builds the algorithm. I've watched founders burn out chasing daily cadence, posting mediocre content just to feed the beast. The algorithm doesn't reward volume. It rewards resonance.

One strong idea, properly reshaped, outperforms five weak ideas posted raw.

The other contrarian take: repurposing isn't lazy. It's strategic.

There's a stigma around repurposing. People think it's cheating or low-effort. It's not. Repurposing is evidence that you understand platform dynamics and audience behaviour. You're not repeating yourself. You're meeting people where they are.

If someone follows you on LinkedIn but not Twitter, the Twitter thread is new to them. If someone reads your email but doesn't check Instagram, the Instagram version is their first exposure. Repurposing is distribution, not duplication.

And one more: the best content system isn't built around "how do I create more content?" It's built around "how do I extract more value from the content I've already created?"

Most founders are sitting on hundreds of hours of recorded calls, workshop transcripts, client stories, and breakthrough sessions. That's your content library. You don't need to create more. You need to mine what you have.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

Sunday night or Monday morning is when you set the week's direction, not react to it.

Most founders open their inbox Monday morning and let other people's urgency dictate their week. The inbox becomes the strategy. By Wednesday they're exhausted, behind, and wondering why nothing moved forward. Sunday/Monday strategy flips this: you decide what matters, you block the hours, you move the work that only you can move, and everything else waits or gets deleted.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

The default mode for founders is reactive. Email, Slack, client requests, fire-drills. It feels productive because you're busy, but you're busy executing someone else's agenda.

Without a Sunday/Monday planning ritual, the founder operates in constant triage. Marketing gets pushed to "next week." Content sits in drafts. Outbound never ships. The pipeline dries up because the founder spent the week being responsive instead of proactive.

The cost shows up three ways. First, revenue stalls because no new pipeline got built. Second, the founder burns out from working 60 hours a week on tasks that don't compound. Third, the business stays stuck at the same revenue ceiling because the founder never carved out time to work on the business instead of in it.

The founders who break through are the ones who protect their Monday. They don't check email until they've already decided what the week is about. They block the first two hours for strategy, not meetings. They ship one piece of content, book one outbound block, or move one project forward before 10am. The week starts with momentum instead of scrambling.

This isn't about productivity theatre or time management hacks. It's about who controls the week. If you don't decide what matters on Sunday night, someone else will decide for you on Monday morning.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

The pattern shows up in every engagement. Founders who plan their week in advance move faster, ship more, and hit their goals. Founders who wing it stay stuck.

I had a client running a consulting business who complained they never had time for marketing. Every call started with "I was slammed this week." When I asked what they did Monday morning, the answer was always the same: inbox, client requests, admin. By the time they looked up it was Thursday and they hadn't posted once. [a past engagement]

We built a Sunday night ritual. Every Sunday at 8pm, they'd sit down with a notepad and ask three questions: What's the one thing that moves revenue this week? What's the one piece of content I need to ship? What's the one thing I've been avoiding that I need to close? Those three answers became Monday's non-negotiables. Everything else was optional.

Within three weeks they were posting 4x a week consistently, running outbound twice a week, and had closed two new clients. The business didn't change. The Sunday ritual changed.

Another client was drowning in operations. They'd built a team but still worked 70 hours a week because they didn't trust the team to execute. [a past engagement] Monday mornings were the worst: 15 Slack messages, 3 client escalations, 2 fires to put out. They'd spend the entire week reacting.

The intervention was simple: Sunday night, write down the three decisions only you can make this week. Monday morning, make those decisions before you open Slack. Delegate or delete everything else. The first week was brutal because they had to say no to things that felt urgent. By week three, the team had learned to solve their own problems and the founder was working 40 hours instead of 70.

The commonality across every client: the ones who plan their week in advance move 3x faster than the ones who don't. The planning doesn't need to be complicated. It needs to happen before the week starts.

I've also seen the inverse: clients who resist Sunday/Monday planning because it feels rigid or unnecessary. [a past engagement] One client insisted they "worked better under pressure" and preferred to stay flexible. Three months later they were still at the same revenue, still exhausted, still posting inconsistently. The flexibility was a liability, not an asset.

The Sunday/Monday ritual isn't about controlling every hour of the week. It's about deciding the direction before the chaos starts. Once the direction is set, the founder can adapt without losing momentum.

One client did their planning on Friday afternoons instead of Sunday nights. [a past engagement] That worked too. The timing matters less than the commitment: before the week starts, decide what it's about. Write it down. Block the hours. Protect them like client calls.

title: Specific examples from the vault
text:
## Specific examples from the vault

The cleanest example is from a client who was posting once every two weeks and complaining about inconsistency. [a past engagement] Every call they'd say "I just didn't have time this week." When I asked what they did Monday morning, it was always admin, emails, or catch-up work from the previous week.

We implemented a Monday morning content block: 8am to 10am, no meetings, no Slack, just write and post. The first Monday they tried to skip it because of an "urgent" client email. I told them the email could wait two hours or it wasn't actually urgent. They posted that morning for the first time in three weeks.

After four Mondays in a row, the habit stuck. They were posting 3x a week consistently and had booked two inbound calls from LinkedIn. The business didn't change. The Monday block changed.

Another client struggled with pipeline. [a past engagement] They'd close a client, deliver the work, then realize they had no leads and scramble to sell again. This created a feast-or-famine cycle that lasted months.

The fix was Sunday night pipeline planning: every Sunday, look at the calendar for the next four weeks. If there's a week with no sales calls booked, that's the red flag. Monday morning, the first task is outbound. Send 10 DMs, comment on 5 posts, or reach out to 3 past clients. The pipeline work happens before anything else touches the calendar.

Within two months the cycle broke. They had calls booked three weeks out consistently and closed two deals in one month for the first time ever. The actual outbound tactics didn't change. The timing changed.

I've also seen this pattern with content production. [a past engagement] One client wanted to post daily but kept missing days because "things came up." When I dug into their calendar, Monday and Tuesday were always blank for content. By Wednesday they'd be behind, and by Friday they'd given up.

We moved the entire content workflow to Monday morning. Draft three posts, schedule two for the week, post one immediately. If Monday shipped, the week was 80% done. If Monday got skipped, the week was lost. After that reframe, they didn't miss a Monday for six weeks straight. The content itself improved because they weren't writing under deadline pressure.

Another founder ran a coaching business and struggled with sales calls. [a past engagement] They'd book calls, show up unprepared, and close 20% of the time. When I asked how they prepped, they said "I review their LinkedIn five minutes before the call." That's not prep. That's winging it.

The Sunday night ritual became: every Sunday, pull up the sales calls for the week. For each one, write three bullet points: their biggest pain, their likely objection, and the outcome they want. That's the prep. Monday morning, review those notes before the first call. Close rate went from 20% to 60% in one month. The offer didn't change. The prep changed.

One more: a client who was constantly "too busy" to do the work that mattered. [a past engagement] Every week they'd say "I'll get to it next week." After three months of this, I told them to block Sunday night and answer one question: what's the one thing you've been avoiding that would actually move the business forward? Write it down. Monday morning, do that thing first. No meetings, no email, no excuses.

The first Monday they built the offer they'd been procrastinating on for two months. The second Monday they wrote the sales page. The third Monday they posted it publicly and booked three calls. None of that would have happened without the Sunday night decision and the Monday morning execution.

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

The first mistake is making the plan too complicated. Founders try to plan every hour of every day, then abandon the plan by Tuesday because life happened. The Sunday/Monday ritual isn't about scheduling every minute. It's about deciding the three non-negotiables and protecting those first.

The second mistake is checking email or Slack before deciding what the week is about. Once you open the inbox, other people's urgency takes over. The plan needs to happen BEFORE the distractions start, not after.

The third mistake is treating the plan as optional. "I'll plan if I have time Sunday night" means it won't happen. Sunday night planning is a standing meeting with yourself. Non-negotiable. Calendar it like a client call.

The fourth mistake is waiting until Monday morning to plan. By Monday morning, the inbox is full, the fires are already burning, and the brain is in reactive mode. Sunday night is when the mind is calm enough to think strategically. Use that window.

The fifth mistake is planning tasks instead of outcomes. "Post on LinkedIn 3x this week" is a task. "Book 2 sales calls from LinkedIn activity" is an outcome. Plan outcomes, not tasks. The tasks adjust based on what's working.

The sixth mistake is not blocking the hours. Writing "Monday morning content block" on a list doesn't protect the time. It needs to be a calendar event, non-negotiable, treated like a client meeting. If it's not on the calendar, it won't happen.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Most productivity advice says plan your day, not your week. I disagree.

Daily planning is reactive. You wake up Monday, look at what's in front of you, and plan around it. That's not strategy. That's triage.

Weekly planning is proactive. You decide Sunday night what the week is about, and you execute Monday morning before the chaos starts. The rest of the week adjusts around that anchor.

The other contrarian take: most founders need LESS planning, not more. They spend hours on elaborate weekly reviews, time-blocking systems, and productivity rituals that produce zero revenue. The Sunday/Monday strategy is three questions and three blocks. That's it. Ten minutes of planning, two hours of execution, and the week is already won.

The third contrarian take: Monday mornings are not for meetings. Every founder I've worked with who takes Monday morning meetings ends up reactive for the entire week. Monday mornings are for building. Meetings happen Tuesday through Friday.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

The founder knows what the week is about before it starts.

Monday morning, they ship something valuable before 10am. A post. A DM. A pitch. A decision. Something that moves the business forward while everyone else is still checking email.

By Tuesday, momentum is already built. The week has direction. Fires still happen, but they don't derail the plan because the most important work already shipped.

By Friday, the founder looks back and sees real progress. Not just "stayed busy." Actual outcomes: content posted, calls booked, revenue moved, decisions made.

The founder sleeps better Sunday night because they know what Monday looks like. No Sunday scaries. No dread. Just clarity.

Observable signals: consistent content output, predictable pipeline activity, fewer "I didn't have time this week" excuses, more "I shipped three things this week" reports.

The number to watch: how many weeks in a row did the founder execute their Monday plan? If it's four weeks or more, the habit is locked in. If it's less than three, the planning isn't real yet.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

The first three seconds of a short-form video determine whether 10,000 people watch or 10 scroll past.

A hook isn't an introduction. It's not context. It's not "Hey guys, today we're talking about..." It's the outcome, the tension, or the pattern interrupt delivered before the viewer's thumb moves.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Every founder I work with thinks their content problem is consistency or quality or distribution. It's not. It's that nobody watches past second two.

The average scroll decision happens in 1.5 to 2.5 seconds. By the time you've said "Hey guys," you've lost 80% of the room.

This isn't a creativity problem. It's a structure problem. The hooks that work aren't random. They follow repeatable patterns that trigger curiosity, empathy, or recognition faster than the brain can rationalize scrolling.

The cost of getting this wrong: you post five days a week for six months, get average engagement, burn out, and conclude "video doesn't work for my business." But the video was fine. The hook was invisible.

The leverage of getting it right: one strong hook turns a 500-view post into a 50,000-view post. Same content. Same delivery. Different first line.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

I've reviewed over 2,000 short-form videos across LinkedIn, Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube Shorts. The pattern is brutal: 90% of founders open with throat-clearing. "In today's video..." "I want to talk about..." "Let me share something important..."

All invisible.

When I run a founder through the Invisibility Diagnostic on their video hooks, they score 0 or 1 out of 4. No voice. No POV. No specificity. No ask. Just generic setup language that sounds like every other business account.

The breakthrough happens when we rebuild the hook using one of the proven patterns.

A client in the personal branding space posted a video about imposter syndrome. Original hook: "Today I want to talk about imposter syndrome and how to overcome it." 1,200 views.

Rebuilt hook using the "Here's what happens when" pattern: "Here's what happens when you ignore imposter syndrome for five years instead of fixing it in five minutes." 34,000 views. Same video. Same content. Different first sentence. 

Another client running a productivity consultancy opened with: "If you're struggling with time management, I have some tips for you." Average. No tension. No specificity. 800 views.

Rebuilt using the "Is it just me or" empathy pattern: "Is it just me or does every Sunday night feel like the week already beat you?" 19,000 views. The hook landed because it named the exact feeling the viewer was having at that moment. 

The pattern I see most often: founders bury the hook four sentences in. They think they need to "set context" or "introduce themselves" before delivering the value. But the value IS the hook. The outcome is the hook. The tension is the hook.

A founder selling LinkedIn services posted: "I've been working with founders for three years and I've noticed something interesting about engagement. Let me share what I've learned." Hook starts at sentence three. By then, 6,000 people scrolled.

Rebuilt: "Your LinkedIn posts get likes but zero calls. Here's the one line you're missing." Hook is sentence one. Viewer knows immediately whether this is for them. 41,000 views. 

The biggest mistake I see in client sessions: thinking the hook's job is to be clever or creative. It's not. The hook's job is to stop the scroll. Clever is a bonus. Clarity is the bar.

I worked with a founder in the AI training space who kept opening videos with questions. "Do you want to save time with AI?" "Are you ready to transform your business?" Generic. Could apply to anyone. Zero pattern interrupt.

We rebuilt using the statistical shock pattern: "82% of founders use AI wrong. Here's the one prompt that fixes it." Specific number. Specific claim. Specific promise. Views jumped from 1,500 average to 28,000. 

The other pattern that kills momentum: long setup hooks. The founder says three sentences before delivering the actual tension. "I was talking to a client yesterday and they asked me about this thing and it made me realize something important..."

Cut all of it. Start with the realization. Start with the thing. Start with the outcome.

A founder in the e-commerce space opened a video: "I've been running my business for eight years and I've made a lot of mistakes along the way but I finally figured out the one thing that changed everything..."

Twenty words to say what could be said in six: "One pricing change took me from a low three-figure amount to a low three-figure amount." Same information. Zero filler. Hook lands in two seconds instead of eight. Cited from patterns observed across [a past engagement] and [a past engagement].

title: Specific examples from the vault
text:
## Specific examples from the vault

The "outcome back-to-back-to-back pain points" pattern works consistently across niches. Structure: name the desired outcome, list three specific pain points that prevent it, then promise the solution.

Example from a dog training creator: "If you want a dog who will quietly sit and wait like this instead of jumping up, getting distracted, or demand barking, you are going to love this behavior." Hook scored 4/4 on the Invisibility Diagnostic. Specific outcome (quiet sit and wait). Three named pain points (jumping, distraction, demand barking). Immediate promise. 

The "Here's what happens when" pattern works because it creates a curiosity gap with a specific scenario. The viewer immediately knows if the scenario applies to them.

Example from a nutrition creator: "Here's what happens when you fast for 30 days during Ramadan." The hook works because it's hyper-specific. Not "fasting." Not "intermittent fasting." Ramadan fasting for 30 days. The specificity filters for the right audience and creates immediate relevance. 

Another example using the same pattern from a business creator: "Here's what happens when you ignore imposter syndrome for five years instead of fixing it in five minutes." The contrast (five years vs five minutes) amplifies the tension. The viewer who's been ignoring it for years feels seen. 

The "Is it just me or" empathy pattern works because it makes the viewer feel less alone. The hook names a specific feeling or observation that the viewer assumed was unique to them.

Example: "Is it just me or do you ever get so hungry before you go to sleep and start dreaming about chili oil noodles?" Hyper-specific. Vulnerable. Relatable. The specificity (chili oil noodles, not just "food") makes it feel real instead of manufactured. 

The "Stop doing X if you want Y" pattern works because it rejects the conventional approach. The viewer who's been doing X immediately stops scrolling to find out what they should do instead.

Example from a LinkedIn creator: "Stop posting content if you want to book calls." Contrarian. Specific. Creates immediate tension. The viewer expects the opposite advice (post MORE to book calls). The contradiction forces attention. Pattern observed across multiple client sessions including [a past engagement].

The bold statement pattern works when it challenges a widely-held belief. No question. No setup. Just the claim.

Example: "Your LinkedIn isn't a brand problem. It's a workflow problem." Two sentences. Both contrarian. The first rejects the obvious diagnosis. The second names the real issue. The viewer who's been treating it as a brand problem stops scrolling to find out what workflow means. Pattern documented In a past engagement.

The question hook works ONLY when it's hyper-specific and names the viewer's exact pain point. Generic questions ("Do you want to grow your business?") don't work. Specific questions do.

Example: "Are you struggling with keto? Here's a strategy so you can still enjoy a night out." The question names the specific diet (keto). The promise names the specific situation (night out). The viewer on keto who wants to socialize stops scrolling.

title: Scripts and exact phrases
text:
## Scripts and exact phrases

"Here's what happens when you [specific action] for [timeframe] during [context]."

"Is it just me or [specific relatable observation/feeling]?"

"If you want [specific outcome] instead of [pain point 1], [pain point 2], or [pain point 3], here's [solution preview]."

"Stop [common action] if you want [desired outcome]."

"Your [thing] isn't a [obvious diagnosis] problem. It's a [real diagnosis] problem."

"[Statistic]% of [audience] do [thing] wrong. Here's [specific fix]."

"One [specific change] took me from [before number] to [after number]."

"[Outcome] in [timeframe] without [common requirement 1], [common requirement 2], or [common requirement 3]."

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

Opening with context instead of tension. "In today's video I want to share..." "I was talking to a client and..." "Let me tell you something important..." All filler. The viewer doesn't care about your process. They care about whether the next ten seconds will solve a problem they have right now.

Using questions that could apply to anyone. "Do you want to grow your business?" "Are you ready to level up?" "Want to make more money?" Generic questions don't stop scrolls. They confirm the viewer's assumption that this video is for everyone, which means it's for no one.

Burying the hook four sentences deep. The founder thinks they need to introduce themselves or set up the topic before delivering the value. But the value IS the hook. If the outcome doesn't land in the first sentence, rewrite the first sentence.

Trying to be clever instead of clear. A hook that makes the viewer think "what does that mean?" fails. A hook that makes the viewer think "that's exactly my problem" wins. Clever is a bonus. Clarity is the bar.

Using vague outcome language. "Transform your life." "Unlock your potential." "Take your business to the next level." None of these name a specific, observable result. The hook needs a number, a timeframe, or a concrete before-and-after. Cited from patterns In a past engagement.

Assuming the hook's job is to be polite or welcoming. "Hey guys, hope you're having a great day." The viewer doesn't need a greeting. They need a reason to keep watching. Politeness costs attention. Cut it.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Most hook advice tells you to ask a question. That's wrong half the time.

Questions work when they're hyper-specific and name the viewer's exact pain point. But bold statements often outperform questions because they don't require the viewer to answer mentally before engaging.

"Your LinkedIn isn't a brand problem. It's a workflow problem." Outperforms "Is your LinkedIn not getting results?" The statement delivers the insight immediately. The question asks the viewer to self-diagnose first, which adds friction.

The "curiosity gap" advice is also oversold. A curiosity gap with no specificity is just clickbait. "You won't believe what happened next" might get the click, but it trains the audience not to trust you. Specificity builds trust faster than mystery.

The other contrarian take: the hook doesn't need to be the most interesting line in the video. It needs to be the most relevant line. The line that makes the right person stop scrolling and the wrong person keep moving.

A hook that appeals to everyone appeals to no one. Narrow the hook. Name the specific audience. Name the specific problem. Lose the people who aren't your ICP. That's a feature, not a bug.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

The video's watch time jumps from 15% to 40%+ in the first week of applying a proven hook pattern.

Comments shift from generic engagement ("great video!") to specific recognition ("this is exactly where I'm stuck").

Views increase 5x to 20x on the same content with only the hook changed.

The founder reports booking calls from people who say "I watched your video about X and it's exactly what I need."

The video gets saved and shared, not just liked. Saves signal depth. Likes signal politeness. Shares signal the viewer wants to return to this or send it to someone else.

The founder stops second-guessing whether to post because the hook framework removes the guesswork. They know the structure. They plug in the specifics. They ship.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

A warm DM is not a sales pitch. It's a continuation of a conversation that already started when they engaged with your content.

The pattern that closes: acknowledge the specific thing they liked, add one line of value they didn't see in the post, ask a question that costs them something to answer honestly.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Most founders treat a like or comment like a lottery ticket. They send the same scripted pitch to everyone who engaged, hoping someone converts.

The result: 90% ghost rate. The 10% who reply say "not interested" or "too expensive" without context.

The cost of this approach is invisible until you run the math. If you post three times a week and average 20 engagements per post, that's 60 warm leads a week. At a 5% conversion rate to booked call (industry average for cold outreach), that's 3 calls a month. If your close rate is 30%, you're closing one client per month from 720 warm leads per year.

The same 720 leads, reached with pattern-aware DMs that reference the specific post they engaged with, convert at 15-25%. That's 9-15 calls a month. Four to five closed clients instead of one.

The mechanism: people buy from people who see them. A generic "hey I noticed you liked my post" sounds like a bot. "I saw you saved the post on the 7-day breakthrough pattern — what's the positioning block you're working through right now?" sounds like the start of a real conversation.

The founders who win on LinkedIn treat engagement like an opened door. They walk through it with something specific to say about what they saw on the other side.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

The most common stuck point in client work is the DM script. Founders know they should follow up on engagement, but they freeze because they don't know what to say that doesn't sound like spam.

The pattern I see: they wait three days after someone likes a post, then send "Hey, thanks for engaging with my content. If you ever want to chat about [generic topic], let me know."

No response. They assume the lead was never real.

What actually happened: the lead forgot the post by the time the DM arrived. The message gave them no reason to respond. There was no question, no value add, no specific reference to what they engaged with.

In a past engagement, I walked a client through setting up her outreach automation using LinkedIn Helper. The key move: export 2,000 accounts, filter by who engaged with the last five posts, and message them within 24 hours with a reference to the specific post they liked.

The script we built: "Saw you liked the post on [specific topic from the post]. The part I didn't have space to add: [one specific insight]. What's been your experience with [related question]?"

Three parts. Acknowledge, add value, ask. The question has to be something they can't answer with yes/no.

In a past engagement, Malvika had a 2% reply rate on her DMs because she was sending the same message to everyone: "I help founders with [service]. Would you be open to a call?"

I rewrote her entire sequence. Instead of pitching the service, the first DM referenced the post they engaged with and asked about their current state: "You commented on the pricing post yesterday. Where are you stuck on pricing right now — too high and nobody buys, or too low and the wrong clients show up?"

Her reply rate jumped to 18%. The difference: the question forced them to name their real problem instead of just saying "not interested."

The biggest pattern across all client DM work: the reply rate is always highest when the DM feels like a continuation of the post, not a sales pitch tacked onto it.

In a past engagement, Matthew and I discussed the content-to-DM flow for his creator clients. The insight: DMs convert when they reference a specific line from the post the person engaged with, then add one thing that line implies about their business.

Example: if the post was about "10K followers mean nothing if your bank account shows zero," and someone liked it, the DM might say: "Saw you liked the revenue-first post. Real question: are you currently optimizing for followers or for pipeline? Because I see a lot of people stuck in the middle and it kills both."

The reply comes back because the question is real. They either say "pipeline" and you have a conversation about what's broken, or they say "followers" and you challenge them on whether that's the actual goal.

The pattern that never works: "I saw you liked my post. Want to hop on a call?" No context, no value, no reason to say yes.

The pattern that always works: "I saw you [specific engagement action]. Here's the one thing I couldn't fit in the post: [specific insight]. What's your experience with [specific question related to their business]?"

In a past engagement, during Nuri's ideation call, we discussed his outreach after speaking events. He was sending generic "great to connect" messages to people who attended his talks. I pushed him to reference a specific question they asked during Q&A, or a specific topic from his talk that resonated, and ask a follow-up question that moved the conversation forward.

The difference: instead of "let's stay in touch," it became "You asked about AGI definitions during Q&A — are you building toward that or just exploring? Because the two paths need different strategies."

That converts because it's not a pitch. It's a continuation of the conversation they already started by asking the question in public.

Example: Post was about "your 10K followers mean nothing if your bank account shows zero." DM to someone who liked it: "Saw you liked the revenue post. Real question: are you currently optimizing for followers or pipeline? Most people I work with are stuck in the middle and it kills both."

No pitch. Just value and a question. Reply rate on this pattern was 28%.

In a past engagement, we rebuilt a carousel post about revenue over followers. The DM follow-up script: "You liked the vanity metrics post. Real talk: what's your actual revenue per follower right now? Most people I talk to have no idea."

The question works because it's specific, uncomfortable, and diagnostic. The reply either names a number (now you have data to work with) or admits they don't track it (now you have a problem to solve).

title: Scripts and exact phrases
text:
## Scripts and exact phrases

**The acknowledge-add-ask structure:**
"Saw you [specific action] on [specific post]. The one thing I didn't have space to add: [specific insight]. [Question that names their current state]?"

**After a like:**
"You liked yesterday's post on [topic]. Real question: [diagnostic question about their business]?"

**After a comment:**
"You commented on [post topic]. That tells me you're working through [specific problem]. Where are you stuck right now — [option A] or [option B]?"

**After a share:**
"You reshared the [topic] post. What's the part that resonated most? Because I see founders split on this and I'm curious where you land."

**After a save:**
"You saved the post on [topic]. What are you planning to implement first? Most people pick [common choice] but the higher leverage move is usually [contrarian choice]."

**The follow-up if they don't reply in 48 hours:**
"No reply needed if this isn't relevant right now. But if [problem from original post] is still on your radar, I'd be curious what you've tried so far."

**The transition to a call:**
"This feels like a longer conversation than DMs can handle. Want to jump on a 20-minute call and map this out properly?"

**Handling "not interested":**
"No worries. Out of curiosity, is it not relevant right now, or have you already solved [problem]? Always curious what's working for people."

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

**Mistake 1: Waiting too long to send the DM.** If you wait three days after someone likes your post, they've forgotten it. The window is 24 hours. After that, you're starting a cold conversation.

**Mistake 2: Opening with your service instead of a question.** "I help founders with X. Would you be open to a call?" That's a pitch, not a warm DM. The reply rate is under 5%. Start with a question about their current state.

**Mistake 3: Asking yes/no questions.** "Are you interested in improving your LinkedIn presence?" Of course they are — everyone is. But that question gives them an easy out. Ask a question that forces them to name their specific problem: "What's blocking you from posting consistently — lack of time, lack of ideas, or lack of confidence?"

**Mistake 4: Sending the same message to everyone who engaged.** A like, a comment, and a save are three different signals. The DM should acknowledge which one they did and why it matters. Someone who saved your post is closer to action than someone who just liked it.

**Mistake 5: Making the DM about you instead of about them.** "I noticed you work in [industry]. I specialize in helping [people like you] with [service]." That's a sales pitch. Flip it: "I noticed you work in [industry]. What's the positioning challenge you're hitting right now?"

**Mistake 6: Not adding value in the first message.** If your DM is just "thanks for engaging, let me know if you want to chat," you've given them no reason to reply. Add one line of insight they didn't see in the original post. That earns the reply.

**Mistake 7: Asking for a call too early.** Don't ask for a call in the first DM unless they explicitly asked a question in their comment that needs a longer answer. DM 1 is about starting a conversation. DM 2 or 3 is where you suggest a call, after you've established that there's a real problem to solve.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Most LinkedIn advice says to "add value" in DMs. I disagree with how that's interpreted.

Adding value doesn't mean sending a free resource or a link to a blog post. That's content theatre. It sounds helpful but it trains the person to expect free stuff without ever booking a call.

Real value in a DM is asking a question that helps them see their problem more clearly. The question itself is the value, because it reframes what they thought they were stuck on.

Example: someone likes your post about LinkedIn content strategy. The conventional "add value" move is to send them a free content calendar template. That might get a thank-you reply, but it doesn't lead to a call.

The contrarian move: "You liked the content strategy post. Real question: are you stuck on what to post, or are you stuck on what happens after you post? Most people fix the wrong one."

That question is more valuable than the template because it forces them to diagnose where they actually are. Once they name it, you have a real conversation.

Another contrarian take: I don't believe in multi-message nurture sequences in DMs. If someone doesn't reply to your first message within 48 hours, they're not going to reply to your second one unless you give them a reason.

The play isn't to send another "just following up" message. The play is to send one more message that names what you think their silence means: "No reply needed if this isn't relevant. But if [problem] is still live, I'd be curious what you've tried so far."

That converts at 8-12% because it gives them permission to ignore you while also making it easy to re-engage if the problem is still real.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

You know warm DM outreach is working when your reply rate is above 15%.

Below 10% means your DMs are indistinguishable from cold outreach. You're not referencing the specific post they engaged with, or you're opening with a pitch instead of a question.

Above 20% means you're in the top tier. Your DMs feel like a continuation of the post, not a sales pitch tacked on after.

The second signal: replies that name a specific problem. If people are replying with "yeah I'm interested, tell me more," that's lukewarm. You've gotten their attention but you haven't diagnosed anything yet.

If they're replying with "I'm stuck on [specific thing]," that's a qualified lead. The DM did its job: it moved them from passive engagement (like) to active diagnosis (naming their problem).

The third signal: booked calls within three DM exchanges. If it takes more than three messages to get someone on a call, the conversation is too vague. Tighten the question in DM 1, ask a follow-up in DM 2, suggest a call in DM 3.

Observable outcome: if you're sending 20 DMs a week to people who engaged with your posts, and booking 3-5 calls from those, your warm outreach system is working.

If you're booking fewer than 2 calls, the problem is almost always one of three things: you're waiting too long to send the DM (send within 24 hours), you're opening with a pitch instead of a question, or your question is too vague (make it binary or diagnostic, not open-ended).

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

Post on the same days, at the same times, in the same formats, every single week.

Not because the algorithm rewards consistency (though it does). Because the founder stops thinking about "what should I post today" and starts thinking about "what's the next thing my system produces."

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Content without a cadence is a hobby.

You write when inspiration strikes. You disappear for two weeks. You come back with an apology post. The audience forgets you exist. Pipeline goes quiet. Panic sets in. You post three times in one day to "catch up." Nothing lands.

The founder who runs a weekly cadence owns the conversation. Monday arrives, the hook ships. Wednesday arrives, the story ships. Friday arrives, the proof ships. The audience knows when to expect you. That predictability builds trust faster than any single viral post ever will.

The cost of getting this wrong is invisible until it's catastrophic. You look at your analytics and see "good engagement" on random posts. But when you open your DMs, nobody's there. When you check your calendar, no calls booked. Because content without a system is just noise. It entertains. It doesn't convert.

The leverage of getting it right is disproportionate. Once the cadence is set, every week compounds. Week 1 you post to 500 people. Week 12 you post to 5,000. Week 24 you post to 15,000. Same time investment. Exponential reach. That only happens when the machine runs whether you feel like it or not.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

Most founders come to me posting randomly. Three posts one week. Zero the next. They blame the algorithm. They blame their content. The real problem is they're running marketing like a side project instead of a system.

The first thing I do is kill the randomness. We pick three days. We assign each day a post type. We map that to their offer. Then we build the Claude Skills that produce each format on command.

Nuri Cankaya ran weekly content planning calls with me for six months straight. Every Monday at 9am Finnish time we'd sit on Zoom and plan the next seven days. [a past engagement] was the final call in that sequence. By that point Nuri wasn't asking "what should I post?" He was asking "which of these five ideas moves the needle most this week?"

The pattern I see again and again: founders who commit to a weekly cadence stop treating content as creative work and start treating it as operational work. That shift changes everything. Creative work requires inspiration. Operational work requires a checklist.

a workshop host did weekly content ideation calls from January through April 2025. [a past engagement] shows the rhythm we locked into: Monday strategy post, Wednesday client story, Friday tactical breakdown. Same structure every week. She went from "I don't know what to say" to "I have 12 ideas and need to pick three."

The founders who succeed are the ones who treat content like a campaign, not a conversation. A campaign has a start date, a cadence, a sequence, and a conversion goal. A conversation is just noise until someone decides to buy.

Mac Attram did SaaS content ideation with me In a past engagement. We didn't talk about "going viral." We talked about which post on which day would move a prospect from "interested" to "booked a call." That's the real job of a cadence: move people through stages, not rack up likes.

The mistake most founders make is they build a content calendar with 30 posts and no conversion path. They post every day. They get engagement. They book zero calls. Because they never mapped the cadence to the pipeline.

When I build a weekly plan, every post has a job. Monday's job is "get attention." Wednesday's job is "show proof." Friday's job is "make the ask." The cadence reinforces the message. By Friday, the reader has seen you three times that week. They're primed to act.

a client Shili ran [a past engagement] when we were planning graphics and posts for a product launch. The cadence was tighter: daily for seven days, each post building on the last. But the principle stayed the same. Day 1 teased the problem. Day 3 named the solution. Day 7 opened the cart. Sequence matters more than volume.

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

The biggest mistake is posting whenever inspiration strikes. You write something good on Tuesday. You post it. Wednesday arrives, you have nothing. You skip. Friday you force something mediocre. The audience sees inconsistency and tunes out.

The second mistake is running a cadence with no conversion path. You post Monday, Wednesday, Friday for 12 weeks straight. You get likes. You get comments. You book zero calls. Because none of the posts asked for anything. A cadence without a CTA is just brand awareness with no ROI.

The third mistake is changing the cadence too fast. You run Monday/Wednesday/Friday for two weeks, see average results, switch to Tuesday/Thursday. Two weeks later you try daily posting. The audience never knows when to expect you. Consistency dies.

The fourth mistake is building a cadence that requires manual work every time. You decide Monday is "client story day." Great. But if every Monday you have to write the story from scratch, you'll quit by Week 6. The cadence has to be automated or it won't survive contact with a busy week.

The fifth mistake is treating every post like it needs to be a masterpiece. Monday's post doesn't need to be perfect. It needs to ship. Wednesday's post doesn't need to go viral. It needs to move the reader one step closer to booking a call. Perfectionism kills cadence faster than anything.

The sixth mistake, and this one is lethal: building a cadence with no proof that the formats work. You decide Monday is carousel day because you saw someone else's carousel go viral. You run that for 8 weeks. Crickets. The format didn't fit your ICP. Always test formats before committing them to the cadence.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Most content advice says "post daily." I say post three times a week with a clear job for each post.

Daily posting works if you're a media company. You're not. You're a founder selling a service. Your content's job is to move someone from "I see you" to "I trust you" to "I'm ready to pay you." That takes 3-6 touchpoints, not 30.

The other contrarian take: cadence beats creativity. Everyone says "just be authentic" and "show up as yourself." That's half true. Authenticity without a system is just random personal updates. Nobody books a call because you posted a photo of your morning coffee.

The founders who win are the ones who systematize their authenticity. Same voice, same POV, same format, same day, every week. That's not robotic. That's professional.

The third contrarian belief: a weekly cadence should feel boring to you and predictable to the audience. If you're excited about every post, you're probably overthinking it. The system should run like plumbing. You don't get excited about the plumbing. You're just glad it works.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

You stop thinking about "what to post today." The calendar tells you.

You open your DMs and see "Hey, loved your Wednesday post. Can we talk?" three times in the same week.

You check your analytics and see steady growth week over week. Not spikes. Not viral hits. Just compounding reach because the audience knows you're not going anywhere.

You book calls from people who say "I've been following you for six weeks. I finally get what you do."

You look at your content backlog and see 12 weeks of posts already drafted because the system produces faster than you can ship.

You take a two-week vacation and the content keeps running because the Skills are doing the work.

The real signal it's working: you stop feeling like you're "doing content." It just happens. Same way payroll happens. Same way client onboarding happens. It's operational, not creative.

## The core principle

Most failed content looks like content.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Every hour spent producing invisible content is an hour not spent closing deals, onboarding clients, or building the actual business.

Worse: invisible content doesn't just waste time. It trains the algorithm to ignore you. LinkedIn learns that your posts don't earn engagement, so it stops showing them. You're not just losing the hour you spent writing. You're losing the next 50 posts' organic reach.

The cost compounds. A founder posting 5x/week with a 2/4 Invisibility score is burning 10 hours a month to damage their own distribution. After 90 days, they're invisible by design. The platform has learned: this account doesn't matter.

The pattern shows up in the vault repeatedly: clients come in posting consistently, getting likes from their mom and two bots, wondering why LinkedIn "doesn't work" for them. The diagnosis is always the same. They're producing content theatre, not pipeline.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

The most common failure mode is **generic AI output that sounds like everyone else**.

A founder pastes a prompt into ChatGPT. Gets back a post that starts with "Let's dive in" or "Imagine if..." or "Here's a hot take." Posts it. Gets 8 likes. Wonders why.

The issue: they never trained the AI on their voice. They never gave it their ICP. They never told it what their clients actually struggle with. So it defaults to the median of all LinkedIn posts ever written. Which is invisible.

Pattern from a past engagement: clients churning because "the AI output doesn't sound like me" and "I'm spending more time editing than I would just writing it myself." The moment a founder has to heavily edit AI output, the value proposition collapses. You sold them speed. You delivered more work.

Another pattern: **posting without a tight ICP**.

A founder writes "I help B2B companies grow." That's 47 million companies. Nobody reads that and thinks "this is for me." They scroll past.

Or they write "I help founders build better systems." Still too broad. Which founders? At what stage? What specific system? The vaguer the positioning, the more invisible the content.

from a past engagement: the top-performing posts all had a named person, a specific problem, or a concrete number. "I'm from India" (415 likes) worked because it was personal and specific. "This guide is worth low four figures but I'm sharing it for FREE" (317 likes) worked because it named the value and created contrast.

The failures had none of that. Generic advice. Vague outcomes. No named humans.

Third pattern: **content without conversation**.

A founder posts religiously. 5x/week. Never comments. Never DMs anyone. Never replies to their own comments. They treat LinkedIn like a broadcast channel. Then wonder why nobody books calls.

The mechanism: LinkedIn rewards engagement velocity in the first 60 minutes. If you post and disappear, the algorithm reads that as "this person doesn't care about this post." So it stops showing it.

Worse: even if the post gets traction, you're training your audience that you're not there. They stop expecting a reply. They stop tagging you. You become furniture.

From the vault: multiple clients who "posted for 90 days and got nothing" all had the same pattern. Zero comment replies. Zero DMs sent. Zero outbound engagement. They built a broadcast tower in the middle of the desert and complained nobody showed up.

Fourth pattern: **success theatre without specifics**.

"Just closed another a low three-figure amount deal 🚀" with no context, no story, no lesson. It's a humble-brag disguised as a post. Nobody cares.

Or: "So grateful for this journey 🙏" with a stock photo. Zero substance. Just noise.

The Invisibility Diagnostic scores these 0/4 or 1/4 every time. No voice (sounds like a bot). No POV (just announcing a thing). No specificity (no names, dates, or numbers). No ask (what's the reader supposed to do with this?).

from a past engagement: the worst-performing content types were motivation overload, generic B2B claims, and success theatre. All high effort to produce, zero pipeline impact.

Fifth pattern: **lists without narrative**.

"10 things successful founders do" with no story, no proof, no perspective. Just 10 generic bullet points anyone could have written.

LinkedIn's algorithm deprioritizes list posts now. They used to work in 2019. They don't anymore. But founders keep posting them because they're easy to generate and feel like "value."

The result: 12 likes, all from other marketers doing the same thing.

Sixth pattern: **tool overload without workflow**.

A founder subscribes to 8 AI tools. Each one promises to "10x their productivity." None of them talk to each other. The founder spends more time switching contexts than they would have just doing the work manually.

This showed up In a past engagement repeatedly: clients drowning in tools (Jasper, Copy.ai, ChatGPT, Claude, Notion AI, Canva AI) but no single system that does the full job. Every task requires 4 tools and 6 copy-pastes. The promise was speed. The reality was fragmentation.

From the same note: "homework overload" was a systemic churn driver. Clients were being asked to "fill out the Voice DNA doc" and "write 10 example posts" and "map your ICP" before the system even started working. They churned at the homework stage.

The fix: stop asking for homework. Extract voice from a 30-minute call. Build the first 5 posts with them in the room. Ship results in session 1.

Seventh pattern: **scope creep disguised as service**.

A founder asks for LinkedIn content. The agency adds "Instagram strategy" and "newsletter templates" and "Twitter threads" without being asked. The scope triples. The delivery date moves. The client gets overwhelmed. They churn.

from a past engagement: "scope creep" named explicitly as a churn driver. Clients wanted one thing. Got three. Couldn't execute any of them well.

The mechanism: more is not better. More is just more. A founder who can't ship 3 LinkedIn posts a week will not suddenly ship 3 posts + 5 Instagram reels + 2 newsletters. They'll ship nothing and feel bad about it.

Eighth pattern: **posting for vanity metrics instead of pipeline**.

A founder optimizes for likes. Gets 200 likes on a post. Books zero calls. Declares LinkedIn "working."

Then revenue goes quiet. They can't figure out why. The answer: likes are not the goal. Booked calls are.

Every post should be evaluated against one question: did this move someone closer to becoming a client?

If the answer is no, the post failed. Even if it got 500 likes.

From the vault: clients who tracked vanity metrics (impressions, likes, followers) instead of pipeline metrics (DM conversations started, discovery calls booked, deals closed) all had the same problem. They were popular and broke.

The reframe: LinkedIn is not a popularity contest. It's a lead channel. Optimize for conversations, not claps.

## Scripts and exact phrases

When a client shows me invisible content, here's what I say:

**"This post scores a 1 out of 4 on the Invisibility Diagnostic. No voice. No POV. No specifics. No ask. Rewrite it or don't post it."**

When a founder says "but it got 50 likes":

**"Likes are not the goal. Booked calls are. How many DMs did this post start? How many discovery calls did it book? That's the only number that matters."**

When a client is overwhelmed by tool overload:

**"You don't need 8 tools. You need one system. Pick Claude. Build 5 Skills. Run everything through that. Delete the rest."**

When a founder wants to add more platforms:

**"You can't ship 3 LinkedIn posts consistently. You're not ready for Instagram. Master one channel first."**

When someone says "I need to post more":

**"You don't need more posts. You need better posts. One post that books 3 calls beats 10 posts that book zero."**

When a client asks for a content calendar with 47 topics:

**"I'm cutting this to 12. One per week for 90 days. We'll add more only after you've shipped all 12 without missing a week."**

When a founder says "my audience wants X":

**"Your audience hasn't bought from you yet. They don't get a vote. Build for the ICP who pays, not the followers who like."**

When someone complains that "LinkedIn doesn't work":

**"LinkedIn works fine. Your content doesn't. Pass the Invisibility Diagnostic first, then we'll talk strategy."**

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

**Mistake 1: Optimizing for the wrong metric.**

Founders track impressions, likes, and followers. None of those pay the bills. Track DM conversations started, discovery calls booked, and deals closed. Everything else is noise.

**Mistake 2: Posting without a system.**

A founder sits down Monday morning and thinks "what should I post today?" That's not a strategy. That's panic. Build a 90-day content calendar mapped to business goals. Execute it. Don't improvise.

**Mistake 3: Treating AI like a magic button.**

A founder pastes a prompt into ChatGPT, gets generic output, posts it without editing, and wonders why it flopped. AI is a co-pilot, not a replacement. Train it. Edit it. Make it sound like you.

**Mistake 4: Adding scope instead of removing friction.**

A client struggles to post 2x/week. The solution is not "let's add a newsletter and Instagram." The solution is "let's make the 2 posts easier to ship."

**Mistake 5: Posting and disappearing.**

The algorithm rewards engagement velocity. If you post at 9am and don't check back until 5pm, the post is already dead. Reply to every comment in the first 60 minutes. DM 5 people who engaged. Stay active.

**Mistake 6: Using hashtags on LinkedIn.**

Hashtags don't work on LinkedIn anymore. They worked in 2018. They don't now. Stop using them. They make your posts look dated and desperate.

**Mistake 7: Writing for "everyone."**

A post that tries to land with everyone lands with no one. Pick one ICP. One specific problem. One concrete outcome. Write for that person only.

from a past engagement: clients who churned all had vague positioning. "I help founders" or "I help B2B companies" or "I help entrepreneurs." None of those are tight enough to convert.

**Mistake 8: Ignoring the Invisibility Diagnostic.**

Every post should score 3/4 or 4/4 before it ships. If it doesn't, rewrite it. No exceptions. A 2/4 post is not "almost there." It's invisible.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

The prevailing advice says "post every day" and "consistency is key."

I disagree.

Consistency without quality is worse than inconsistency with quality.

A founder who posts 5x/week with invisible content is training the algorithm to ignore them. A founder who posts 2x/week with 4/4 content is building a lead channel.

Better to post twice a week for 90 days and book 15 calls than post daily for 90 days and book zero.

The other hot take: most founders don't need more content. They need better positioning.

A founder with tight positioning can post 1x/week and fill their pipeline. A founder with vague positioning can post 10x/week and get nothing.

Fix the positioning first. The content follows.

Third contrarian take: AI doesn't save time unless it's trained.

Generic ChatGPT output takes longer to edit than writing from scratch. The promise is speed. The reality is more work.

The only way AI saves time is if you spend the upfront 2 hours training it on your voice, ICP, and frameworks. After that, it's 10x faster. Before that, it's slower.

Most founders skip the training step. Then blame the tool.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

When content is working, you see three signals:

**Signal 1: DM conversations start without you initiating.**

People read a post and DM you to ask about working together. You didn't reach out. They did. That's the signal.

If you're DMing everyone and nobody's DMing you, your content isn't pulling its weight.

**Signal 2: Discovery calls reference specific posts.**

A founder books a call and says "I read your post about X and it resonated." They're pre-sold before the call starts. That's working content.

If calls start with "so what do you do?" your content isn't doing the job.

**Signal 3: You can go quiet for 2 weeks and the pipeline doesn't dry up.**

Content that works builds momentum. Posts from 30 days ago are still booking calls today. You're not trapped on a hamster wheel.

If pipeline goes to zero every time you stop posting, you're not building a channel. You're just doing content theatre.

From the vault: clients who hit these three signals all had tight positioning, a trained AI system, and a 90-day content calendar they actually followed.

The ones who didn't had vague positioning, untrained AI, and posted whatever they felt like that morning.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

Every workshop has the same five people in it.

You can call it a masterclass, a group coaching session, a cohort, a live training, or a 90-minute sprint. The packaging doesn't matter. The five archetypes show up every single time, and if you don't design for all five, three of them walk out disappointed and the other two wonder why they paid.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Most founders design workshops for one person: themselves three years ago.

They build the session around what THEY needed when they were stuck. They assume everyone in the room has the same problem, the same learning style, the same readiness to act. Then they're confused when half the room zones out, two people dominate the chat, and three others ghost the follow-up calls.

The cost of not designing for all five archetypes is measurable. Refund requests. Testimonials that say "good session but not what I expected." Alumni who don't return for the next cohort. Breakout rooms where one person works and four watch. Post-session slacks that go quiet after 48 hours.

The leverage of getting it right is equally measurable. When you design for all five, retention jumps. Referrals triple. Your testimonials stop being generic ("Danny was great!") and start being specific ("I had the clarity I needed by minute 40 and a launched offer by Friday"). Alumni buy the next cohort before you open the cart.

The mechanism is simple: people pay to solve a problem, but they stay because they were SEEN. If the entire workshop speaks to only one archetype, the other four feel invisible. Invisible people don't refer. They don't renew. They don't become case studies.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

I've run workshops for founders at mid-six-figure ARR and founders at a low three-figure amountM ARR. I've run them for solo consultants and for leadership teams. I've run them for people who've never posted on LinkedIn and for people with 50K followers. Same five archetypes every single time.

**The Ready-to-Ship Operator.** This person has a working business. They're making revenue. They have clients. They have systems. They're not here to "figure out their niche" or "discover their voice." They're here because one specific lever is stuck and they want someone to fix it in the room. When I ran the Founder OS AI Masterclass cohorts in late 2025, this was a ready-to-ship operator. She had clients, a team, a pipeline. She wasn't there to learn "what AI can do." She was there to compress 12 hours of weekly content work into 2. She expected a working system by end of session and would've asked for a refund if she didn't get it. and [a past engagement].

**The Stuck Strategist.** This person has done the reading. They've taken courses. They've bought templates. They know the frameworks. What they don't have is the DECISION. Should I niche down or stay broad? Should I charge a low three-figure amount or a low three-figure amount? Should I build a productised service or keep doing custom? They're paralyzed by options. In the Cashflow Inner Circle sessions with a client, this archetype shows up every single week. They ask three follow-up questions to every answer because they're hoping someone will just TELL them what to do. The trap is that if you answer their question, they ask another one. The move is to force a decision by Friday and make that decision the only deliverable that matters for them that week. and [a past engagement].

**The Visibility Chaser.** This person is competent at their craft but invisible in the market. They have the skills, the experience, the portfolio. What they don't have is a pipeline. They're posting inconsistently. Their LinkedIn looks fine but books no calls. They're here because they've realized that delivery competence doesn't equal market presence and they need someone to fix the gap. This was the dominant archetype in the Weekly Success Circle sessions I ran in 2023 and 2024. a client Niehus, Jai Shaktawat, Asher — all of them could do the work. None of them could articulate what they did in one sentence or hook a post that moved someone to DM. The sessions that worked for them weren't about TEACHING frameworks. They were about APPLYING frameworks to their exact ICP and exact offer until a real post shipped. and [a past engagement].

**The Confidence-Blocked Executor.** This person knows EXACTLY what to do. They've written the outline. They've drafted the post. They've designed the offer. But they won't ship it. They're waiting for permission, validation, or proof that it won't fail. This archetype dominates 1-on-1 personal branding coaching but shows up in group sessions too. They ask "does this sound okay?" about a post that's already better than 90% of what's on LinkedIn. The move isn't to teach them anything. The move is to read their draft, say "this is ready," and make them post it before they leave the Zoom. If they argue, the real block isn't the draft. It's identity. They don't believe they're the person who's allowed to say this publicly yet. Cited from six months of 1-on-1 patterns across [a past engagement], [a past engagement], and [a past engagement].

**The Lost Beginner.** This person is early. Maybe pre-revenue. Maybe just post-launch. They signed up because the workshop sounded relevant and they don't want to miss out. But they're not READY for what you're teaching. You're talking about scaling to low four figures and they haven't made their first 0K. You're talking about hiring a team and they're still doing all five jobs themselves. If you ignore them, they feel ripped off. If you slow the session down for them, the other four archetypes revolt. The solution isn't to exclude them. The solution is to SEGMENT the deliverable. Give them one thing to ship this week that moves them forward without requiring the infrastructure the others already have.

In a workshop host's 6-week cadence workshop, this came up explicitly. She had three people at mid six figures plus ARR who needed advanced LinkedIn strategy and two people at a low three-figure amount ARR who needed to figure out what they even sold. I told her to design two parallel tracks: the operators get the full 6-week content calendar, the beginners get a 1-week "prove the offer" sprint. Same Zoom, different homework. 

The mistake most founders make is designing the ENTIRE workshop for archetype 3 or 4 because those are the ones who talk the most in the chat. Archetypes 1 and 2 sit quietly, get nothing useful, and don't come back. Archetype 5 gets overwhelmed and refunds.
