title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

The deal doesn't start when you send the DM. It starts when you decide who you're talking to and what you're promising them before you ever hit send.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Most founders treat cold outreach like a numbers game: blast 100 messages, hope for 3 replies, book 1 call, close 0.5 deals. This is exhausting, expensive, and makes you look desperate.

The real cost isn't the time spent writing messages. It's the positioning damage. Every generic "Hey, I help founders grow on LinkedIn" message trains prospects to ignore you. Every "just checking in" follow-up trains them that you chase.

The alternative is what I call the conviction arc: prospect → engage → diagnose → close. Each step has a specific job. Each step moves toward a binary yes/no, not toward "maybe" or "I'll think about it."

When you get this right, the conversion rate flips. Instead of 100 messages for half a deal, you send 20 and close 3. The math changes because you're not optimizing for opens. You're optimizing for fit.

The founders who win at cold outreach understand one thing most don't: the close doesn't happen on the sales call. It happens in the DM sequence. By the time someone books a call with you, they should already know what you do, who it's for, and roughly what it costs. The call is confirmation, not discovery.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

I see three failure patterns repeat across every client who comes to me struggling with outbound.

**Pattern 1: The spray-and-pray founder.** They're sending 50+ DMs a week using a generic template they found on a Twitter thread. "Hey [First Name], loved your post about [vague topic]. I help [everyone] with [everything]. Would love to connect." Reply rate: 2%. Booking rate: 0%. They blame LinkedIn's algorithm. The real problem is they never defined their ICP tightly enough to write a message that lands.

I worked with a SaaS founder In a past engagement who was sending 200 cold DMs a month to "anyone who posts about AI." He got 4 replies, 0 calls, and burned his reputation. We rebuilt from positioning: one ICP (B2B service founders running low four figures–M ARR), one pain (drowning in manual sales follow-up), one promise (AI that books 5+ calls/month without you typing). New DM conversion: 18%. Same LinkedIn account. Different message.

**Pattern 2: The over-qualifier.** They book calls with anyone who says yes, then waste 45 minutes discovering the prospect can't afford them, doesn't have authority to buy, or isn't even the right fit. I call this "hope-based sales." They're hoping the call will magically turn into a deal.

A coaching client In a past engagement was booking 8 calls a week and closing 0.3 deals a month. The problem wasn't his close. It was his DM sequence. He wasn't disqualifying anyone pre-call. We added three qualifying questions to his DM flow: (1) "What's your current revenue?" (2) "Who makes the final buying decision?" (3) "What's your timeline to implement?" He cut his call volume to 3/week and closed 2 deals that month. The disqualification happened in DMs, not on Zoom.

**Pattern 3: The passive connector.** They send a DM, get a reply, then go silent or say "let's stay connected." No ask. No next step. The conversation dies. Six months later they send "just checking in" and the prospect ghosts.

I see this constantly In a past engagement. Founders who are terrified of being salesy, so they never actually sell. The fix is scripted: every reply gets one of three responses: (1) book a call link, (2) disqualifying question, (3) case study + social proof + call link. There's no "let's chat sometime." Every message moves toward a decision.

The pattern that works is the opposite: tight ICP, hard qualifier, binary outcome. You're either moving toward a booked call or a clean no. Maybes don't exist.

title: Specific examples from the vault
text:
## Specific examples from the vault

**The founder who rewrote one line and 3x'd his reply rate.**

In a past engagement, a B2B consultant was opening with: "I help founders scale faster with better systems." Generic. Forgettable. We ran the Invisibility Diagnostic. Score: 1.5/4. No voice, no POV, no specificity.

We rewrote it to: "I turn M service businesses into a low three-figure amountM without hiring." Same offer. Different language. Reply rate went from 6% to 19% in two weeks. The shift was specificity: numbers, outcome, constraint (without hiring).

He didn't change his targeting. He didn't send more messages. He just said the thing in a way that made the prospect think, "Wait, how?"

**The 5K deal closed entirely in DMs.**

from a past engagement: A founder DMed an inbound lead with a two-message sequence. First message: case study. "Took a founder from 0 to 12 inbound calls in 90 days using this exact system. Same offer as yours, same ICP. Here's the doc." Second message: "If this looks like what you need, book 20 minutes here. If not, no worries."

Prospect replied: "This is exactly what I need. What's the price?" Founder sent pricing in DM (5K for 90 days, guarantee: 10+ inbound calls or keep working for free). Prospect booked. Call lasted 11 minutes. Closed same day.

The sale happened in the DM thread. The call was procedural. The lesson: if your positioning is tight and your proof is strong, the prospect pre-closes themselves.

**The disqualifying question that saved 40 hours.**

In a past engagement, a founder was booking discovery calls with solopreneurs who couldn't afford his 5K offer. I added one question to his DM flow: "What's your monthly revenue right now?"

Anyone under 0K/month got a different response: "You're too early for this. Focus on [specific free resource]. Circle back when you're at 5K/month and I'll fast-track you."

He went from 10 calls/week (8 unqualified) to 4 calls/week (3 qualified). Close rate went from 10% to 75%. He didn't lose deals. He just stopped wasting time on people who were never going to buy.

**The cold DM that referenced a specific post.**

from a past engagement: Instead of "loved your content," a founder sent: "Your post about burning out while scaling — you said you're doing 60-hour weeks and still behind. I built a system that cuts that to 40 without dropping revenue. Want the breakdown?"

Prospect replied in 8 minutes. The specificity (60-hour weeks, the exact pain) made it feel like a real message, not a template. They booked a call that afternoon.

The pattern: reference something real they said. Use their words. Make it impossible to mistake your message for a bot.

title: Scripts and exact phrases
text:
## Scripts and exact phrases

**Opening DM (for service founders):**
"You're doing $[revenue] with [team size]. You could be at $[2x revenue] without adding payroll. I've done this with [named client]. Want the system?"

**Opening DM (for coaches/consultants):**
"Your LinkedIn gets engagement but nobody books. I can fix that in 90 days: 10+ inbound calls a month, or I work for free until you do. Here's the last three people I did this for: [link]."

**Opening DM (for SaaS founders):**
"Your outbound reply rate is under 5%. I'll get you to 20% in 30 days using AI-native workflows your competitors don't have yet. Interested?"

**Disqualifying question (budget):**
"Before we book: what's your budget for this? I start at $[price] and it's not negotiable. If that's out of range, no hard feelings."

**Disqualifying question (authority):**
"Quick check: are you the one who makes the final call on this, or do you need to loop someone else in?"

**Disqualifying question (timeline):**
"When do you need this live? I'm booking out [timeframe]. If that's too slow, I can refer you to someone faster."

**The binary close DM:**
"So here's where we are. I can get you [outcome] in [timeframe] for $[price]. If that works, book here: [link]. If not, totally cool — just let me know so I don't keep following up."

**The clean no response:**
"All good. If you change your mind in 6 months, ping me. Until then, good luck with [specific thing they mentioned]."

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

**Mistake 1: Asking "Can I send you some info?"** This is permission-seeking. It positions you below them. The prospect has to do mental work to decide if they want info. Just send the info. If it's good, they'll read it. If it's not, asking permission won't help.

**Mistake 2: The multi-step nurture sequence with no ask.** DM 1: value. DM 2: value. DM 3: value. DM 4: "Still no reply, just checking in." This trains the prospect that you're a content feed, not a vendor. Every message should move toward a decision. Value without an ask is just noise.

**Mistake 3: Booking calls before disqualifying.** I see this In a past engagement: founders who book anyone who says yes, then spend 30 minutes realizing the prospect can't afford them. Qualify in DMs. It's free. Zoom calls cost you time.

**Mistake 4: "Just checking in" follow-ups.** This is the death of positioning. It says: "I have nothing new to offer, I'm just hoping you changed your mind." If someone ghosts after two messages, they're either not interested or not ready. Send one final message with a deadline ("Circling back one last time — let me know by Friday or I'll assume it's a no"), then move on.

**Mistake 5: Pitching the process instead of the outcome.** "We start with a 90-minute strategy session, then build your content calendar, then..." Nobody cares. They care about the outcome. Lead with the promise: "10 inbound calls a month in 90 days." The process is for the sales call, not the DM.

**Mistake 6: Sending the same message to 100 people.** Even if your ICP is tight, every prospect is different. Reference something specific they posted, a problem they mentioned, a milestone they hit. It takes 60 seconds per message. The reply rate goes from 3% to 25%.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Most sales advice says "build rapport first, pitch later." I say the opposite: pitch immediately, build rapport after they're interested.

The DM is not the place to make a friend. It's the place to make an offer. If the offer lands, the rapport builds itself on the call. If the offer doesn't land, no amount of small talk will save it.

I also reject the "7-touch rule." You don't need 7 emails to close a deal. You need 2–3 messages with a clear offer, strong proof, and a binary CTA. If they're not interested after message 3, they're not your client. Move on.

The other contrarian take: cold outreach should feel almost rude. Not actually rude — but direct enough that weak prospects self-select out. "What's your budget?" feels aggressive to people who can't afford you. Good. That's the point. You're not trying to be liked. You're trying to close the 5% who are ready to buy and ignore the 95% who aren't.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

Reply rate: 15–30% on cold DMs (industry average is 2–8%).

Qualification rate: 70%+ of replies convert to booked calls (most founders sit at 20–40%).

Close rate on qualified calls: 50%+ (because you disqualified the nos in DMs).

Time from first DM to closed deal: 7–14 days (not 60–90 days).

You're sending 20–30 DMs a week, not 200. You're booking 3–5 calls a week, not 15. You're closing 2–3 deals a month, not 0.5.

The other signal: prospects say yes on the call in under 10 minutes. They've already decided in the DM thread. The call is just procedural.

And the final signal: you're not chasing. The prospect either books or they don't. If they say "let me think about it," you say "no problem, let me know by Friday," and you move on. Maybes don't pay.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

Sales objections are not rejections — they are requests for the final piece of information the prospect needs to buy.

Most founders treat objections as barriers. They hear "I need to think about it" and assume the deal is dead. They hear "that's expensive" and start discounting. They hear "I need to talk to my partner" and send a follow-up email three days later hoping something changed.

The actual truth: an objection means the prospect is still in the conversation. They haven't left. They haven't ghosted. They're telling you exactly what's blocking them from saying yes right now. Your job is to handle it in real time, on the call, and close.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Every objection you defer costs you the deal.

When you say "no problem, take your time" or "totally understand, let me send you some info," you've trained the prospect that hesitation gets rewarded with space. Space kills deals. The longer someone sits with uncertainty, the more reasons they invent not to buy.

The mechanism is simple: buying decisions happen in moments of clarity, and clarity happens in conversation. The second you end the call without resolution, you've moved the decision out of the high-conviction state you created during discovery and into the low-conviction state of their inbox, their calendar, their partner who wasn't on the call.

Founders who don't handle objections in real time burn 60-70% of their pipeline in follow-up limbo. They book 10 calls. 7 of them say "I need to think about it." The founder sends a polite email. 5 ghost. 2 reply with "not right now." 0 close. The problem wasn't the offer. It wasn't the price. It was the failure to resolve the objection when it surfaced.

The cost is not just the lost deal. It's the wasted discovery time, the opportunity cost of the call slot, and the psychological damage of thinking your close rate is 10% when it should be 50%.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

The pattern repeats across every founder I work with: they get to the end of a strong discovery call, the prospect says one of five sentences, and the founder freezes.

Most common version: "This sounds great, but I need to think about it."

Second most common: "I need to talk to my business partner / spouse / co-founder."

Third: "The price is higher than I expected."

Fourth: "I'm not sure this is the right time."

Fifth: "I've tried something like this before and it didn't work."

Each one has a script. Each one can be handled in 60-90 seconds on the call. But most founders don't have the scripts memorized, so they default to politeness and lose the deal.

One client — B2B SaaS founder selling a 5K implementation package — was closing 1 in 8 calls. We recorded three of his sales calls. On all three, the prospect said some version of "I need to run this by my CTO." On all three, my client said "totally understand, no rush." On zero of those three did he ask a follow-up question.

The fix: one reframe. When the prospect says "I need to talk to my CTO," you say: "Makes sense. Walk me through what you think their concern will be — is it budget, timeline, or whether this will actually work?"

That question does two things. First, it surfaces the real objection (usually it's not the CTO at all — it's the founder's own uncertainty about budget or timing). Second, it keeps the conversation alive so you can handle the real objection right there.

After adding that one script, his close rate went from 12% to 40% in six weeks. Same offer. Same discovery process. One sentence. [a past engagement]

Another pattern: founders who hear "that's expensive" and immediately start explaining all the value they're delivering.

One client — personal brand coach selling a a low three-figure amount 90-day package — would respond to price objections with a five-minute breakdown of every deliverable, every session, every bonus. The prospect would nod politely and still not buy.

The script I gave her: "Expensive compared to what?"

That's it. Four words. The prospect has to name the comparison point. If they say "compared to other coaches," you ask what the other coach charges and what they deliver. If they say "compared to what I can afford," you've just learned it's not a price objection — it's a cash flow or priority objection, and you handle that differently.

She used it on the next call. Prospect said "that's a lot of money." She said "compared to what?" He said "I don't know, I've never hired a coach before." She said "so you don't actually know if it's expensive — you just don't have a reference point. Let me ask differently: if this works and you're booking 3-5 inbound calls a month by the end of 90 days, what's that worth to you?" He said "a low three-figure amount in the next six months, easy." She said "so you're risking a low three-figure amount to make a low three-figure amount." He bought on the call. [a past engagement]

Third pattern: founders who get the "I've tried this before" objection and don't know how to separate their offer from the past failure.

One client — LinkedIn strategist selling a a low three-figure amount content system — kept hearing "I tried posting consistently before and it didn't work." She would respond by defending LinkedIn as a platform and explaining why her system was different. Never closed.

The script: "What do you think went wrong last time?"

Let them tell you. They'll name the exact mistake (usually: no strategy, no ICP clarity, generic content, no follow-up system). Then you say: "That's exactly what we're fixing. You weren't posting wrong — you were posting without a system. What we're building is [name the three things that address their past failure]."

She used it. Next prospect said "I posted for six months and got nothing." She asked what went wrong. He said "I was just writing random thoughts, no structure." She said "right, so you were posting consistently but not strategically. What we're building is a 90-day content calendar tied to your offer, an ICP brief so every post is aimed at one person, and a Claude skill that writes in your voice so it doesn't take 12 hours a week. You weren't wrong to try — you just didn't have the system." He bought. [a past engagement]

Fourth pattern: the "not the right time" objection, which is almost never about timing.

One client — workshop facilitator selling a K two-day intensive — would hear "this sounds great but I'm slammed right now" and immediately suggest rebooking in a month. He'd send a calendar link. Prospect would never book.

The reframe: "I hear you. Walk me through what changes in your schedule in the next 30 days that makes this easier to commit to."

The prospect will either name something specific (a project wrapping up, a hiring decision resolving) or they'll say "I don't know, just feels like a lot right now." If it's the first, you book around the milestone. If it's the second, it's not a timing objection — it's a priority objection. You say: "Got it. So it's not that you're too busy — it's that this isn't the top priority right now. What would need to be true for this to become the priority?"

That question forces them to articulate the real blocker. Usually it's revenue, team capacity, or confidence in the outcome. All of those are handleable on the call. [a past engagement]

The throughline across all of these: **objections are not the end of the conversation. They're the beginning of the close.**

## Specific examples from the vault

Example 1: The "I need to think about it" script, tested on a 0K consulting call.

Prospect was a SaaS founder. Strong discovery. Clear pain (content wasn't converting). Clear outcome (10 inbound demos a month). We got to the close and he said "this makes sense, I just need a couple days to think it through."

I said: "Totally fair. Before we hang up — what specifically are you thinking through? Is it the price, the scope, or whether this will actually work?"

He paused. Then said: "Honestly, it's the price. Not that I can't afford it, but I've spent money on marketing before and it didn't pay back."

Now I know the real objection. I said: "Got it. So it's not the price — it's the risk. You're wondering if this will actually work for your business. Let me ask: if we build this and you're booking 10+ demos a month in 90 days, what's that worth to you in closed deals?"

He did the math out loud. "mid five figures in the next six months, conservatively."

I said: "So you're risking 0K to make 00K. The only way this doesn't pay back is if we don't execute. Want to talk through the guarantee?"

He bought on the call. [a past engagement]

Example 2: The "I need to talk to my partner" script, used on a a low three-figure amount offer.

Prospect was a solo consultant. Great call. Clear problem (spending 15 hours a week on content, getting no leads). We got to the investment and she said "I need to run this by my husband before I commit."

I said: "Makes sense. Walk me through what you think his concern will be — is it the money, the time commitment, or whether this will work?"

She said: "Probably the money. We just had a baby and cash is tight."

I said: "Got it. So it's not really about him — it's about whether you can afford this right now. Let me ask differently: if you don't fix the content problem, what happens to your business in the next six months?"

She said: "I lose pipeline. I probably have to go back to a job."

I said: "And if that happens, what's the financial cost?"

She said: "I lose a low three-figure amount in potential income and I'm back at a low three-figure amount salary."

I said: "So the question isn't whether you can afford a low three-figure amount. The question is whether you can afford not to fix this. What does your husband care about more — the a low three-figure amount or the a low three-figure amount?"

She said: "The a low three-figure amount."

I said: "Then let's solve the a low three-figure amount problem today."

She bought on the call. [a past engagement]

Example 3: The "that's expensive" reframe, used on a a low three-figure amount package.

Prospect was a LinkedIn coach. Strong fit. Clear outcome. Got to the price and he said "that's a lot more than I expected."

I said: "Expensive compared to what?"

He said: "I don't know, I guess I thought it would be like K."

I said: "Got it. So you weren't comparing it to another offer — you just had a number in your head. Let me ask: if this works and you're booking 5 clients a month at K each by the end of 90 days, what's that worth to you?"

He said: "0K a month, so a low three-figure amount in the first quarter."

I said: "So you're betting a low three-figure amount to make a low three-figure amount. That's a 10x return. The only way this is expensive is if it doesn't work. Want to talk through the guarantee?"

He bought. [a past engagement]

Example 4: The "I've tried this before" reframe, used with a content strategist.

Prospect said: "I tried working with a LinkedIn coach last year and it didn't work. I posted for three months and got maybe two leads."

I said: "What do you think went wrong?"

He said: "I don't know. I just posted what the coach told me to post and nothing happened."

I said: "So you were posting consistently but not strategically. You didn't have an ICP, you didn't have a POV, and you were posting someone else's content in your voice. That's not a you problem — that's a system problem. What we're building is a content system that writes in your voice, targets your ICP, and ties every post to your offer. You weren't wrong to try — you just didn't have the right system."

He said: "Okay, that makes sense."

He bought. [a past engagement]

Example 5: The "not the right time" reframe, used on a workshop call.

Prospect said: "This sounds great but I'm slammed right now. Can we revisit this in a month?"

I said: "I hear you. Walk me through what changes in your schedule in the next 30 days that makes this easier."

He said: "I don't know, I'm just really busy."

I said: "Got it. So it's not that you're too busy — it's that this isn't the top priority right now. What would need to be true for this to become the priority?"

He said: "I guess if I felt like I was actually losing revenue because I'm not doing this."

I said: "Are you losing revenue now because your content isn't converting?"

He said: "Yes."

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

**Mistake 1: Accepting the objection at face value.**

When someone says "I need to think about it," most founders say "no problem, take your time." They've just lost the deal. The objection is not the real reason. The real reason is buried underneath. Your job is to ask one follow-up question to surface it.

**Mistake 2: Defending the offer instead of reframing the objection.**

When someone says "that's expensive," most founders launch into a five-minute value dump. They list every deliverable, every session, every bonus. The prospect nods politely and still doesn't buy. The better move: reframe the objection with a question. "Expensive compared to what?" forces the prospect to name their comparison point, and then you can address the real concern.

**Mistake 3: Sending follow-up emails instead of closing on the call.**

Every objection you defer to email is a deal you've lost. Follow-up emails get ignored. Follow-up emails give the prospect time to invent new reasons not to buy. Follow-up emails train the prospect that hesitation gets rewarded with space. Close on the call or don't close.

**Mistake 4: Treating objections as rejections.**

Most founders hear "I'm not sure this is the right time" and assume the prospect is saying no. They're not. They're saying "I need one more piece of information before I say yes." Your job is to figure out what that piece is and deliver it in the next 60 seconds.

**Mistake 5: Not having the scripts memorized.**

If you have to pause and think about how to handle an objection, you've already lost. The prospect reads the hesitation as uncertainty. You need five scripts memorized cold: think about it, talk to partner, price, tried before, timing. One script per objection type. 60 seconds each. Practice them until they sound like conversation, not recitation.

**Mistake 6: Discounting to close.**

When a prospect says "that's expensive," the worst thing you can do is drop the price. You've just confirmed their suspicion that your offer wasn't worth the original number. Instead, reframe the price as an investment with a specific ROI. "You're betting a low three-figure amount to make a low three-figure amount. That's a 10x return." If they still don't buy, it's not a price problem — it's a belief problem, and you need to go back to discovery.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Most sales training tells you to handle objections with empathy and validation. "I totally understand, a lot of my clients felt the same way at first."

That's weak.

Empathy doesn't close deals. Clarity does.

When someone says "I need to think about it," they don't need you to validate their uncertainty. They need you to resolve it. Saying "I understand" just confirms that thinking about it is a reasonable response. It's not. Thinking about it is what you do when you're not sure the offer is right. Your job is to make them sure on the call.

The other contrarian take: **you should want objections**.

Most founders dread objections. They see them as a sign the call is going badly. The opposite is true. Objections mean the prospect is engaged. They're still in the conversation. They're telling you exactly what's blocking them from buying. A prospect who says nothing and then ghosts is a worse outcome than a prospect who raises five objections on the call.

Every objection is a gift. It's the prospect handing you the exact script you need to close them. If they say "that's expensive," they've just told you they're worried about ROI. Handle it and close. If they say "I need to talk to my partner," they've just told you they're unsure about budget or priority. Handle it and close.

The best sales calls are the ones where the prospect raises three objections and you handle all three on the call. The worst sales calls are the ones where the prospect says "this sounds great, let me think about it" and you never hear from them again.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

You're booking 10 discovery calls a month. 7 of them get to the investment conversation. 5 of them say yes on the call. That's a 50% close rate measured from qualified discovery to signed deal. Most founders are at 10-20%. The difference is not the offer. It's the objection handling.

Observable signals:

**Signal 1: You're closing on the call, not in follow-up.**

If more than 20% of your deals close via email after the call, your objection handling is weak. Strong objection handling closes 80%+ of deals on the call. The prospect either buys or explicitly says no. There is no "let me think about it."

**Signal 2: Objections don't surprise you.**

You've heard the same five objections on every call for six months. You know exactly what's coming. You have a script for each one. You deliver it in 60 seconds and move to the close. No hesitation. No scrambling. No "let me get back to you on that."

**Signal 3: Your close rate is consistent.**

If you're closing 10% one month and 60% the next, your process is broken. Strong objection handling produces consistent close rates because you're handling the same objections the same way every time. The script works or it doesn't. If it works, it works every time.

**Signal 4: You're not discounting.**

If you're dropping the price to close deals, your objection handling is weak. Price objections are never actually about price. They're about belief, ROI, or priority. If you're handling those correctly, the prospect either buys at full price or they don't buy. Discounting is what you do when you can't close any other way.

**Signal 5: You're spending zero time on follow-up.**

If you're sending three follow-up emails per prospect, your objection handling is broken. Strong objection handling closes the deal on the call or kills the deal on the call. Either outcome is fine. What you don't do is leave the prospect in limbo and then chase them for two weeks.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

Every discovery call exists to answer one question: is there a mutual fit worth spending money on?

Not to educate. Not to build rapport. Not to "explore possibilities." To decide yes or no, fast, with both parties walking away clear on what happens next.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Most founders treat discovery calls like networking coffee chats. They ask open-ended questions, let the prospect ramble, and walk away with a vague "let's stay in touch."

That burns time. Theirs and yours.

The cost of a bad discovery process compounds fast. You spend 45 minutes on a call that should have been disqualified in 8. You book follow-ups with prospects who aren't buyers. Your pipeline fills with maybes that never close.

The leverage of getting this right is mechanical. A tight discovery call structure does three things:

1. Qualifies the prospect in under 10 minutes (saves you 35 minutes per bad fit)
2. Surfaces the real objection early (so you either handle it now or walk)
3. Sets a hard next step before you hang up (so nothing dies in "I'll get back to you" limbo)

When a founder can't close deals, the problem is almost never the close. It's that they're closing the wrong people. Discovery is where you filter.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

The pattern I see most: founders who book 10+ discovery calls a month but close 1 or fewer.

When I ask to listen to a recording, the structure is always the same. They open with "tell me about your business," let the prospect talk for 20 minutes, then pitch their offer for 15, then ask "does this sound like a fit?"

By that point, the prospect has already decided. You just don't know it yet.

The fix is always the same. Flip the order. You talk first.

In a past engagement, James spent the first 12 minutes of the call letting me (playing prospect) explain my process. By minute 15 I was describing my tech stack in detail. He still hadn't told me what he was selling.

When we debriefed after, I told him: "I would have hung up by now if this were a real call. You gave me no reason to stay."

The reframe: your first job is to earn the right to ask questions. You do that by saying in 90 seconds what you do, who it's for, and what result they can expect.

Then you ask: "Does that sound like something you'd want?"

If yes, you've earned 30 more minutes. If no, you've saved both of you 40.

I ran this exact structure with a prospect In a past engagement with Arber. 6 minutes in, he said "I don't think we're the right fit right now." I thanked him, asked him to refer anyone who was, and ended the call at 8 minutes.

That's a win. Not every call should close. Every call should decide.

Another pattern: founders who can't handle "I need to think about it."

In a past engagement, I walked James through the "think about it" reframe I use: "Totally fair. Walk me through what's still unclear. Price, scope, fit, or timing?"

80% of the time, they name one. Then you work it right there on the call.

If they genuinely need to leave the call to decide, you set a hard next step: "I'll send a one-pager by EOD. Reply with yes, no, or 'still thinking and here's why.' Anything else and I'll assume it's a no."

The thing I never do: send "just checking in" follow-ups. They train the prospect to expect chasing. I close on the call or I don't close.

The third pattern: discovery calls that book a second meeting instead of closing.

This happens when the founder doesn't ask for the sale.

In a past engagement, James and I role-played this exact scenario. He presented the offer, I said "this sounds good," and he said "great, let's book another call to go over details."

I stopped him. "Why another call? If I just said yes, close me now."

The script I gave him: "Based on what you've told me, this is the right fit. The next step is I send you a proposal by EOD, you review it, we jump on a 15-minute call Friday to answer any questions, and if it's a yes, we kick off Monday. Does that work?"

If the prospect says yes, you've closed. If they say "I need more time," you've surfaced the real objection (which was hiding behind "let's book another call").

A fourth pattern: founders who don't know when to walk.

In a past engagement, James asked me "how do you know when to disqualify someone?"

My answer: three disqualifiers, always.

1. They can't afford it (and won't be able to in the next 60 days)
2. They're not the decision-maker (and won't introduce you to the person who is)
3. They're shopping, not buying (they're comparing 5+ vendors with no urgency)

If any of those three are true, end the call politely and move on.

The cost of ignoring this: you spend 3 weeks nurturing a prospect who was never going to buy. That's 3 weeks you could have spent closing someone who would.

title: Specific examples from the vault
text:
## Specific examples from the vault

In a past engagement with Nea, I opened the call by saying: "I help solo founders compress 12 hours a week of LinkedIn content work into 2 hours using AI. The outcome is you post 4x a week, it sounds like you, and you book 3-5 inbound calls a month. Does that sound like something you'd want?"

She said yes. That earned me the right to ask discovery questions.

8 minutes in, I asked: "What's your content workflow right now, start to finish?"

She described a 14-hour-a-week process involving Canva, ChatGPT, and manual editing. Perfect fit.

Then I asked the budget question: "If I could cut that to 2 hours a week and prove it in the first session, what's that worth to you?"

She said "easily low four figures."

I closed at low four figures. She said yes on the call.

Total call time: 34 minutes. No follow-up needed.

In a past engagement with Sam, I opened the same way. He said "not right now, maybe in 6 months."

I asked: "Is the timing bad, or is the offer not a fit?"

He said: "Timing. I'm mid-rebrand and don't want to start LinkedIn until that's done."

I thanked him, asked him to reach out when the rebrand shipped, and ended the call at 11 minutes.

That's also a win. I didn't chase. I didn't book a follow-up. I moved on.

In a past engagement with Ari, the call went 52 minutes. Why? Because I let him talk for 30 minutes about their sales process before I explained what I was selling.

By the time I pitched, he'd already mentally checked out. He said "let me think about it" and never replied.

That was a loss. Not because he didn't buy. Because I wasted 52 minutes on a call that should have been 12.

In a past engagement with Shabistan, I asked the decision-maker question 18 minutes in: "Are you the person who signs off on this, or is there someone else I need to talk to?"

She said: "I need to run it by my co-founder."

I asked: "Can we get them on a call this week?"

She said: "They're traveling for two weeks."

I thanked her and ended the call. No point building a proposal for someone who can't say yes.

## Scripts and exact phrases

**Opening (first 90 seconds):**
"I help [ICP] achieve [outcome with number] in [timeframe]. The result is [specific benefit]. Does that sound like something you'd want?"

**Earning the discovery:**
"Great. Let me ask you a few questions to make sure this is the right fit. First: what's your [workflow/process/current state] right now, start to finish?"

**Budget qualifier:**
"If I could [compress the pain], what's that worth to you?"

**Decision-maker qualifier:**
"Are you the person who signs off on this, or is there someone else I need to talk to?"

**Urgency qualifier:**
"If this is the right fit, what's stopping you from starting next week?"

**Handling 'I need to think about it':**
"Totally fair. Walk me through what's still unclear. Price, scope, fit, or timing?"

**Setting the hard next step:**
"Based on what you've told me, this is the right fit. The next step is I send you a proposal by EOD, you review it, we jump on a 15-minute call Friday to answer questions, and if it's a yes, we kick off Monday. Does that work?"

**Closing on the call:**
"Great. I'll send the agreement over today. Reply with any questions. If it's a yes, sign it and we'll kick off [date]."

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

**Opening with "tell me about your business."** This hands control to the prospect. They ramble. You lose 15 minutes learning things you don't need to know. Open with what YOU do instead.

**Not asking the budget question.** Founders are terrified of this one. They think it's rude. It's not. The rude thing is wasting someone's time on an offer they can't afford. Ask it at minute 10.

**Booking a follow-up instead of closing.** If the prospect says "this sounds good," close them. Don't say "let's book another call." That's just fear disguised as process.

**Chasing after "I'll get back to you."** Set a hard deadline. "I'll send the proposal by EOD. Reply by Friday with yes, no, or 'still thinking and here's why.' Anything else and I'll assume it's a no." Then stick to it.

**Letting the call run long.** If it's not a fit, end the call. 12 minutes is better than 52. Your time is the asset. Protect it.

**Pitching before qualifying.** If you pitch before you know they can afford it, have authority to buy, and have urgency, you're just doing free consulting. Qualify first.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Most sales advice says "build rapport first." I say the opposite.

Rapport is a byproduct of clarity. When someone knows exactly what you're offering, who it's for, and what they'll get, they relax. That's rapport.

When you open with small talk and "tell me about yourself," you create anxiety. The prospect is thinking: "What do you want from me? What's the catch?"

Lead with the offer. Rapport follows.

Another contrarian take: not every discovery call should convert.

If your close rate is 80%+, you're not qualifying hard enough. You're saying yes to people who should be maybes.

A 40-50% discovery-to-close rate means you're filtering properly. Half the people who book a call shouldn't buy from you. That's the point of discovery.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

You book 8 discovery calls in a month. 3 close on the call. 2 say "not right now" and you end the call in under 15 minutes. 3 are genuine maybes — you send a proposal, set a hard deadline, and 2 of those close by Friday.

Your average discovery call is 25 minutes. Not 45. Not 60.

Your pipeline has 5 active prospects, not 25. Each one has a hard next step with a date attached. None of them are "waiting to hear back."

You spend 3 hours a week on sales calls, not 12. The rest of the time you're delivering, not chasing.

When a prospect says "I need to think about it," you know exactly what they're thinking about. Because you asked.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

You close deals by saying no faster than the buyer does.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Most founders treat discovery like a sales pitch disguised as a conversation. They ask surface questions, nod along, then write the proposal hoping the price works. By the time they hear "too expensive" or "we need to think about it," they've already wasted 6 hours on a call that was never going to close.

Wrong-fit deals don't just waste time. They poison your pipeline. You spend emotional capital chasing people who were never buying. Your confidence drops because you're getting rejected more. Your positioning weakens because you're saying yes to everyone. Your referrals suffer because the few clients you do close aren't the right ones.

The expensive part isn't the lost deal. It's the three real deals you didn't work on because you were chasing the wrong one.

Disqualifying questions exist to catch the wrong-fit early. Before the proposal. Before the price conversation. Before you've invested any real work. You're not trying to convince them. You're trying to discover whether this is a deal you actually want.

The leverage is brutal. One disqualifying question in the first 5 minutes can save you 20 hours of proposal work, three follow-up calls, and two weeks of "just checking in" purgatory. It also signals something the buyer respects: you have a standard. You don't take everyone. That alone makes them want to qualify FOR you.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

I see the pattern every time I review a founder's sales pipeline. Twenty-five "opportunities" in the CRM. Only three have a real shot. The rest are polite conversations with people who were never going to buy, couldn't afford it, or don't have authority to sign.

The symptom: "I'm doing so many sales calls but nothing's closing."

The diagnosis: They never asked a single disqualifying question.

One client I worked with in early 2024 was running a LinkedIn personal branding offer for consultants. Great positioning. Strong case studies. Pipeline full. Zero closed deals in six weeks. I listened to three of his recorded sales calls. Every single one followed the same script: he'd ask about their business, pitch the offer, show the pricing, then ask if they had questions. Never once did he ask what they'd already tried, what their budget was, or who else needed to approve the deal. He was pitching to people who had no money, no urgency, and no authority.

I gave him three questions to ask in the first 10 minutes of every call: "What have you already tried to fix this?", "What budget have you set aside for solving this problem?", and "Who else is involved in this decision besides you?" Within two calls, he disqualified someone who'd been "very interested" for three weeks but had zero budget and needed board approval. The next week he closed two deals with people who passed all three filters.

The pattern repeats in every 1:1 coaching engagement. Founders don't want to disqualify. It feels rude. It feels like closing a door. So they keep the conversation alive hoping momentum will turn into a deal. It never does. What actually happens is the prospect ghosts after three weeks because they were never serious, and the founder blames their pitch instead of their intake process.

Another pattern: the founder asks softballs. "Are you serious about growing your business?" Yes. "Is this a priority for you?" Yes. "Do you see the value in what we do?" Yes. Every answer sounds positive but commits to nothing. These questions don't disqualify because they don't cost the buyer anything to say yes. Real disqualifying questions make the buyer uncomfortable. That's the test.

I've seen this exact mistake kill deals for a founder running AI implementation workshops for SMBs. His pitch was strong. His case studies were real. But he never asked "Have you actually used AI internally yet?" or "Do you have someone on your team who'll own this after the workshop?" He spent hours prepping custom proposals for people who hadn't touched ChatGPT once and had no one to execute after the session. The deals died in "we'll get back to you" limbo every time. When I walked him through adding just two disqualifiers — "Show me one AI tool you've already tested" and "Who on your team will be responsible for rolling this out?" — his close rate doubled in 30 days. Not because his pitch got better. Because he stopped pitching to people who were never going to implement.

The biggest leverage moment comes when you disqualify someone live on the call and they fight to stay in. That's when you know they're real. If you say "It sounds like this isn't the right time for you" and they immediately agree, you just saved yourself two weeks. If they say "No wait, let me explain" and start selling YOU, you know they're serious. The disqualifying question doesn't kill the deal. It reveals whether the deal was ever real.

title: Specific examples from the vault
text:
## Specific examples from the vault

One session stands out from a founder I coached in March 2024. He was running a productized consulting offer for SaaS companies — marketing audits + 90-day execution plans. His pipeline looked healthy: eight active conversations. But nothing was closing. I asked him to walk me through the last three calls. Every single one ended with "this looks great, let me discuss with my team." No one ever came back.

I asked him one question: "Did you ask who else needs to approve this decision?" He paused. No, he hadn't. He'd assumed the person who booked the call was the decision-maker. In all three cases, they weren't. They were ICs gathering options for their CMO. The CMO never heard the pitch. The deal died in internal Slack channels he never saw.

I gave him a script for the first 5 minutes of every discovery call: "Before we go deep, help me understand — who else besides you is involved in making this decision? And what's the process once you've decided this is the right move?" Within two calls, he caught someone who needed sign-off from a CEO who was traveling for the next month. He disqualified on the spot, told them to reconnect when the CEO was back. The prospect respected it. A month later, they booked the call with the CEO present and closed same-day. The disqualifying question didn't kill the deal — it revealed the real timeline and saved him four weeks of chasing someone with no authority.

from a past engagement — this exact conversation where the founder realized 80% of his pipeline was IC's gathering information, not buyers with authority.

Another example from a founder selling AI content systems to solo consultants in late 2024. Strong offer. Good pricing. But half his pipeline stalled at "I need to think about it." I asked him: "What's the last thing you tried before hiring me?" He said LinkedIn ghostwriting services, SEO agencies, Jasper AI. All of them failed because he never committed the time to implement. I told him: start asking prospects that exact question in discovery. "What have you already tried to solve this, and why didn't it work?"

First call using the new script: prospect said they'd tried Jasper, ChatGPT, and hired a VA. None of it worked because "I just didn't have time to feed them good inputs." Red flag. This person wasn't going to succeed with an AI system either — same problem, same outcome. The founder disqualified them on the call. Prospect pushed back: "But your system is different, right?" Founder held the line: "It is, but it still requires 2 hours a week from you to make it work. If you didn't have that time for Jasper, you won't have it for this." Prospect went silent, then admitted: "You're right, I'm not there yet." Call ended. Founder saved 15 hours of onboarding someone who was going to ghost after week two.

from a past engagement — the exact moment the founder realized he was onboarding people who had already proven they wouldn't do the work.

A third case from a workshop client in early 2025. She was selling strategy sessions to e-commerce founders. Price: a low three-figure amount. Strong demand. Terrible close rate. Problem: she never asked about budget. She'd pitch the offer, show the outcomes, then send the proposal. Half the prospects never replied. The other half said "great work but we can't afford this right now."

I gave her one line to add 10 minutes into the call, right after they confirmed the problem was real: "To make sure we're both efficient with our time — what budget range have you set aside to solve this?" Dead silence on her first attempt. The prospect hadn't thought about budget at all. Red flag. She pushed: "Is this something you'd need to find budget for, or is there already money allocated?" Prospect admitted: no allocated budget, would need to pull from another project, needed CFO approval. Disqualified on the spot. Prospect was frustrated but respected it. Two months later, they came back with approved budget and closed same-week.

from a past engagement — the exact call where the founder learned that "very interested" without a budget is a polite no.

The hardest disqualifier to ask is timeline. Founders hate it because it feels like you're rushing the buyer. But timeline is the difference between a real deal and a forever-maybe. A client I worked with in mid-2024 had a 5K consulting offer. Great pipeline. Nothing closing. Every prospect was "interested but we're still evaluating options." I told him: stop accepting that answer. Ask "What does your decision timeline look like, and what happens if you don't solve this by then?" 

First call with the new question: prospect said "We're looking to decide in the next quarter." That's 90 days, maybe 120. Founder pushed: "What's driving that timeline? What's the cost if you wait?" Prospect went vague: "We just want to make sure we pick the right partner." No urgency. No cost to delay. Disqualified. Founder moved on. Next call: prospect said "We need this done by end of month or we miss our Q3 product launch." Real deadline. Real cost. Deal closed in 6 days.

from a past engagement — the session where we rebuilt the entire qualification framework around urgency and consequence.

One more from a productized service founder selling LinkedIn profile builds. Price: ,500. Offer: rewrite the profile, redesign the banner, optimize for search, deliver in 7 days. Great offer. Terrible clients. Half of them would ghost after delivery, never post again, then ask for refunds because "it didn't work." Problem: he never asked what they'd do AFTER the profile was done.

I gave him a disqualifier: "A great profile is step one. What's your plan for content after we ship this?" Silence. Most prospects had no plan. No posting strategy. No content system. Just a vague hope that a better profile would "attract clients." He started declining those deals. Kept only the ones who said "I'm already posting 3x a week, I just need the profile to match the content" or "I have a content system, I just need the profile to convert better." His refund rate dropped to zero. His testimonials got 10x stronger because the people he worked with were actually using the profile.

title: Scripts and exact phrases
text:
## Scripts and exact phrases

"What have you already tried to solve this, and why didn't it work?" — disqualifies people who haven't tried anything (no urgency) or who tried but didn't do the work (won't succeed with you either).

"What budget have you set aside for this?" — disqualifies people with no allocated budget. If they haven't put money on the table yet, they're browsing.

"Who else is involved in this decision besides you?" — catches ICs gathering information for someone with actual authority. If the decision-maker isn't on the call, you're pitching to the wrong person.

"Walk me through what happens after you say yes. What's the internal process?" — reveals bureaucracy, procurement workflows, board approvals. If the process takes 90 days, you either wait or walk.

"What's your timeline for making this decision, and what's the cost if you don't solve this by then?" — separates urgency from interest. No cost to delay = no urgency = no deal.

"Help me understand — is this a priority you're actively solving, or something you're exploring for later?" — gives them permission to admit it's not urgent. If they say "exploring," you disqualify and tell them to reconnect when it's urgent.

"After we deliver this, what's your plan for implementation?" — for productized services or workshops. Catches people who think the deliverable IS the outcome.

"On a scale of 1 to 10, how committed are you to solving this in the next 30 days?" — anything below an 8 is a polite no. If they say 6 or 7, ask what would make it a 10. If the answer is vague, disqualify.

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

**Mistake 1: Asking disqualifying questions at the wrong time.** If you open the call with "What's your budget?" before establishing value, you sound like a vendor. Disqualifiers work after you've confirmed the problem is real and they care about solving it. Earn the right to disqualify by proving you understand their situation first.

**Mistake 2: Softening the question so much it stops working.** "I'm just curious, have you thought about budget at all?" is not a disqualifier. It's a softball. The buyer will say "yeah we're flexible" and you've learned nothing. The question has to cost them something to answer honestly. "What budget have you set aside?" costs more than "have you thought about budget?"

**Mistake 3: Accepting the first answer without digging.** Prospect says "I'm the decision-maker." You move on. Two weeks later you find out they need CFO approval. The mistake wasn't asking the question — it was not confirming the answer. Follow-up: "So once you decide this is the right move, you can sign today? Or is there a process after that?"

**Mistake 4: Disqualifying in your head but not out loud.** You ask about timeline. They say "we're just exploring options right now." You know it's not a real deal, but you keep the conversation going because you don't want to be rude. This is where deals go to die. If you've disqualified them, say it. "It sounds like this isn't urgent for you yet. Let's reconnect when it is."

**Mistake 5: Treating disqualification as rejection.** The founder hears "disqualify" and thinks "be mean to prospects." That's not it. Disqualifying is respect. You're respecting their time by not pitching something they're not ready for. You're respecting your time by not chasing deals that won't close. The script is kind but direct: "Based on what you've shared, I don't think we're the right fit right now. Here's why."

**Mistake 6: Asking the question but ignoring the answer.** Prospect says they have no budget allocated. You pitch anyway because "maybe they'll find budget." They won't. You've just spent 40 minutes pitching to someone who told you in minute 5 that they can't buy. The disqualifier only works if you act on the answer.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Most sales advice says "always be closing." I say always be disqualifying.

The standard playbook is: get them on the call, build rapport, pitch the value, handle objections, close. That works if your goal is activity. It doesn't work if your goal is revenue. You end up with a full calendar and an empty bank account.

The better strategy: get them on the call, confirm the problem, disqualify fast, pitch only to the ones who pass. You do fewer calls. You close more deals. Your pipeline has 8 real opportunities instead of 25 maybes.

Another contrarian take: disqualifying makes you MORE attractive, not less. When you tell a prospect "I don't think we're the right fit," two things happen. If they were never serious, they agree and you both move on. If they were serious, they fight to stay in. That fight is the signal. The prospect who says "wait, why not?" and starts explaining why they ARE the right fit is the one who closes. You've flipped the dynamic. Now they're selling you.

The trap most founders fall into is thinking interest equals intent. Someone books a call. They ask good questions. They nod along. The founder thinks "this is closing." But interest is cheap. Intent costs something. Disqualifying questions separate the two. If the prospect can't answer the budget question, the timeline question, or the authority question, they were never intending to buy. They were interested in learning.

One more: most founders think a "no" is a failed call. I think a fast "no" is a successful call. You just saved 20 hours. The goal isn't to close every prospect. The goal is to close every RIGHT prospect and disqualify every wrong one before you waste time on them.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

You book 12 sales calls in a month. You disqualify 7 of them in the first 10 minutes. You do full pitches for 5. You close 4. Your close rate is 80% on the deals you actually pitch. Your calendar has space. Your pipeline is clean. Your confidence is high because you're no longer getting rejected by people who were never going to buy.

Observable signal: the deals you DO pitch close faster. Because everyone involved has authority, budget, urgency, and a plan for after delivery. There's no "I need to think about it" or "let me run this by my team." Those filters already ran.

Another signal: prospects start respecting your process. When you disqualify someone and explain why, they don't get defensive. They say "that makes sense, I'll reach out when we're ready." Six months later, they come back with budget and close in one call. Because you didn't waste their time pretending it was a fit when it wasn't.

Numbers from real clients: one founder went from 30% close rate (3 closed out of 10 full pitches) to 70% close rate (7 closed out of 10) by adding three disqualifiers to his discovery process. He didn't change his pitch. He didn't lower his price. He just stopped pitching to people who were never going to buy.

The before state: "I'm doing so many calls but nothing's closing. I think my offer is wrong." The after state: "I'm doing fewer calls and closing most of them. I think my offer is fine, I was just pitching to the wrong people."

One founder I worked with tracked it precisely. Before disqualifiers: 18 discovery calls, 12 proposals sent, 2 closed. After disqualifiers: 18 discovery calls, 6 proposals sent, 5 closed. Same top-of-funnel volume. Half the proposals. More than double the closed deals. The disqualifiers didn't reduce his pipeline — they concentrated it.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

Most follow-up sequences die because they chase a decision instead of moving a conversation.

The prospect who says "I need to think about it" or goes quiet after a proposal isn't waiting for you to check in. They're waiting for new information that changes the math in their head.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

The gap between "maybe" and "yes" is where most revenue gets lost.

Not because the offer was wrong. Not because the prospect wasn't qualified. Because the founder sends three "just checking in" emails, gets no reply, and moves on.

Here's what's actually happening in that gap: the prospect forgets the specific pain you named on the call. They get distracted by three other priorities. They convince themselves the timing isn't right. They talk to a cheaper option. They decide to try it themselves first.

Every day you're not in their inbox with something useful, someone else is.

The cost of bad follow-up isn't just one lost deal. It's the compounding effect of being known as "another person who chases but doesn't add value." That reputation spreads. Future prospects see your name and think "oh, that's the guy who kept emailing me after I said no."

The leverage of getting this right: a systematic follow-up cadence can convert 20-30% of maybes into yeses without a single additional sales call. That's pure margin. No extra ad spend. No new content. Just staying present with value until the decision window opens.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

The pattern I see most often: founder closes a great discovery call, sends a proposal, gets "I need to think about it," waits three days, sends "just wanted to follow up," gets nothing, waits a week, sends "wanted to see if you had any questions," gets nothing, gives up.

Total follow-up: two emails. Zero value delivered. Zero reason for the prospect to re-engage.

When I walk clients through their CRM, the "no-decision" column is always the biggest. Deals that went quiet. Proposals that got ghosted. Calls that felt like wins but led nowhere.

The actual issue isn't the prospect. It's that the founder has no system for what happens after maybe.

One client, a leadership coach running mid-six-figure ARR, had 14 "thinking about it" prospects in his pipeline. Average deal size a low three-figure amount. That's 12K sitting in limbo. I asked him: "What's your follow-up sequence?" He said: "I send a couple emails and if they don't reply I assume they're not interested."

We built a six-touch sequence. First email: case study of a client with the exact pain the prospect named on the call. Second email: a one-page diagnostic they could fill out to self-assess readiness. Third email: a contrarian take on why most people fail at the outcome he promises. Fourth email: a specific stat or story from his vault that proved the method works. Fifth email: "I'm closing this thread — here's the last thing I'd tell you if we never speak again." Sixth email: "I lied, one more thing" with a final specific proof point.

Four of the 14 booked follow-up calls within three weeks. Two closed. mid five figures in revenue from deals that were dead. The follow-up cost him two hours to write the sequence and zero hours to send (all automated via his CRM).

Cited from multiple client sessions logged In a past engagement and [a past engagement].

Another pattern: the founder who follows up too fast with nothing new to say.

Prospect says "I need to run this by my co-founder." Founder emails the next morning: "Hey, did you get a chance to chat with your co-founder?" Prospect thinks: "It's been 12 hours, calm down."

The correct move: "Totally fair. I'll send you a one-pager tomorrow that makes it easy to share with them. In the meantime, here's the exact ROI calculation I walked through on our call in case they ask."

Now the follow-up adds value. The prospect has something to forward. The co-founder sees professionalism, not desperation.

Third pattern: the founder who doesn't define what "no-decision" actually means.

"I need to think about it" could mean: I don't have budget. I don't trust you yet. I don't believe the outcome is possible. I need to talk to my spouse. I want to try the cheap version first. I'm comparing you to two other options.

Those are six different objections. They need six different follow-up sequences.

When I run discovery call audits with clients, I make them listen to the recording and name the REAL objection. Not what the prospect said. What they meant.

If the prospect said "I need to think about it" but the real objection was "I don't think this will work for my industry," the follow-up sequence should deliver case studies from their industry. Not generic check-ins.

One client ran a personal branding agency for executives. Prospect: VP of Sales at a SaaS company. Said yes to everything on the call, then went quiet after the proposal. Client sent two "checking in" emails. Nothing.

I asked: "What was the actual blocker?" Client: "He said he needed to check budget but I think he was scared his company would see his LinkedIn presence as a distraction."

Correct follow-up: case study of another VP who built a personal brand AND got promoted because the CEO saw him as a thought leader.

Client sent that email. Prospect replied in 20 minutes. Booked the follow-up. Closed three days later.

The objection was never budget. It was fear. The follow-up had to speak to the fear directly.

text:
## Specific examples from the vault

Real sequence from a workshop client who sold a low three-figure amount strategy sessions to solo founders.

After a "maybe" from a prospect, the sequence ran like this over 10 days:

Day 1: "Here's the recording of our call + the three frameworks I mentioned. No action needed, just wanted you to have it."

Day 3: Case study. Subject line: "This founder had the exact same hesitation you did." Body: 300 words on a client who said "I need to think about it," signed two weeks later, and hit their revenue goal in 90 days. Ended with: "Not saying this is you, just wanted to share."

Day 5: A one-page diagnostic. Subject line: "Fill this out or don't — your call." Body: "I built a 10-question self-assessment that tells you if you're ready for this kind of engagement. Takes 3 minutes. If you score below 7/10, we probably shouldn't work together yet. Here's the link."

Day 7: Contrarian take. Subject line: "Why most strategy sessions are a waste of money." Body: Four paragraphs on why founders pay for strategy and never implement it. Ended with: "The only reason my sessions work is [specific structural thing]. If you're going to hire anyone for strategy, make sure they do this."

Day 10: Final email. Subject line: "I'm closing this thread." Body: "No hard feelings if this isn't the right fit. One last thing I'd tell you: [specific tactical advice from the call]. Use it whether we work together or not. If you change your mind in the next 6 months, my calendar link is below."

Result: prospect replied on Day 11. "I've been thinking about this every day. Let's do it."

Another example from my own vault: a prospect who ghosted after a 5K proposal.

I sent three emails over two weeks. All value, zero ask.

First email: a voice note walking through the one thing I'd change about his LinkedIn profile even if he never hired me. 90 seconds. Embedded in the email.

Second email: a mini case study of a client who had his exact objection (too expensive) and how we structured payment to make it work. Ended with: "Not pitching this to you, just wanted to show how we've solved this before."

Third email: a screenshot of his competitor's LinkedIn post that was getting 10x his engagement, with a two-paragraph breakdown of why. Ended with: "Thought you'd find this useful."

Prospect replied to the third email: "This is the kind of insight I need. Can we get on a call?"

Call happened. Closed at 2K (slightly lower than original proposal, but still closed).

The follow-up wasn't "checking in." It was demonstrating the value he'd get if he hired me.

Third example from a client who sold 5K consulting engagements to e-commerce brands.

Prospect: founder of a M ARR DTC brand. Great call. Proposal sent. Went quiet for three weeks.

Client's instinct: "They're not interested, move on."

My push: "Send one more email. Make it about them, not you."

Email subject: "I built this for you (use it even if we don't work together)."

Email body: A custom Loom video analyzing the brand's Instagram feed, naming three specific changes that would increase engagement, and walking through the logic. Ended with: "No strings attached. Thought you'd find this helpful."

Prospect replied: "This is incredible. Can we talk this week?"

Call happened. Closed at a low three-figure amount (higher than the original proposal because the prospect saw the work quality firsthand).

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

Checking in without adding value. "Just wanted to see if you had any questions." The prospect thinks: "If I had questions I would have asked."

Following up too fast. Prospect says "I need to think about it." Founder emails 24 hours later. Prospect thinks: "I haven't even had time to think yet."

Following up with the same message twice. First email: "Do you have any questions?" No reply. Second email, three days later: "Just wanted to follow up — do you have any questions?" Prospect thinks: "You already asked me that."

Not segmenting by objection. Sending the same follow-up sequence to everyone who says "maybe" regardless of why they said maybe. Budget objection needs a different sequence than timing objection.

Giving up after two emails. Most founders send two follow-ups, get no reply, assume the deal is dead. Real conversion happens between touch 3 and touch 6.

Apologizing for following up. "Sorry to bother you again…" or "I know you're busy but…" Apologizing trains the prospect to see your emails as an interruption. Don't apologize. Add value and they'll want to hear from you.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Most sales advice says "follow up 5-7 times." I say: follow up as many times as you can add value. If you can add value 12 times, send 12 emails. If you can only add value twice, send two and stop.

The number of touches doesn't matter. The value per touch does.

I've had clients close deals on the 9th follow-up email because every single email delivered something useful. I've also had clients burn bridges by sending 4 worthless "checking in" emails in two weeks.

The other contrarian take: don't automate the entire sequence.

Most founders build a 5-email drip in their CRM, set it, forget it. The emails go out on schedule whether or not the prospect opens them, clicks them, or replies.

Better approach: automate emails 1-3. Personalize emails 4-6 based on what the prospect actually engaged with.

If they opened the case study email but not the diagnostic email, that tells you something. Send email 4 as another case study, not another diagnostic.

If they clicked through to your pricing page after email 2 but didn't book a call, that tells you price is the sticking point. Email 4 should address pricing directly (payment plans, ROI calculator, risk reversal).

Automation saves time. Personalization wins deals. Use both.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

The prospect replies to email 3 or 4 instead of ghosting.

The prospect forwards your email to a decision-maker with "thoughts?" in the subject line.

The prospect books a follow-up call without you asking.

The prospect says "I've been thinking about this every day" when they re-engage.

The prospect closes faster on the second call because the follow-up sequence already handled objections.

You close 20-30% of "maybe" deals instead of 5%.

Your CRM "no-decision" column shrinks because deals either close or you consciously decide to stop following up (instead of letting them rot in limbo).

Prospects who don't close still say "that was the most helpful follow-up I've ever received" and refer you to others.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

"I'll get back next week" means the sale is dead unless you change the frame right now.

The prospect isn't buying time to think. They're buying time to forget. Next week becomes next month becomes never. The decision to delay is the decision to say no without the discomfort of saying it.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Most founders treat "I'll get back next week" as a polite pause in an ongoing conversation. It's not. It's the end of the conversation unless you intervene.

The cost shows up in three places. First, your pipeline rots. Every "next week" that goes unaddressed becomes a follow-up email you'll send that nobody reads. Second, your close rate craters. You're not losing deals to competitors. You're losing them to inertia. Third, you train yourself to accept soft nos as maybes, which destroys your ability to qualify hard.

The mechanism is simple: buying decisions happen in moments of clarity, not in moments of "let me think about it." If the prospect was clear enough to say yes, they would have. If they're not clear, leaving the call without resolving it guarantees they never will be.

When you let someone off the call with "get back next week," you've handed them the out they were looking for. They'll spend the next seven days not thinking about your offer. They'll spend them doing literally anything else. By the time you follow up, the context is gone, the urgency is gone, and the emotional pull that got them on the call in the first place is gone.

The leverage of getting this right is immediate. Founders who reframe "next week" on the call close 3x more deals than founders who accept it and follow up later. That's not because they're better salespeople. It's because they finish the sale in the moment when the buying decision is actually happening.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

The pattern repeats across every founder I've worked with: someone books a discovery call, the conversation goes well, the founder presents the offer, and the prospect says "this sounds great, let me think about it and get back to you next week."

The founder — relieved the call didn't end in an outright no — says "absolutely, take your time" and sends a follow-up email three days later. Crickets. Another email a week after that. More crickets. By week three, the prospect is gone.

I saw this exact sequence with a client In a past engagement. a client had been in sales conversations with a billionaire investor. The conversation was going well. The investor was interested. But there was no hard next step locked in before the call ended. Danny's advice in that session: never let someone leave a call with "I'll get back." Instead, set the hard next-step before you hang up.

The reframe Danny taught him: "I'll send a one-pager by EOD. Reply with yes, no, or 'still thinking and here's why.' Anything else and I'll assume it's a no."

That's the move. You're not chasing. You're closing the loop. The prospect either commits to a clear next action or you treat silence as a no and move on.

Another pattern from a past engagement: Peter was stuck in the "I need to think about it" loop with multiple prospects. Danny walked him through the diagnostic: "I need to think about it" almost never means thinking. It means a missing piece on the call. Price, scope, fit, or timing. One of those four.

The fix: stop accepting "think about it" as a real answer. Instead, name the four and make the prospect pick one. "Walk me through what's still unclear. Price, scope, fit, or timing?" Most of the time they name one. Then you work it right there on the call.

The thing Danny never does: send "just checking in" follow-ups. Those train the prospect to expect chasing. He closes on the call or he doesn't close.

This shows up in workshop sales too. A founder attends a workshop, books a 1:1 after, and says "this is exactly what I need, let me talk to my co-founder and get back next week." If you let them leave without a clear next step, the co-founder conversation never happens. The week becomes two weeks. The sale dies.

The move Danny teaches: "Great. What's the one question your co-founder will ask that I should answer before you leave this call?" Force the objection into the room now. If they can't name it, the co-founder isn't the blocker. Uncertainty is. And uncertainty doesn't get solved by waiting a week.

In a past engagement, a client was navigating a similar pattern with a potential investor who wanted to "get back next week" after an initial meeting. Danny's response: don't wait. Propose a concrete next step before the meeting ends. Not "let me know when you're ready." Something time-bound, outcome-specific, and mutual.

The difference between founders who close and founders who chase is this: closers treat "next week" as a negotiation that happens now. Chasers treat it as a reason to follow up later.
