title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

You can hire your way out of every problem except the one where you're still figuring out what the problem actually is.

The moment you delegate something you don't understand, you hand the steering wheel to someone who's guessing what you meant.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Most founders treat hiring like a solution to overwhelm. Calendar full, inbox drowning, content not shipping — the instinct is to find someone who can "take it off your plate."

That instinct kills businesses.

When you hire before you've run the system yourself, you can't tell the difference between someone executing poorly and someone executing a bad brief. You can't coach. You can't course-correct. You can't fire intelligently. You're just hoping they figure it out.

The cost shows up in three places. First, you burn cash paying someone to learn what you should have already documented. Second, you lose months to a hire who was never set up to succeed because the role wasn't real yet. Third, you train yourself to be helpless — every time something breaks, you look for someone to hire instead of asking if the system itself is broken.

The founders who scale without collapsing are the ones who can toggle. They know exactly which work only they can do, which work can be delegated today, and which work needs to stay with them until the system is repeatable enough that handing it off won't destroy it.

This isn't about being a control freak. It's about being the only person in the business who can afford to waste time figuring out what actually works. Everyone you hire after that depends on you having done that work first.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

The pattern shows up in every 1:1 coaching engagement within the first three calls. Founder says they need to hire a VA, a content manager, a marketing person, a LinkedIn ghostwriter. I ask them to walk me through their current workflow. They can't. They describe the outcome they want, not the system that produces it.

That's the diagnostic moment. If you can't document it, you can't delegate it.

The fastest version of this showed up with a founder who was posting 3x a week on LinkedIn and getting solid engagement [a past engagement]. He wanted to hire someone to "handle LinkedIn" so he could focus on sales. I asked him to record himself writing one post and send me the video. He couldn't finish. He kept restarting, second-guessing, checking other people's posts, abandoning the draft. The workflow didn't exist. What he actually had was talent — an instinct for what resonated — and he was trying to hire someone to reverse-engineer that instinct without ever documenting it himself.

The fix wasn't hiring. The fix was forcing him to write 20 posts in two weeks and narrate his decision-making process out loud while he did it. By post 15, the pattern was obvious: he opened with a contrarian take, backed it with a client name and a number, then closed with a one-line question. That became the SOP. Once we had that, we could hand it to a VA who populated the template with raw material from his call transcripts. Now the VA was executing a system, not guessing at his voice.

Another client ran a productized consulting offer and wanted to hire a CSM to handle onboarding [a past engagement]. I asked what the first 7 days of a new client looked like. He sent me a Notion doc with 8 tasks and no context. "Send welcome email. Schedule kickoff. Deliver template pack. Check in on progress." I asked him to actually run one client through it while screen-recording. By day 3, he was improvising. The template pack link was broken. The kickoff call had no agenda. The check-in happened whenever he remembered. The system was fake.

We spent two weeks with him running onboarding himself while documenting every decision point, every question clients asked, every moment where he had to improvise. That became the real onboarding SOP. Only then could a CSM execute it. The difference: the first version would have resulted in a confused CSM, angry clients, and the founder jumping back in to "save" every onboarding. The second version produced a CSM who closed 9 out of 10 onboardings without founder involvement.

The inverse pattern also shows up constantly: founders who refuse to delegate anything because they've convinced themselves they're the only ones who can do it right [a past engagement]. That's not craftsmanship. That's identity debt. They're terrified that if someone else does the work, they'll become irrelevant. So they stay trapped in execution while the business can't scale.

The clearest example was a founder running a a low three-figure amount/year coaching practice entirely solo. No VA, no admin, no help. He was manually scheduling every call, writing every invoice, sending every follow-up. I asked him what would break if he hired someone to handle scheduling. He said, "Clients expect me to handle it personally." I asked him to test it. He hired a Calendly VA for one month. Not a single client mentioned it. He saved 6 hours a week.

The lesson: he was confusing being the talent with being the system. Clients were paying for his coaching, not his calendar management. But because he'd been doing both for five years, he couldn't see the difference anymore.

The most expensive version of this shows up in content. Founder builds an audience by posting consistently for 6 months. Then they try to hand it to a ghostwriter or a content VA without ever documenting what made their posts work [a past engagement]. The ghostwriter starts posting. Engagement drops by 60% in two weeks. The founder panics, fires the ghostwriter, goes back to doing it themselves, and swears off delegation forever.

The mistake: they handed off the output without documenting the system. They never wrote down their hook formulas, their story structure, their voice rules, their banned phrases. The ghostwriter was guessing. Of course it failed.

The fix in every case is the same: DIY long enough to make the system legible, then hire someone to run the system you documented.

title: Specific examples from the vault
text:
## Specific examples from the vault

The clearest application of this framework came during a session with a founder who wanted to build an AI content team [a past engagement]. He'd been using Claude to write LinkedIn posts but kept getting generic outputs. He thought the solution was to hire a better prompt engineer. I asked him to walk through his actual workflow. He'd type "write a LinkedIn post about [topic]" and paste whatever came back. No voice doc. No examples. No constraints.

I had him document one post he'd written himself that performed well, then narrate why each sentence worked. We turned that into a Voice DNA document and a constraints list (no em dashes, no hashtags, no "let's dive in"). Then we fed that into Claude and tested again. The output was 80% closer to his voice immediately. No hire needed. The problem wasn't the tool. The problem was he'd never documented what good looked like.

Another example from the vault: a founder running AI School operations wanted to build a team for session documentation [a past engagement]. He had a vision for an app that would take session transcripts, generate summaries, create worksheets, and send follow-up emails to attendees. He wanted to hire a developer and a content writer to handle it. I asked what the output should actually look like. He couldn't describe it. We paused the hiring plan and spent two weeks having him manually produce the documentation for three sessions himself — transcribing, summarizing, building the worksheets by hand. By session three, the pattern was obvious. Only then did we spec the app. The developer built exactly what was needed because the founder had done the work to know what "done" looked like.

A counterexample from a session where a founder was building a workshop curriculum [a past engagement]: he wanted to teach participants how to build their first AI teammate in Claude. He'd never built one himself. He wanted to hire a curriculum designer. I told him that was backwards. The curriculum designer can't design what doesn't exist yet. He needed to run the workshop once himself, document what worked, identify where participants got stuck, then hand that learning to a designer. He resisted for two weeks, then ran a pilot session with five people. Three of them stalled on Step 3 (writing custom instructions). That became the place where the designer added extra scaffolding and examples. If he'd hired the designer first, they'd have guessed wrong about where to add support.

The LPG distribution system project showed the opposite dynamic — where DIY was the wrong move [a past engagement]. The client needed a full operations platform: inventory tracking, billing, debt collection, multi-location warehouse management. The founder wanted to build it himself in Notion and spreadsheets because "it's cheaper than hiring a developer." I walked him through what building it himself would actually require: learning database design, learning how to structure RLS policies, learning how to write Supabase functions, learning how to deploy on Replit. At his skill level, that was 6 months of learning before he'd ship anything. Meanwhile, his business was losing money daily because the manual process was breaking. This was a hire scenario. We brought in a developer, and the system was live in three weeks.

The decision rule that emerged from that session: if the work is in your domain of expertise, DIY until you can document it. If the work is outside your domain and the cost of learning it exceeds the cost of hiring someone who already knows it, hire immediately.

title: Scripts and exact phrases
text:
## Scripts and exact phrases

"Can you narrate your workflow out loud while you do it? I want to hear every decision you make." — The diagnostic I use when a founder says they want to hire for something. If they can't narrate it, they don't understand it well enough to delegate it.

"If you hired someone tomorrow, what would you tell them to do on day one?" — Forces the founder to articulate the system before they delegate it.

"You're not hiring a person. You're hiring an executor of a system you haven't documented yet." — The reframe when a founder treats hiring as the solution to not having a process.

"The system lives in your head. Your job is to get it onto paper before you hand it to anyone else." — Used when a founder resists documenting because "it's just obvious."

"You can't delegate what you can't explain." — The one-line version of the entire framework.

"The question isn't 'Can someone else do this?' The question is 'Have I done it enough times to know what good looks like?'" — The decision filter before any hiring conversation.

"You're confusing being the talent with being the system." — When a founder refuses to delegate because they think only they can do it right.

"Hire for execution, not for figuring it out." — The line I use when a founder wants to hire someone to solve a problem they haven't defined yet.

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

**Hiring to solve overwhelm instead of hiring to scale a system.** The founder is drowning, so they hire someone to "take things off their plate." The hire starts working. The founder realizes they still have to explain everything, answer every question, and redo half the work. The time saved was an illusion. The actual fix: pause hiring, document the workflow, then hire someone to execute the documented system.

**Delegating before documenting.** Founder hands a task to a VA with no SOP, no examples, no constraints. The VA guesses. The output is wrong. The founder concludes the VA is incompetent and does it themselves forever. The real issue: they delegated a task that lived entirely in their head.

**Confusing delegation with abdication.** The founder believes "hiring someone" means they never have to think about that function again. They hand off product, marketing, or sales to a hire and step away completely. Three months later, everything is off-course. Delegation means you hand off execution while staying accountable for the outcome. Abdication means you hand off the outcome and hope for the best.

**Staying in DIY mode for identity reasons, not strategic reasons.** The founder is capable of delegating but won't because "no one will care as much as I do" or "I'm a perfectionist." That's ego masquerading as quality control. If you've documented the system and trained someone competently, and they're still not performing, the issue is hiring quality or training quality — not the concept of delegation itself.

**Hiring for a role before the role is real.** Founder decides they need a CMO, a Head of Product, or a COO before the business has defined what that role actually does day-to-day. The hire shows up and spends three months "figuring out the strategy" because the role was a title, not a job. Real roles emerge from work that's already happening and needs to scale. Fake roles emerge from org charts and aspiration.

**DIY-ing outside your zone of genius as a cost-saving measure.** Founder spends six months learning to code because "hiring a developer is expensive," when their time would generate 10x more value doing founder-level work (sales, fundraising, product vision). DIY is smart when you're learning a system you need to own. DIY is expensive when you're learning a skill you'll never use again after this one task.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

The standard advice is "hire fast, fire fast" or "delegate everything that's not in your zone of genius." Both are wrong for early-stage founders.

Hiring fast works if you're a funded startup with room for experimentation. For a bootstrapped founder running a low four figures business, a bad hire costs three months of runway and six months of momentum. You can't afford to hire fast. You have to hire right.

Delegating everything outside your zone of genius assumes you've already figured out what your genius is. Most founders haven't. What looks like "not your zone" might just be "not yet systematized." The founder who thinks they're bad at sales is often just bad at the unstructured early sales process. Once they run 20 sales calls and document what works, they realize they're competent at it — they just hadn't built the system yet.

The deeper contrarian take: DIY is underrated in a world that worships delegation. Every great operator I know spent years doing the work themselves before they hired anyone. They didn't outsource early. They built the machine by hand, documented every bolt and wire, then hired people to run the machine they designed.

That's the opposite of the "4-Hour Workweek" fantasy where you hire a VA on day one and disappear to a beach. The founders who disappear early come back to businesses that collapsed because nobody understood how it actually worked.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

The founder can describe their business in systems, not tasks. They don't say "I need someone to handle LinkedIn." They say "I have a LinkedIn production workflow: pull raw material from call transcripts, apply the hook formula, run it through the voice doc, design the carousel in Canva, schedule in Buffer. I'm delegating step 3 and step 4. I'm keeping step 1, 2, and 5."

New hires ramp in days, not months. Because the system is documented, onboarding is "here's the SOP, here's the last five examples, here's the checklist, here's where you ask questions." The hire starts producing output on day two.

The founder can leave for a week and nothing breaks. Not because they've abdicated, but because the system runs without them needing to narrate every move. They check in. They course-correct. But they're not in the weeds.

Delegation doesn't feel like a risk anymore. The founder knows exactly what good looks like because they did it themselves 50 times. When the VA submits work, they can evaluate it in 30 seconds. No second-guessing. No "I guess that's fine." Just "yes, ship it" or "redo step 3."

Output quality stays consistent when the founder steps back. The content still sounds like them. The client onboarding still converts. The SOPs still get followed. The business doesn't collapse the moment the founder isn't personally doing the work.

The founder's calendar shifts from execution to decision-making. They're no longer writing every post, scheduling every call, invoicing every client. They're reviewing systems, coaching hires, and working on the next phase of the business.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

Walk away before the money is wasted, not after.

The best projects are the ones you don't start. The second-best are the ones you kill before they kill you.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Most founders confuse motion with progress.

They see a shiny new app idea, a potential partnership, a "we should totally build this" moment, and they start moving. They prototype. They hire. They book calls. They invest weeks into something that should have died in the first conversation.

The cost is invisible until it's catastrophic. Six weeks vanish. A developer burns through retainer hours. A client relationship sours because you oversold a half-baked concept. Your own time gets swallowed by a project that was never going to make money.

The leverage of killing early is enormous. One hour of ruthless pre-mortem saves twenty hours of recovery. One "no" protects your entire month. One hard stop at the right moment keeps your pipeline clean, your focus sharp, and your business from drowning in half-finished commitments.

The problem is most people don't have the criteria. They can't tell the difference between a real problem worth solving and a vanity project dressed up as strategy. They can't separate "this feels exciting" from "this will actually close." They can't name the moment when they should stop.

This category exists to give you the criteria.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

The pattern repeats across dozens of calls: the client comes in excited about a new project, I ask three questions, and the project is dead within ten minutes.

Not because the idea is bad. Because the conditions for success aren't there.

I saw this with Maven Course planning In a past engagement. Ross had been chasing a travel brand partnership for weeks. He'd already delivered one video that flopped. They'd promised more work. They'd teased a Guatemala tourism board connection. He was burning hours on follow-ups and feeling like he was about to break through.

The red flags were everywhere. The video they asked him to post didn't match his style. They made him post at midnight instead of his peak time. They wouldn't commit to pricing until after the "test." They kept saying "we'll see" instead of "here's the next step."

I didn't have to tell Ross to walk away. I just had to show him he was already walking toward nothing.

The kill signal was simple: they were using him to test ideas, not to execute a plan. No real brief. No locked budget. No timeline. Just "do this and maybe we'll talk about the next thing."

That's not a client. That's a time drain dressed up as an opportunity.

Same pattern with Maria In a past engagement. She came in struggling to define her ICP because she didn't have a business yet. She was trying to build a personal brand without knowing what she was selling. She was about to get fired and wanted to start "softly contacting people" about freelance work.

The mistake most coaches make here is they'd help her write better LinkedIn posts. I stopped the whole thing.

If you don't know what you're selling, you can't build a brand. If you can't name your offer, posting content is theatre. The project isn't "build Maria's brand." The project is "help Maria figure out what she does."

We ran the Ikigai GPT. We extracted her actual expertise (consumer insights, shopper research, competitor strategy). We named the one thing people already ask her for. Then we could talk about positioning.

The kill decision was killing the "let's work on LinkedIn" project and replacing it with "let's define the offer first."

In a past engagement, a client came in wanting feedback on a video. The video was fine. The real issue was he wanted to add a "join the community" CTA at the end. I asked what the community was. He said "we're not ready for that yet."

That's the kill signal right there. If you're not ready to deliver on the thing you're asking people to sign up for, don't ask.

The instinct is to build momentum. Get the signups. Figure it out later. That instinct destroys credibility faster than doing nothing. People remember when you overpromise. They forget when you underpromise.

We cut the community line from the video. The video still worked. The ask was clearer. The follow-through was real.

The a platform partner project In a past engagement is the opposite pattern: a project that should have been killed but wasn't. Eight sessions deep. Sixteen pages of features. PDF exports. AI session summaries. Weekly metric tracking. Challenge progress tables. Voyage AI embeddings for feedback clustering.

The build was technically flawless. The problem was never defined.

The user wanted "an app that looks exactly like this" and attached a screenshot. The goal was vague: "make sure this app is actually something we want to build for a platform partner." The use cases were broad: transcript-to-doc generation, Taki Moore-style email writing, campaign cadence automation.

That's not a brief. That's a wishlist.

A real brief has one sentence: "This app solves [specific problem] for [specific person] and ships [specific outcome] in [specific timeframe]." If you can't write that sentence, you don't have a project. You have motion.

The kill criteria I use with every new project:

1. Can the client name the one person this is for?
2. Can they describe the before-and-after in numbers?
3. Can they commit to using the first version within 7 days of delivery?
4. Do they already have 3+ examples of the problem costing them money or time?
5. Is this solving a workflow problem or a "wouldn't it be cool if" problem?

If the answer to any of those is no, the project gets killed or scoped down to a proof-of-concept. No exceptions.

The LPG system In a past engagement passed every test. The client had 8 product types, manual stock tracking, paper-based invoicing, and a debt collection process that required physical TT slips. They could name the exact cost: hours per week on manual admin, delayed payments from missing invoices, cylinder stock they couldn't track.

That project shipped. Because the conditions were there.

The EngagementFlow AI project In a past engagement is the cleanest example of a project that survived the kill test. a client and a client had one specific problem: the knowledge transfer gap between sales and customer success. They could describe the cost: senior leaders spending hours writing SOWs manually, no peer review mechanism, no audit trail from promise to delivery.

Twenty-six features got built. The platform went live. Because the problem was real, the buyer was clear, and the outcome was measurable.

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

**Mistake 1: Confusing excitement with viability**

The client comes in energized about a new idea. They've been thinking about it for weeks. They've told their team. They've sketched wireframes. The energy feels like validation.

It's not. Excitement is a starting point, not proof. The question isn't "does this feel good." The question is "will this close deals in 90 days."

**Mistake 2: Starting before the conditions are in place**

I see this constantly in app builds. The client wants to start coding before they've validated the problem. They want to design the UI before they've talked to 5 users. They want to hire a team before they've scoped the MVP.

Starting too early doesn't save time. It creates debt. You build the wrong thing, then rebuild it, then rebuild it again. Three times the cost, zero learning.

**Mistake 3: Treating "maybe" as "yes"**

"They said they're interested" is not a commitment. "They want to see a proposal" is not a green light. "They'll let us know" is not a timeline.

If the client or partner can't commit to a next step with a date, you don't have a deal. You have a conversation.

**Mistake 4: Solving the surface problem instead of the real one**

Maria wanted help with LinkedIn. The real problem was she didn't know what she was selling. Irving wanted content strategy. The real problem was he hadn't decided if he was moving to Thailand.

If you solve the surface problem, you waste time and the client stays stuck. If you name the real problem, you either solve it or you kill the project and replace it with the right one.

**Mistake 5: Keeping a project alive because you've already invested time**

Sunk cost fallacy kills more projects than bad ideas. You've already spent three weeks on the prototype. You've already had four client calls. You've already pitched it internally.

None of that matters. The only question is: if you knew then what you know now, would you start this project today? If the answer is no, kill it.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Most business advice says "don't quit too early" and "persistence beats talent." That's true for the right projects. It's poison for the wrong ones.

The conventional wisdom is you need to push through the hard part. You need to test longer. You need to give it more time. You need to see if it works.

I think that's backwards. The hard part isn't the sign you should keep going. It's the sign you should check if you're solving the right problem.

If a project feels like pulling a truck uphill, you're probably pulling the wrong truck. The right projects have friction, but they don't feel like drowning. They feel like sprinting uphill: hard, but forward.

The other contrarian take: killing a project isn't failure. It's discipline.

Founders who can't kill projects end up with ten half-finished commitments and no wins. Founders who kill fast end up with three completed projects that actually ship.

The scorecard isn't how many projects you started. It's how many you finished. Killing the wrong ones is how you finish the right ones.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

You have a one-page kill checklist. Five questions. If the answer to any question is no, the project parks or dies.

You run every new idea through the checklist within 24 hours of the initial conversation. Not next week. Not after the prototype. Within 24 hours.

Your project list shrinks by 60%. Your shipping rate doubles.

You stop saying "let me think about it" and start saying "this doesn't pass the test yet, here's why." The client either fixes the conditions or they move on. Either outcome is better than six weeks of maybes.

When someone pitches you a partnership, you ask: "What's the specific next step with a date?" If they can't answer, you don't follow up. You let it die.

You stop confusing motion with progress. You stop booking calls to "explore ideas." You book calls to decide yes or no on a specific question by end of session.

Your calendar clears. Your focus sharpens. The projects you do start actually finish.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

When a client can't name their ICP in one sharp sentence, they don't have a positioning problem — they have a revenue problem waiting to happen.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

A broad ICP isn't neutral. It actively destroys the business.

Every dollar spent on content that tries to speak to "anyone who needs this" is a dollar lighting itself on fire. Every sales call with someone outside the bullseye is an hour the founder will never get back. Every piece of positioning that hedges — "we help coaches and consultants and entrepreneurs" — trains the market to scroll past.

The cost shows up in three places. First, the founder burns out. They're writing content for five different audiences, running five different value propositions, testing five different hooks. None of them land because none of them are specific enough to make one person stop and say "this is exactly me."

Second, the sales cycle stretches. A vague ICP means vague messaging. Vague messaging means the prospect has to do translation work in their head to figure out if this applies to them. Most won't bother. The ones who book a call spend the first 20 minutes asking clarifying questions instead of buying.

Third, the founder becomes a order-taker instead of a specialist. When you serve everyone, you command average rates. When you serve one person better than anyone else on the planet, you can charge what the outcome is worth.

The leverage of getting this right is the opposite of all three. Content that speaks to one person resonates with hundreds who match that profile. Sales calls with the right ICP close faster because the prospect already knows you built this for them. Pricing conversations shift from "why does this cost so much" to "when can we start."

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

I see the broad ICP pattern in 80% of first calls. The founder opens with some version of: "I help people grow their business" or "I work with anyone who wants to get better at X."

The diagnostic is simple. I ask: "Who's your last three paying clients?" They name them. Then I ask: "What do those three have in common?" Nine times out of ten, the answer is "not much."

That's the problem. Not the lack of clients. The lack of a pattern in who's buying.

One client I worked with in late 2024 was a leadership coach. Her initial ICP: "executives who want to lead better." When I pushed, she listed: a VP at a SaaS company, a solo consultant, and a mid-level manager at a nonprofit. Three completely different people with three completely different problems.

We spent the first 30 minutes of the call forcing constraints. I asked: "If you could only work with one of those three types for the next 12 months, which one would make you the most money?" She picked the VP. Then: "Why that one?" Answer: "They have budget, they make decisions fast, and the results are visible."

That's the real ICP. Not the one you wish you had. The one that actually pays and actually gets results. [a past engagement]

Another pattern: the founder who's afraid to narrow because they think they'll lose opportunities. Dr. Subra came in saying she worked with "professionals who want to learn mind mapping." The word "professionals" is a red flag. It means nothing.

I asked her to name the last ten people who actually paid. She listed them. Eight were mid-career professionals stuck in corporate jobs who wanted a side business. Two were retirees.

I told her: cut the retirees. Not because they're bad people. Because they're a different business. Mid-career professionals buy differently, consume differently, refer differently. Trying to serve both means your messaging appeals to neither.

She resisted for 20 minutes. Then she admitted: "The retirees take twice as long to close and they haggle on price." That's the signal. Your real ICP is the one who buys fast, pays what you ask, and gets results that make you look good. [a past engagement]

The Founder OS workshop in November 2025 had a live example of this playing out. One attendee was building an AI productivity course. His ICP: "anyone who wants to use AI better."

I stopped him. "That's not an ICP. That's a Google search query."

We did the constraint exercise in real time. I asked: "Who's the one person who, if they got results, would tell ten other people exactly like them?" He thought for a minute. Then: "Solo founders running service businesses who are drowning in admin work."

That's an ICP. It's specific enough that you can picture the person. It's narrow enough that you can build a solution they'll pay for. It's connected enough that one success story creates ten referrals. [a past engagement]

The pattern I see in every narrowing conversation: the founder fights it until they see the math. A broad ICP means you're competing with everyone. A narrow ICP means you're the only option for that exact person.

One founder I worked with was building an AI consulting offer. Initial ICP: "businesses that want to implement AI." We spent 45 minutes narrowing. Final ICP: "Solo founders running low four figures service businesses who are the face of their brand and spending 12+ hours a week on content."

That's not narrower because it sounds good. It's narrower because every word is a filter that increases close rate. "Solo founders" means one decision-maker, no procurement, fast deals. "low four figures" means they have budget but not a marketing team. "Face of their brand" means they care about voice and POV. "12+ hours a week on content" means they feel the pain daily.

The result: his close rate went from 20% to 60% in 90 days. Not because his offer changed. Because he stopped talking to people who were never going to buy. [a past engagement]

Another version of this: the founder who narrows to the wrong ICP. They pick the avatar they *want* to work with instead of the one who actually buys.

One client came in saying his ICP was "enterprise CMOs." I asked him to show me his last five closed deals. None of them were enterprise CMOs. They were all solo founders or small team leads.

The enterprise CMOs sounded sexier. They had bigger titles, bigger budgets, bigger logos. But they also had six-month sales cycles, procurement processes, and legal reviews. The solo founders bought in one call and paid upfront.

I told him: your real ICP is the one who's already buying. Build for them first. Once you have case studies and recurring revenue, you can move upmarket. But if you optimize for the sexy ICP who never buys, you go broke before you get there. [a past engagement]

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

**Mistake 1: Confusing ICP with total addressable market.** The founder says "my ICP is small business owners" because that's who could theoretically buy. But ICP isn't TAM. ICP is the one person you can serve better than anyone else. Small business owners is a TAM. "Solo founders running low four figures service businesses" is an ICP.

**Mistake 2: Narrowing to the sexy avatar instead of the real buyer.** The founder picks "enterprise CMOs" because it sounds impressive. But the last five deals were all solo founders. Your ICP is who's actually buying, not who you wish was buying.

**Mistake 3: Thinking narrow means small.** The founder resists narrowing because they think they're limiting their revenue. The opposite is true. Narrow positioning lets you charge more, close faster, and build a category of one. Broad positioning makes you a commodity competing on price.

**Mistake 4: Defining the ICP by demographics instead of behavior.** "My ICP is 35-50 year old professionals in tech" is demographics. "My ICP is solo founders who post on LinkedIn 3x a week but hate every minute of it" is behavior. Demographics don't buy. People with specific pains and frustrations buy.

**Mistake 5: Trying to serve two ICPs at once.** The founder says "I work with corporate executives and solo founders." Those are two completely different businesses. Different pains, different buying cycles, different pricing models, different content strategies. Pick one. Build for them. Then expand.

**Mistake 6: Narrowing but not committing.** The founder writes a narrow ICP in their positioning doc, then writes broad content because they're afraid to exclude anyone. The ICP only works if every piece of content, every hook, every sales page speaks directly to that one person.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

The conventional wisdom is "niche down so you stand out." That's not wrong, but it misses the actual mechanism.

You don't narrow to stand out. You narrow to stop burning money on people who were never going to buy.

Every founder I've worked with who resisted narrowing had the same fear: "If I narrow, I'll miss opportunities." The reality: you're already missing opportunities by being so broad that no one knows what you do.

The second contrarian take: narrowing isn't about exclusion. It's about efficiency.

A broad ICP means you're writing five different value propositions, testing five different hooks, running five different campaigns. A narrow ICP means you write one thing that works, test one hook that lands, and scale what's already converting.

The third take: your ICP should make you slightly uncomfortable.

If your ICP feels safe and inclusive, it's too broad. The right ICP makes you nervous because you're leaving people out. That discomfort is the signal you've actually committed to a position.

Fourth: the best ICP is fractal.

The solo founder running a 00K service business today becomes the agency owner with ten team members in two years. If you narrow to solo founders and serve them well, you don't lose them when they scale — they bring you with them. Narrow at the entry point, grow with them over time.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

The founder can describe their ICP in one sentence without hedging. No "mostly" or "usually" or "we work with a range of." Just: "I work with solo founders running low four figures service businesses who are the face of their brand."

Content starts landing. Hooks that used to get 10 likes now get 50. Comments shift from "interesting" to "this is exactly me." DMs start with "I feel like you wrote this for me."

Sales calls get shorter. The prospect already knows the offer is built for them. The first 20 minutes aren't spent explaining what you do — they're spent confirming fit and closing.

Close rate goes up. In one case I worked with, narrowing the ICP took close rate from 20% to 60% in 90 days. Same offer, same pricing, same sales process. The only difference: every conversation was with someone who was already 80% sold before they booked the call.

Referrals become predictable. When your ICP is narrow and connected, one client tells ten others exactly like them. Broad ICP means every referral is random. Narrow ICP means every referral looks like your best client.

The founder stops second-guessing. No more "should I post this?" or "will this alienate people?" Every piece of content either serves the ICP or it doesn't. The decision is binary.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

If you are afraid to say the price, the problem is not the number. The problem is the promise.

When a founder hesitates to raise prices, they are always solving the wrong problem. They think they need to justify the increase. They think they need better sales skills. They think they need more proof. None of that is true. What they need is a promise that makes the price irrelevant.

Price is a signal of value. If the value is unclear, any price feels high. If the value is specific and desirable and easy to believe, the price conversation becomes a formality.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Most founders are trapped in a race to the bottom they did not choose. They set their price based on what they think the market will tolerate, then spend the rest of their business justifying why they are worth it. That is backwards.

The cost of underpricing is not just money. It is positioning. When you charge less than the value you create, the market reads you as less capable. Clients treat you as replaceable. You attract buyers who negotiate hard and pay slowly and demand revisions. You build a pipeline full of people who can barely afford you, which means every conversation feels like convincing them you are worth the risk.

Underpricing also kills margin. When margin is thin, you cannot invest in the assets that would make your business stronger. You cannot hire the team. You cannot take the time to build the systems. You stay trapped in delivery mode because you need every client just to stay afloat.

The leverage of getting pricing right is existential. A founder who raises prices and holds the line earns back their positioning, their calendar, and their confidence. They start attracting clients who can afford to pay and who expect results instead of excuses. They build a business with margin. Margin buys options. Options buy freedom.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

The most common pattern is the founder who knows they are undercharging but cannot bring themselves to change the number. They have been charging a low three-figure amount for a service that takes 40 hours and they know it should be a low three-figure amount. But they are terrified that if they raise it, nobody will buy.

The conversation always starts the same way. They ask me how to justify the increase to their existing clients. I tell them we are not justifying anything. We are rebuilding the promise.

In one session with a LinkedIn ghostwriter charging ,500 a month, I asked what the client was actually buying. She said "four posts a week, one carousel, two newsletters." I said that is not what they are buying. Nobody wakes up wanting four posts. They want pipeline. So what is the real promise?

She hesitated. Then she said "more inbound leads." I asked how many. She said "I don't know, it depends." I said that is why you cannot raise prices. You are selling inputs, not outcomes. Inputs have a market rate. Outcomes command a premium. [a past engagement]

We rebuilt the offer. The new promise was "10 qualified inbound DMs a month or I write until you get them." The price went to low four figures. She closed three clients in two weeks. The objection rate did not change. The quality of buyer did.

Another client was a brand strategist charging a low three-figure amount for a positioning package. She wanted to go to 2K but was stuck. I asked her what the client was left with after the engagement. She said "a positioning document, a messaging house, and a brand story." I said nobody wants documents. What do they actually want?

She said "clarity." I said that is still too vague. Clarity about what? She thought for a minute. Then she said "they want to know what to say when someone asks what they do, and they want it to land." Bingo.

We restructured the deliverable. Instead of three documents, she now delivered one outcome: a 60-second positioning script that the founder could say on a sales call and have the prospect lean in. That was the promise. The 2K price became a non-issue. [a past engagement]

The pattern repeats. Founders get stuck on price because they are selling the wrong thing. They are selling their time, their process, their deliverables. None of those things justify a premium. The only thing that justifies a premium is a result the buyer cannot get anywhere else.

A workshop client was charging low four figures for a 90-minute AI training. He wanted to charge ,997 but felt like he needed to add more content. I told him content is free. Every founder can watch a YouTube video. What they cannot do is walk out of a 90-minute session with a working system they can use on Monday.

We rebuilt the workshop around that promise. Instead of teaching AI tools, he built their first automated workflow live in the room. By the end of the session, they had a working email drafter, a working content repurposer, or a working client onboarding sequence. The workshop went to ,997. Nobody balked. [a past engagement]

The other common pattern is the founder who raises prices but immediately caves when the prospect hesitates. They panic and offer a discount. Or they offer to split the price across more deliverables. Or they apologize and say "I can work with you on that."

That is a confidence problem, not a pricing problem. If you do not believe the price, the prospect will not either.

I ran a live pricing workshop where a consultant said she wanted to charge 5K for a three-month engagement but kept getting "that is too expensive." I asked her to pitch me. She said "It is 5K for three months of consulting, but we can structure it however works for you."

I stopped her. The moment you say "we can structure it however works for you," you have told the prospect the price is negotiable. That is a signal. Signals matter more than words.

I had her redo it. This time she said "5K. Three months. Here is what ships in month one." No hedge. No apology. No offer to customize. The prospect either buys or they do not. That is the frame. [a past engagement]

The third pattern is the founder who raises prices and then tries to justify them with more deliverables. They add bonuses. They add extra calls. They add a bonus module. That is the wrong move. More deliverables do not make a higher price feel justified. A stronger promise does.

A client was selling a 0K consulting package and wanted to go to 0K. She asked if she should add more check-ins. I said no. Adding more inputs does not double the value. Doubling the outcome does.

We did not add anything. We changed the promise from "I will help you build your marketing strategy" to "You will have five qualified sales calls booked in the first 30 days or I keep working until you do." The price doubled. The deliverables stayed the same. The objection rate dropped. [a past engagement]

title: Specific examples from the vault
text:
## Specific examples from the vault

The clearest example is a founder who came to me charging ,500 for a personal branding package. She wanted to raise it to a low three-figure amount but could not close anyone at that price. She kept getting "I need to think about it."

I asked her to walk me through the last sales call. She said "I explained the deliverables, showed them examples of past client work, and then told them the price. They said it was more than they expected."

I said the problem is not the price. The problem is the order. You are selling the deliverables before you have sold the outcome. That is backwards.

I had her redo the call structure. Open with the outcome. "In 90 days you will have a LinkedIn profile that books three inbound calls a month. That is the promise." Then ask if that outcome is worth a low three-figure amount to them. If yes, then show the deliverables. If no, the call is over.

She ran the next call that way. The prospect said yes before she even explained what was included. She closed at a low three-figure amount. [a past engagement]

Another example from a workshop. A founder was selling a a low three-figure amount offer and wanted to go to a low three-figure amount. He asked if he should add a bonus. I said no. Instead, I had him cut a deliverable.

He was selling five one-hour strategy sessions plus a written plan. I told him to drop the plan. Nobody wants a plan. They want the first action taken. So instead of five sessions and a plan, he sold three sessions and one implemented system. The price went to a low three-figure amount. Nobody complained. The perceived value went up because the promise got clearer. [a past engagement]

A third example is a client who was afraid to raise prices because her current clients could not afford the increase. She was charging K a month for LinkedIn ghostwriting and wanted to go to a low three-figure amount. She thought she would lose everyone.

I told her she would not lose everyone. She would lose the wrong people. The clients who could barely afford K were never going to be great clients. They negotiated on scope. They asked for revisions. They paid late. Losing them was the goal.

She raised prices. Four clients left. Three new clients signed at a low three-figure amount in the first month. Her revenue went up and her workload went down. [a past engagement]

The pattern that shows up over and over is the founder who thinks they need to ease into a price increase. They want to raise low four figures this quarter, then another low four figures next quarter. I tell them that is the wrong move. Incremental increases train the market to expect negotiation.

If the new price is 0K, charge 0K today. Not a low three-figure amount with a plan to go to 0K later. The market does not care about your internal pricing roadmap. They care about whether the promise is worth the price right now. [a past engagement]

title: Scripts and exact phrases
text:
## Scripts and exact phrases

"The price is $X. Here is what you get in the first 30 days."

No justification. No apology. Just the number and the first outcome.

"If I can deliver [specific result] in [specific timeframe], is $X a fair price?"

This is the qualifying question. If they say no, the call is over. If they say yes, the rest of the conversation is just logistics.

"I used to charge $Y. That was underpriced. The new price is $X because the promise is now [specific outcome]."

This is the script for transitioning existing clients or reactivating old leads. You are not justifying the increase. You are stating that the old price reflected an old promise and the new price reflects a new one.

"This is not for everyone. If budget is tight, I can refer you to someone else. But if you want [specific outcome], this is the investment."

This is the disqualification script. It gives them permission to walk away and it positions the price as non-negotiable.

"The price is $X. The payment plan is [structure]. Which one works for you?"

This is the closing question. You are not asking if they want to buy. You are asking how they want to pay. The frame assumes the sale.

"Most people think they need [deliverable]. What they actually need is [outcome]. That is what I sell."

This is the reframe for prospects who are focused on inputs instead of outcomes.

"I do not discount. If the price does not work, I can recommend someone at a lower price point."

This is the objection handler for "can you do it for less?" The answer is no, and you give them an out.

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

The first mistake is raising prices without changing the promise. If the promise is the same and the price goes up, you just made the offer worse. The prospect is paying more for the same thing. That is a bad trade.

The second mistake is apologizing for the price. The moment you say "I know it is a lot, but..." you have told the prospect the price is too high. They will believe you.

The third mistake is adding more deliverables to justify a higher price. More is not better. More is just more. A stronger outcome justifies a higher price. More check-ins do not.

The fourth mistake is negotiating before the prospect asks. Founders preemptively offer payment plans or discounts because they are afraid of losing the deal. That is a signal that the price is soft. The prospect will push.

The fifth mistake is anchoring on hourly rate. If you charge 00 an hour and the project takes 40 hours, you think the price should be a low three-figure amount. That is wrong. The price should be whatever the outcome is worth to the buyer. Hourly rate is an input cost. Inputs do not set price. Outcomes do.

The sixth mistake is running a "soft launch" at the new price with the plan to go higher later. That trains the market to expect increases and it makes every client wonder if they overpaid.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

The conventional wisdom is that you need social proof, testimonials, and case studies before you can raise prices. That is wrong.

You can charge a premium on day one if the promise is clear and the guarantee removes the risk. Social proof helps, but it is not the bottleneck. The bottleneck is whether the prospect believes you can deliver the outcome you promised.

Another piece of conventional wisdom is that you should raise prices gradually so you do not shock the market. I disagree. If the old price was wrong, fix it now. Incremental increases drag out the pain and train prospects to wait for the next discount.

The most damaging conventional wisdom is that you need to be the best in your category before you can charge premium prices. That is backwards. Premium pricing is what creates the margin to become the best. If you stay cheap, you stay stuck. You cannot invest in the systems, the team, or the positioning that would make you premium-worthy.

Premium pricing is not the reward for being great. It is the requirement.

title: What it looks like when it is working
text:
## What it looks like when it is working

You stop getting "I need to think about it" as an objection. When the promise is clear and the guarantee is strong, the prospect either buys or they self-disqualify. Hesitation means something is unclear.

You start closing faster. When the price is justified by the outcome, the sales cycle compresses. There is less back-and-forth. Less negotiation. The prospect knows what they are buying and they either want it or they do not.

You start attracting better clients. Premium pricing filters out the tire-kickers and the budget shoppers. The clients who sign are serious. They expect results. They do not ask for discounts. They pay on time.

Your close rate does not drop. Most founders think raising prices will cut their close rate in half. It does not. The close rate on qualified prospects stays roughly the same. What changes is the quality of the pipeline.

You get paid what the work is worth. Not what the market thinks it should cost. Not what you think you can get away with. What the outcome is actually worth to the buyer.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

Strategy is the category. Tactics are the execution.

Most founders get this backwards. They open a call asking "Should I post daily on LinkedIn?" when they haven't answered "Who am I talking to and what do I want them to do?" They build features before they know what problem they're solving. They hire before they know what role the business actually needs.

The question isn't whether you need strategy or tactics. You need both. The question is: what level is the actual problem at?

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Getting the level wrong costs months.

A founder comes to a call stuck on "My content isn't working." They want better hooks. They want a new post format. They want to know if video performs better than carousels.

Those are tactical questions. But when you dig, the real issue is positioning. They can't say what they do in one line. They have three ICPs. They're selling to everyone and no one.

No hook fixes that. You can teach them ten frameworks, they'll still sound generic because the strategy layer is broken.

The opposite happens too. A founder spends three months "refining their positioning" when the real problem is they haven't shipped anything. They're stuck in strategy paralysis. The business doesn't need another brand workshop. It needs five LinkedIn posts this week and three outbound DMs.

The cost of misdiagnosis is time. Time you don't get back. Time the business bleeds while you solve the wrong problem.

The mechanism is simple: strategy sets direction, tactics cover ground. If the direction is wrong, speed makes it worse. If the direction is right but you're not moving, nothing happens.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

This shows up in every single 1:1 call.

The pattern: founder comes in with a tactical problem. "My posts get likes but no DMs." "I need better cold email copy." "Should I launch on Product Hunt?"

First move: name the level. Ask one question that surfaces whether this is a strategy or a tactics issue.

"Who exactly are you trying to reach with this post?" If they can't answer in one sentence, it's not a hooks problem. It's a positioning problem. Strategy layer.

"What happens after someone replies to that cold email?" If the answer is "I don't know" or "I figure it out," it's not a copy problem. It's an offer problem. Strategy layer.

"What does success on Product Hunt actually give your business?" If the answer is "visibility" or "traffic," and they can't connect that to revenue in three steps, it's not a launch tactics problem. It's a business model problem. Strategy layer.

from a past engagement: Client came in asking how to write better LinkedIn posts. Five minutes in, he couldn't name his ICP. He was posting for "business leaders in cybersecurity." That's 50,000 people. The posts were invisible because the strategy was invisible. We parked content work entirely. Spent the session defining one ICP (SaaS founders in regulated industries, M-0M ARR, hiring their first security lead). Two weeks later he posted content for THAT person. Booked three calls in ten days.

from a past engagement: Founder came in with a pipeline problem. Wanted to know which lead magnet to build. I asked what happens after someone downloads it. He said "I send them an email." I asked what the email says. He said "I haven't written it yet." The lead magnet question was a distraction. The real issue: no nurture sequence, no offer, no sales process. Strategy missing. We didn't touch tactics for four weeks. Built the offer first, then the sales process, then the lead magnet last.

from a past engagement: Couple running a consulting business. Came in asking about social media calendars and posting frequency. Classic tactics question. I asked "What do you want social to DO for your business?" They looked at each other. Silence. Then: "We don't know. Everyone says we should post." That's not a content tactics problem. That's a channel strategy problem. We killed social entirely for 90 days. Focused on one outbound channel (cold LinkedIn). Revenue up 40% in 8 weeks because they stopped doing theatre and started doing sales.

The diagnostic comes down to one test: if I give you the tactical answer right now, can you execute it today? If yes, it's a tactics problem. If no, something strategic is missing.

Example: "Should I use video or text posts?" If the founder knows their ICP, knows their message, knows what they're asking the reader to do, they can test it today. Tactics problem. Answer: test both, measure replies, double down.

But if they don't know who they're talking to? Video vs text doesn't matter. Strategy problem. Park the question. Fix positioning first.

from a past engagement: Founder came in with a classic tactics question: "Should I hire a VA to help with content?" I asked "What's the content doing for the business right now?" She said "Not much." I asked "Why not?" She said "I'm not sure who I'm talking to." Hiring a VA to make more of what isn't working is expensive theatre. We didn't hire anyone. We fixed the ICP and the messaging. Three months later she asked the same question and the answer was different: yes, hire, because now you know what good looks like.

The other pattern: founders who never leave strategy.

They refine their positioning for six months. They rewrite their About page twelve times. They do brand audits, hire consultants, buy courses, and never ship.

from a past engagement: Client had been "working on her brand" for eight months. She had three versions of her positioning doc. She had hired two brand strategists before me. She'd done workshops, exercises, Vision boards, the full circus.

I asked her to show me what she'd shipped in the last 90 days. Nothing. She was stuck in strategy theatre.

The move: I told her to park strategy entirely. Pick one offer. Pick one person it's for. Write five LinkedIn posts this week about problems that person has. DM ten people. Do that for 30 days. Identity emerges from the work, not the planning.

She resisted. "But I don't know my brand yet." I said: "Your brand is what people say about you after they work with you. You can't plan that. You earn it by doing the work."

She shipped. Thirty days later, she knew exactly who she was because the market had told her. Three clients in 90 days. The brand clarity followed the work, not the other way around.

The posts had no POV. They restated obvious things. That's not a hooks problem. That's a positioning problem. You can't write a sharp hook if you don't have a sharp position. We parked hooks. from a past engagement: Follow-up session after the initial strategy call. Client had executed the positioning work. Now he came in with a tactical question that actually WAS tactical: "How do I structure a cold DM to a SaaS founder?" This time the answer was tactical because the strategy was solid. I gave him a three-line script. He sent 20 DMs that week. Booked 4 calls. Tactics work when strategy is handled.

from a past engagement: Client came in wanting to build "an app." That's a tactics request disguised as a build. I asked "What problem does this app solve?" He listed five problems. I asked "Which one costs you the most money today?" He said "We lose track of cylinder inventory and customers don't pay on time." That narrowed it. The app wasn't the strategy. The app was the tactic to solve a specific inventory and collections problem. We built for that. If I'd just built "an app," it would've been feature soup.

He said "Turn session transcripts into formatted documents in 10 minutes instead of 2 hours." That's the strategy. from a past engagement: This was a masterclass in getting the level wrong. Client asked me to help him build a solo business. I started asking tactical questions: pricing tiers, customer acquisition strategy, cost structure. Halfway through I stopped myself. I asked "Why did you exit your last business?" He said "I was burned out." That's the strategy question. Before we build anything, we need to know: what does success actually look like for YOU? Is it revenue? Freedom? Time? Until that's clear, every tactical decision is a guess.

title: Scripts and exact phrases
text:
## Scripts and exact phrases

When a founder brings a tactical question and the real issue is strategic:

"That's a great question, but I'm going to push back on it. Here's why: [name the missing strategic piece]. Let's handle that first, then the tactical answer becomes obvious."

When a founder is stuck in strategy theatre and needs to ship:

"I hear you. But here's what I'd do: park strategy for 30 days. Pick one thing. Ship it. The clarity you're looking for comes from the work, not from more planning."

When diagnosing the level on a call:

"Before we answer that, help me understand: [ask the one question that surfaces strategy or tactics]. If it's X, this is a tactics problem. If it's Y, we need to go one level up."

When a founder asks "Should I...?" about a tactic:

"Maybe. Depends. What's the business goal behind this? If we do this and it works, what changes?" (If they can't answer, it's not a tactics problem.)

When closing a strategy session:

"Here's what we're NOT doing next: [list the tactics they wanted to jump to]. Here's what we ARE doing: [name the one strategic move]. Once that's handled, those tactics will be ten times easier."

When a tactic IS the right answer:

"Yes. Do that. Here's exactly how. [Give the specific script/process/tool]. Test it this week. Report back Friday."

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

**Mistake 1: Answering the question the founder asks instead of the question they need answered.**

Founder asks "What's the best time to post on LinkedIn?" You give them the data: Tuesday mornings, 8-10am. They go post at 8am Tuesday. Nothing happens. Why? Because posting time wasn't the problem. The posts were generic. They didn't know who they were talking to. You solved a tactics problem that didn't matter because the strategy was missing.

The fix: name the level FIRST, then answer.

**Mistake 2: Forcing strategy when the founder just needs to ship.**

Founder comes in, ready to execute, asks "Should I send 10 cold DMs today or write a LinkedIn post?" You say "Let's step back and think about your overall go-to-market strategy." They glaze over. You lose them.

They didn't need strategy. They needed permission and a script. The strategy was already handled (they know their ICP, they know their offer). They just wanted to know which channel to hit today.

The fix: if the strategic foundation is solid, give the tactical answer and get out of the way.

**Mistake 3: Treating every call like a strategy session.**

Not every call needs frameworks. Sometimes the founder just needs you to say "Yes, that works, go do it" or "No, that's a distraction, kill it." Overcomplicating simple decisions is expensive.

**Mistake 4: Building tactics in isolation from business goals.**

Founder wants to "grow their email list." You help them build a lead magnet, set up a funnel, run ads. List grows. Revenue doesn't. Why? Because you never asked what the email list was supposed to DO for the business. Was it meant to nurture cold leads? Replace a sales call? Sell a course? Without the strategy layer, the tactic becomes theatre.

**Mistake 5: Confusing activity with progress.**

Posting daily on LinkedIn feels like strategy execution. It's not. It's tactics. If the positioning is wrong, posting daily just scales the wrong message. More activity doesn't fix a strategy problem. It amplifies it.

**Mistake 6: Never moving from strategy to tactics.**

The founder who's been "working on their brand" for six months, attending workshops, refining messaging, and never shipping. Strategy becomes procrastination. The brand doesn't exist until it's in the market.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Most people think strategy is big and tactics are small.

Wrong.

Strategy is fast. Tactics are slow.

Defining your ICP takes one session. Writing 100 posts for that ICP takes three months.

Choosing your offer takes an afternoon. Building a sales funnel takes weeks.

Deciding to kill a channel takes five minutes. Ramping up a new channel takes 90 days.

The hard part isn't strategy. The hard part is committing to one strategy long enough to execute the tactics that make it real.

Here's the other contrarian take: most "strategic" advice is just expensive tactics disguised as vision.

Brand positioning workshops. Vision boards. "North Star" documents. OKRs for solopreneurs. These are tactical outputs pretending to be strategic. They're theatre.

Real strategy is boring. It's answering three questions:

1. Who am I serving?
2. What do I want them to do?
3. What's the one thing I'm betting on to make that happen?

That's it. Everything else is tactics or distraction.

If your "strategy session" takes longer than two hours, you're doing it wrong.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

You're on a call with a founder. They ask a tactical question. You name the level in 30 seconds. If it's strategy, you stop them, handle the strategy, and the tactics become obvious. If it's tactics, you give the specific answer and move on.

No wasted time. No strategy theatre. No solving the wrong problem.

The founder leaves with one clear move. Not twelve. One.

And that move is at the right level. If they're stuck on positioning, they're not building lead magnets. If positioning is handled, they're not rewriting their About page for the fifth time.

Observable signals:

- Founder can articulate their ICP in one sentence without hesitation.
- Founder can name what they're asking their content/outreach/sales process to DO.
- Founder ships weekly because the strategy is clear enough that tactics don't require constant re-decision.
- Revenue moves because the tactics are aligned to a strategy that actually connects to business outcomes.

From client work: when strategy is handled, tactics conversations take 10 minutes. When strategy is missing, tactics conversations spiral for an hour and produce nothing actionable.

The test: if you can't execute the answer from the call THIS WEEK, the call was at the wrong level.

title: The core principle
text:
## The core principle

Session notes are real-time operating records, not summaries written after the fact.

They capture what happened, what was said, what changed, and what ships next — written live while the session unfolds, not reconstructed from memory two hours later when half the decisions are already forgotten.

title: Why this matters
text:
## Why this matters

Bad session notes kill momentum.

When you reconstruct a call from memory, you lose the exact language the client used. You lose the moment they shifted. You lose the specific objection they raised before they said yes. You lose the next action they committed to in the room.

Three days later when you're writing the follow-up email, you're guessing. The client notices. They feel like you weren't listening. Trust drops.

Good session notes preserve the operating state of the engagement. You can pick up exactly where you left off. You can quote the client's exact words back to them. You can hold them to the commitment they made in minute 47 of the call. You can reference the specific pain point that made them book in the first place.

The leverage is in the details. Names. Numbers. Direct quotes. The specific phrase that landed. The exact deliverable they asked for. The reason they said no to the first version of the offer. The timeline they committed to. The obstacle that showed up mid-session.

Without those details, every session becomes generic. With them, every session becomes a specific, citable, actionable record you can build the next move from.

title: How it shows up in client work
text:
## How it shows up in client work

Every call gets documented live in a structured format: participant list, transcript extract, key decisions, next actions, direct quotes.

The format stays consistent across hundreds of sessions because consistency makes the notes searchable. When a client says "Remember that thing we talked about in October?" you can find it in under 30 seconds because every October session follows the same structure.

For workshop builds, the notes capture more than just what was taught. They capture attendance, engagement signals, which examples landed, which sections ran long, what questions came up in chat, what broke technically. [a past engagement] shows a 3-hour live build session with 80+ participants — the notes track not just the content but the participant reactions, the technical issues with Base44 credits burning out mid-demo, the specific features announced (thumbnail generator, newsletter composer, integrated CRM), and the exact subscription offer made at the end (a low three-figure amount annual, includes weekly expert sessions).

For 1:1 coaching calls, the notes prioritize direct quotes. When a client is stuck on positioning, the note captures their exact fumbling attempt to describe what they do — not a cleaned-up summary. That fumble IS the positioning problem. [a past engagement] captures Ross and Danny prepping for a workshop, including the honest moment where Danny admits "I haven't done a lot, I just want to quickly run through" — that admission of incomplete prep becomes part of the learning. The note also captures Ross's push on slide structure: "I think that can be part of our big introduction" — a small redirect that changes the flow.

For operations and curriculum work, notes document the decisions that shaped the product. [a past engagement] records a multi-hour session building the April 2026 AI School schedule. The note captures which sessions were cut (laptop AI, hiring session, HeyGen multilingual, give-Claude-your-business), which were added (Growth Track sessions on ad copy, conversion diagnostics, P&L building), and the exact style rules that govern every title: no "How to" openings, no em dashes, no model version numbers, no technical acronyms, outcome visible in the title itself.

The note also names the people whose input shaped the decisions. Alex contributed curriculum suggestions. Nuseir's plain-English style governs all titles. James hosts Orientation Party. Jeremiah hosts Roast Sunday. Alexa, Martin, Jiaa, Gelo, and Jullia are the ops team executing. When you read that note six months later, you know who made which call and why.

For client transformation work, notes track the before-state and the shift. [a past engagement] documents the full arc of a cybersecurity executive transitioning from corporate roles into his own consulting practice. The note captures his starting challenge (low LinkedIn engagement despite regular posting), the pivot strategy (from niche leadership content to engagement-focused trending topics), the productized consulting model being reverse-engineered (fixed-fee a low three-figure amount-00K engagements), and the specific frameworks applied to every piece of content (AIDA, SLAY, SCOPE, SMART, PAS, 3E).

That note becomes the operating manual for the engagement. When a client asks "Where were we on the LinkedIn strategy?" the answer is in the note. When he forgets why we're positioning security as a growth engine instead of a cost center, the note holds the reasoning.

For problem diagnosis sessions, notes preserve the exact language of the problem as stated by the client before any solution was proposed. [a past engagement] captures Alex's opening question verbatim: "The goal of March Madness was to have a much higher attendance than a normal session because we said it would springboard to trying to boost... it didn't look like that was necessarily the case. So I want to understand what were the learnings and why weren't we able to achieve that?"

The note then lists the five problems identified: wrong day (Sunday, historically lowest attendance), marketing started too late, no promotional strategy across regular sessions, competing priorities with Nasir's sessions, too much content in too little time. Each problem gets its own line. Each line can be cited independently. The note becomes the foundation for the debrief document that ships three hours later.

For technical build sessions, notes track not just what was built but the iteration path. [a past engagement] captures an 8-session a platform partner build for a Next.js dashboard. The note lists every feature built (Participant Intelligence tab, Command Center multi-file upload, collapsible sidebar, Voyage AI embeddings, Weekly Summary zone, Challenge Tracker), every fix attempted (Session AI URL extraction took five iterations, Command Center PDF parsing took three), and the client's exact working style preferences (one file changed at a time, hardcoded hex values, brand system strictly enforced).

That note becomes the handoff document when another developer picks up the project. They don't have to ask "How does Danny like to work?" — it's in the note.

For content planning sessions, notes capture the strategic decisions and the tactical next moves in one document. [a past engagement] shows a session where Danny walks Juvy through uploading session recordings to the student portal. The note captures the technical steps (download from Zoom recordings, upload to live session recording section) but also the context: a client didn't join, the meeting moved to Friday, Danny had to take another call mid-session and made Juvy the host.

Those context details matter. When you review the note two weeks later trying to remember why a task didn't ship, the answer is there: Danny got pulled into an urgent call. Juvy spent 10 minutes exploring the platform solo. That delay rippled.

For design and branding work, notes preserve the aesthetic decisions and the rejections. [a past engagement] captures Danny's request to rebuild a training document in a platform partner branding. The note specifies the exact colors (yellow #FFBE0B, orange #FB5607, black text), the fonts (Plus Jakarta Sans), the visual style (glass-morphism pills, gradient headers), and the explicit rejections (no week theme labels on curriculum docs, no AI emojis in any communications).

When the next document needs to be built six months later, the note holds the brand system. No need to re-decide. No need to ask. The note is the source of truth.

title: Common mistakes
text:
## Common mistakes

Writing summaries instead of records. A summary says "We discussed pricing." A record says "Client balked at 5K, said yes at 8K with 90-day guarantee, signed in the room."

Cleaning up the client's language. When a client says "I don't know, like, we help people with, um, strategy stuff I guess?" that's the note. Rewriting it as "They provide strategic consulting services" erases the positioning problem.

Skipping the participant list. Six months later when you need to loop someone into a follow-up, you can't remember if they were on the original call. The participant list preserves who was in the room.

Leaving out the interruptions and constraints. "Danny had kidney stones but ran the rehearsal anyway" explains why the slides were incomplete. Without that context, the incomplete slides look like poor prep.

Not citing the source of decisions. "Alex suggested the Growth Track" is useful. "We added a Growth Track" is not. When someone challenges the decision later, you need to know who made the call.

Writing notes in narrative prose instead of structured sections. Narrative is hard to search. Structure is easy to search. Consistent structure across 200 notes means you can find the pricing conversation from any call in under 30 seconds.

title: The contrarian read
text:
## The contrarian read

Most people think session notes are for the client. They're not. They're for you.

The client was on the call. They heard what was said. The note is so YOU can reload the context three weeks later when you're writing the follow-up and can't remember if they said a low three-figure amount or 5K.

Most people think good notes require a notetaker or a VA or Otter.ai. They don't. Good notes require a format and the discipline to fill it in live while the session runs.

Most people think long notes are better. They're not. The best notes are short, structured, and searchable. A 200-word note with 4 direct quotes and 3 next actions beats a 2,000-word narrative summary every time.

The real purpose of session notes is to preserve your own operating state so you can pick up where you left off without re-explaining the context to yourself. If the note makes the client feel heard, that's a bonus. But the primary user is you.

title: What it looks like when it's working
text:
## What it looks like when it's working

You can read a note from six months ago and remember the exact state of the engagement in under 60 seconds.

You can quote the client's exact words back to them in a follow-up email without checking the transcript.

You can hand a note to another team member and they can run the next session without asking you a single clarifying question.

You can search "positioning fumble" across 200 notes and find every session where a client struggled to articulate what they do.

You can read the "next actions" section from the last call and know exactly what ships today.

The client feels heard because you're citing their exact language, their exact objection, their exact commitment from the call three weeks ago.

Other team members can read your notes and learn how you work, how you diagnose problems, how you structure a session, how you close a sale.

Your notes become the source of truth for the engagement, the project, the workshop series, the curriculum build.
